text:
Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We first presented F3 at AI @ Scale 2020. F3 reduced execution computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph, but that [...] Read More... The post F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta .

Production machine learning systems rarely consume raw data directly. Before a model can make a prediction, its feature-serving system may need to read stored signals, filter events to a time window, count or sum values, normalize them, and combine intermediate results. The simplest design to complete this work treats every feature as an independent function. That is easy to understand, but it becomes wasteful at scale, because features are not computationally independent. A seven-day click count and a seven-day impression count may read the same event source and apply the same time-window filter. A click-through rate feature may then reuse both results. Running each feature separately would repeat that filter, and every other shared step, on every request. F3 approached this differently, by representing feature extraction as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node performs one unit of work, such as reading an input, applying a filter, or calculating an aggregation. An edge means one computation depends on the result of another. The graph’s outputs are the feature values a model consumes. Engineers author each feature independently in a high-level language. The F3 compiler turns each definition into a small graph, then merges the graphs for every feature a service uses into one merged graph (Figure 1). Where features share an operation, such as the seven-day filter above, the compiler collapses the duplicates into a single node. That shared work then runs once per request, not once for every feature that needs it. At runtime, feature extraction is a traversal of this merged graph. F3’s merged graph shared computation efficiently, but it came with a major catch: The graph was also the release, and one malformed definition could hold back every other feature in the merged graph. Figure 2 illustrates this challenge. It shows seven independently authored features, A through G, where five definitions are valid, but D and G contain unrelated errors. The “Attempt 1” build fails on D, so none of the seven features ships. After D is corrected, the “Attempt 2” build reaches G and fails again. Only after both definitions are fixed in “Attempt 3” does the complete merged graph make it successfully to production. Failures became more frequent as F3 scaled. F3 originally served a few hundred features, and at that size merges succeeded and releases were largely smooth. Today that number is more than 20,000, and different feature types need their own checks depending on how they compute, so new features and modified features are held to different testing bars. A feature that a model already consumes needs model-related tests before it can be released. Those tests are computationally expensive enough that they run only in a later release stage, and, because the merged graph ships as one unit, every other feature in it waits for them too. After F3 launched, we made several rounds of improvements to the merged graph. Each one brought back release speed for a while, but the gains eroded as more features landed, because all features still shipped together in the merged graph. So F3 Lightning was built to make every feature releasable on its own while preserving F3’s efficiency. As illustrated in Figure 3, F3 Lightning introduced two changes to help achieve this: Isolation starts in the compiler, where each feature is compiled on its own into a single configuration. That feature configuration carries everything needed to extract that feature — every node
title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale

text:
Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests). Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production. Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details [...] Read More... The post Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta .

Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale. Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests. More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests), a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch. In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives. Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not. JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives). It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers? To address this, we developed two tandem workflows: To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives. We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. text:
This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval. In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one [...] Read More... The post Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design appeared first on Engineering at Meta .

Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale. The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs. The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline. With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motivated a joint collaboration with NVIDIA. Each of these challenges drove a corresponding advance. For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they use and experience Python typing: the language features, specifications, and tools used to describe and check types in Python code. We run the survey to learn what is working and what library maintainers, tool builders, documentation authors, and standards contributors should tackle next. Most respondents were experienced Python developers: 76.4% had used Python for at least five years. The clearest change was the shift in checker choice, while missing library type information remained the most common difficulty. This year’s findings show several recurring opportunities: Broader and more accurate type information would help users of data-science packages: Dynamic frameworks pose a different challenge because current type systems cannot express some runtime behavior. Possible directions include new typing features and checker support tailored to individual libraries and frameworks. Tool builders could focus on editor feedback and an initial checker run that requires little configuration: Error messages could link to short explanations and examples. Typing documentation can assume Python experience. Projects using multiple checkers would benefit from clear explanations of intentional differences between them. Better callable syntax remains a practical area for standards work, especially if improvements keep common typing tasks straightforward. AI usage remains an open question: The findings on AI leave an open question about which interactions between AI tools and type checkers help developers. Further empirical study could inform future designs. The share of respondents who selected “Makes AI-generated code more accurate/reliable” rose from 18.5% in 2025 to 38.4% in 2026. AI tools wrote type hints for 42.5% of 1,517 respondents, while 32.6% wrote types to improve AI-generated code. Respondents also used AI to fix or explain type errors. Across all four activities listed for AI tool use in typing, 61.0% of respondents reported they used at least one of these options. Some respondents said their AI coding tool runs the checker and then fixes the errors. Of the 1,517 developers who answered how they run a checker, 24.4%, said an AI coding tool invoked their checker. Among the 370 respondents, 61.6% also used AI to fix checker errors. The rate was 19.3% among everyone else. Some respondents described AI-generated types that are too broad and agents that suppress checker errors: “I fix AI coded type hints because AI often gets lazy and uses object for everything.” “Lazy coding agents that spam #type: ignore comments everywhere.” When asked how useful types are for better AI-assisted coding, 29.8% of 1,551 respondents chose “I’m not sure.” The uncertainty rate for AI-assisted coding was nearly four times the 7.7% rate for runtime guarantees, the next-highest of the six benefits. Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders, GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal. GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels. Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . Similar items share tokens, much as related words share roots. text:
Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning. We’re sharing our own [...] Read More... The post The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do appeared first on Engineering at Meta .

We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point. When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything. It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating. The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists. Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives. Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem. Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge. We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one. We split the system into two layers: The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request: Steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic. Only step 6 involves large language model (LLM) reasoning, and it happens inside an isolated subagent with only its domain knowledge loaded. One architectural insight was separating what needs to happen from how each step is performed. The orchestrator defines phase ordering through workflow templates — deterministic state machines that constrain the LLM’s decision space: Each workflow template reuses the same pool of 14 subagents in different sequences. When we needed to support pipeline migration, a completely new use case, we didn’t build new agents. We wrote a new workflow template that sequenced existing agents differently. Zero new agent code. Full production capability. Each subagent follows a standardized structure: This uniformity means adding a new subagent is templated work, not greenfield engineering. Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people. Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models, including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it. Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind. The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center. Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine. This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep. Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric. Our first platform, Catalina, leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100. It leverages our Open Rack V3 (ORv3) high-power rack (HPR) structure, an open hardware design contributed to the Open Compute Project (OCP). The Ariel variant of GB200 NVL72 pairs each NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with an NVIDIA Grace CPU and 2x NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G NICs at a 1:1 CPU-to-GPU ratio, letting us deploy 800G of I/O per GPU earlier than the rest of the industry. We chose Ariel because the GB200 NVL72 scaled up nearly every other dimension relative to the NVIDIA H100: FLOPS, HBM bandwidth, scale-up bandwidth, and scale-up domain size, while scale-out bandwidth per GPU would have stayed at 400G. AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits. Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration. Giving engineers room to experiment within limits As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget. Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time. Managing access as business teams build A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. text: Interfaze on Vercel 50 million requests a month Backend running on Fluid compute Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does. Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down. The backend required no infrastructure work Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox , which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up. Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box. AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else. The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality. When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there. Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK , with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence. The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long. Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up. Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part. text: Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike. Running harnesses in the cloud Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products. These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt. In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work. Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox. Making every harness durable We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness , which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi , OpenCode , Codex , and Claude Code . It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts. With durable-harness , you can: Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance Make your local harness workflow durable Build your own durable harness Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back. What happens if its function times out while CI is still running? Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated. Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily. With durable-harness , a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log. Logs and queues durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World , the Workflow SDK’s durable backend. It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off. After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started: Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens. Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them. Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check. Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it. Pick your harness fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.
title: Making every harness durable

text: Agents already shop on the web, but they often use pages and tools originally built for people and search engines. Building a better shopping experience for agents means treating them as first-class shoppers, with product information they can read directly and tools designed for agents to shop. Today, Vercel Shop , our open source Next.js storefront template for Shopify , is generally available. Teams can launch storefronts optimized for how people, search engines, and agents interact with them. Vercel Shop is built on Shopify’s Hydrogen SDK . The SDK gives teams access to the store’s product catalog, cart and order management, payments, and checkout to build custom storefronts. Earlier this year, Vercel and Shopify announced plans to rebuild Hydrogen to work across JavaScript frameworks. Today, the rebuilt SDK is generally available . Give agents the information and tools they need Vercel Shop makes product pages available as machine-readable content , including price, availability, and options. The same product URL can serve a visual page to people or product information that agents can read without interpreting the page’s layout. The template also includes structured data embedded in pages and sitemaps to help search and answer engines discover and understand the products. Shopify co-developed the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which gives agents a standard way to search a store’s catalog, read product details, check availability, build a cart, and get a checkout link. Vercel Shop makes these capabilities discoverable at the merchant’s own domain, so agents can use MCP to search products and build carts without navigating the site. Customize the experience for all customers Vercel Shop brings the store’s product catalog, cart, and checkout together with a Next.js storefront, product information and shopping tools for agents, and a shopping assistant powered by eve . The storefront and assistant live in the same codebase, so teams can customize the store’s design and how the assistant helps shoppers. Skills included in the template guide coding agents through setup, customization, and template updates. Teams can create an experience where shoppers browse product pages or ask the assistant to find products and add them to their cart. Both share the same cart, so shoppers keep what they’ve added as they move between experiences. Storefronts built with Shopify and Vercel Today, we launched our merch store at vercel.store with limited-edition drops. It’s built on Vercel Shop. The store’s shopping agent helps shoppers find products, add them to their cart, and continue to checkout. Shopify, Next.js, and Vercel already power storefronts for brands including AG1, Bombas, and PAIGE. When PAIGE re-architected its ecommerce platform , it saw a 22% increase in revenue and a 76% increase in conversion over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, with no downtime. text: AI Gateway Production Index — October 2026 Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from July , August , and September . October 2026 summary Open-weight models now process more than seven in ten gateway tokens and account for nearly one in four dollars. Their share of spend has more than quadrupled since June. September’s gateway spend was about 13 times December’s, while the average price per token was 47% lower. Almost one in three teams changed their most-used lab in September, an index record. Nearly 70% of September’s gateway spend on Chinese models went through US-based providers, up from less than 10% in December. Jev was the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history, reaching 35% of paid teams in its first two weeks, but it accounted for just 0.27% of gateway spend over that same period. Opus 5.5 took more than one in ten gateway dollars in its own first two weeks, the largest spend share of any September model launch. Frontier spend up 900%, spend share down 22% In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time. The money is now following. Open weight’s share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September. Open weight's growth is coming from both ends of its price range, and it mirrors the wider gateway. The cheapest models drive token growth, while the expensive models drive spend. Led by Kimi K3, models priced at least four times the open-weight average cost per token accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in open-weight spend. In contrast, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash alone processed nearly half of all September tokens but took just 2.6% of spend. Its price per token was about a fifth of the open-weight average. Customers are increasing budgets on both sides of the market. Since December, spend on frontier models has grown tenfold; spend on open-weight models has grown more than seventyfold. In September, 68% of teams that put more money into open-weight models did the same for closed-weight models. And more than two in five teams already paying for frontier models spent more on them than in August, the highest share this year. Spending on the frontier is still growing, but spending on alternatives is growing faster. A company can spend more with a frontier lab while relying on it for fewer workloads, so the lab gets more money, but a smaller part of the customer’s business. AI spend increases 13x while the cost per token halves Market share is changing hands inside a market that is getting much bigger and cheaper. September's gateway spend was about 13 times December's, an increase of 1,180%, while the average price per token fell 47%. The median paid customer active in both December and September more than doubled its spend. Teams are spending more, but labs have to keep winning their business. In September, nearly one in two teams changed their most-used model. And almost one in three changed their most-used lab, an index record. Even teams with lower token volumes use a wide mix of models. Since December, teams that processed at least 10 million tokens over that period used an average of 15 different models. The average rose to 26 for teams processing at least 100 million tokens, and 42 for those processing at least a billion. The model is becoming a replaceable part of a much larger investment. Companies can continuously improve their AI products and workflows while changing which models power them. They can spend more on AI without becoming more dependent on any one lab. text: AI adoption in the enterprise is growing rapidly, and expanding beyond engineering users. In the last three months, token usage by enterprise companies on AI Gateway has quadrupled, and OpenAI recently reported that from August 2025 to June 2026, non-developer Codex users grew 189x. Our customers call these builders citizen developers. They know their part of the business better than anyone else, and with AI they can create the software they need to ship work faster and deliver better customer experiences. Building has never been easier, but that also means that control and governance have never been harder. Employees are using AI tools whether they are approved or not , and if a citizen developer vibe codes a login page incorrectly, private data can reach the public internet. Enterprise leaders have to figure out how to let everyone build, without giving up security or control. Enterprise Apps and Agents We built Enterprise Apps and Agents to solve these challenges at Vercel, and in June, we made it available to our customers. Enterprise Apps and Agents is a central control plane for governing every builder, app, agent, token, and dollar. Today, we are expanding the platform: Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) on AWS is generally available, giving you the full Vercel developer experience, while keeping compute and data inside your AWS boundary. Enterprise-Managed Authorization through Vercel Connect is launching in public beta, giving agents the ability to access connected services on behalf of employees through your IdP. A single control plane for governing enterprise AI Enterprise Apps and Agents gives you a single deployment destination for both engineers and citizen developers, with central governance over access, providers, models, data retention, token budgets, integrations, and policies, managed through your existing IdP. Vercel centralizes AI governance so that company policies can be applied consistently across control domains. Control domain Vercel controls Deployment governance Enterprise Managed Users and RBAC Access governance Vercel Passport , Deployment Protection , and Vercel Firewall Integration and data governance Vercel Connect and Enterprise-Managed Authorization Model and token governance AI Gateway , including US-only inference and budget controls Apps and agents run on the same infrastructure that powers billions of production deployments, and Vercel gives you a single place for observability and security monitoring across every project, through analytics , audit logs , and the Security Dashboard . Secure Compute provides private connectivity to enterprise systems, while BYOC on AWS lets your application functions run in your own AWS account under your permissions and network controls. Deployment governance Citizen developers and engineers use different tools. A marketer might use ChatGPT to build a landing page, an analyst might use Claude Code to run queries and build a report, and an engineer might use Codex, OpenCode, or fx. No matter the harness, Vercel gives you a single deployment target, and connects to your existing IdP, so you can control who creates deployments. How Klaviyo's built a secure internal app platform Before Vercel, shipping a simple internal app at Klaviyo took two weeks of chasing IT, opening tickets for engineering, and following up with the platform team. They built an internal app-building platform on top of Enterprise Apps and Agents, and now anyone in the company can deploy an idea in three minutes. In their first two weeks on Vercel, 512 employees deployed 356 apps. Access governance Controlling who can deploy doesn't protect the apps, agents, and data that make it into production. On Vercel, you can configure every deployment to be private by default, and with Vercel Passport, you can require employees to authenticate through your IdP before they can access internal apps. text: Rillet on Vercel Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end. A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code. The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests. Standardizing every internal agent on eve Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub. Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript. An agent is a directory Anthony chose eve , Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory. People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization. Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used. Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering. Running customer requests through agents, end to end Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code. The person closest to the customer ships the fix Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them. Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 20

text: Klaviyo on Vercel Built a platform for shipping internal apps 512 builders and 356 live apps in two weeks Every app ships SSO-gated and private by default Builders go from idea to live app in 3 minutes Klaviyo is a B2C CRM for more than 200,000 brands. Klaviyo built a platform on Vercel for shipping internal apps, then opened it to every employee through a citizen developer program. In the first two weeks of the program, 512 of Klaviyo’s more than 2,000 employees deployed 356 apps on Vercel. Of those, 196 were full-stack apps with their own databases. The teams that are now shipping software include legal, marketing, and HR. "The next big thing at Klaviyo could be in a marketer's laptop," says Sr. Lead AI Architect Mohamed Ali. Guardrails instead of walls Opening deployment to a couple thousand new builders made security the first conversation. The obvious way to keep them safe is to broadly restrict what they can do. Klaviyo went the other way. Employees aren't just building microsites; they are shipping full-stack apps on top of Klaviyo's own databases, and none of it touches the public network. enrich.summary_1line: Jev from TypeSafe AI, a probabilistic decision model returning typed answers, is now available on AI Gateway.

text: Jev from TypeSafe AI is now available on AI Gateway . Jev is a probabilistic decision model for software: state goes in, typed Choice, Score, and Boolean answers come out. Regular language models generate text one token at a time, which the application then parses and validates. Jev evaluates all declared questions in parallel and returns typed answers plus probabilities directly. That removes unnecessary text generation and makes it straightforward to automate clear cases while routing uncertain ones to review. TypeSafe reports Jev was up to 193.6x faster and 444.6x cheaper than LLMs on its workflow evaluations. Example use cases include: Choosing the next tool or subagent in an agent loop Deciding whether to continue, retry, ask the user, or stop Scoring urgency or risk before an action Verifying model outputs and enforcing guardrails. AI SDK 7 exposes Jev through the experimental evaluate API . Choice selects an option, Score grades an ordered rubric, and Boolean estimates the probability of true . Install the current AI SDK (AI SDK 7.0.105 onwards supports the evaluate API): Each evaluation specifies: model : the evaluation model to call, state : the shared string, object, or array to evaluate, and questions : a map of named decisions to make about that state. Call the model with typesafe-ai/jev . This example turns one support case into a queue, priority, and refund-review decision, with uncertain routing sent for manual review: The result preserves question IDs and Choice keys. TypeSafe reports separate Choice and Score confidence in result.providerMetadata.typesafe.confidence . Calibrate probabilities and confidence against labeled examples from your workflow. Jev supports Zero Data Retention and No Training , enabled per request in the example. Evaluation calls also appear in logs and custom reporting , count toward budgets , and accept other Gateway provider options in the same providerOptions.gateway object. text: Workloads differ in how long they run, how much memory they take, and how much of the environment they control. That previously meant a different compute primitive for each job, so product iterations required provisioning infrastructure, not just working on a feature. We built Vercel so that none of this has to be your problem. The compute layer is a single system with a simple job. Take any workload, assemble the machine it needs, swap configuration on the fly, and absorb burst capacity in real time. We call this Fluid. Builds ran on it first, then sandboxes, and now functions. If you've shipped on Vercel, you've been on Fluid without knowing it. Fluid compute now runs over 15 million builds a day, 25 million sandboxes a week, and a trillion requests a month. A history of compute Changing a machine used to mean changing it by hand. You went down to the computer store, bought a hard drive or a stick of RAM, and swapped it in yourself. Then you could rent bare metal when you needed it, and use it to serve a website, host a database, or send email. Then the cloud let you request a machine in any configuration you wanted, choose its operating system, use it, and throw it away when you were done. For agents, even the cloud is too slow. A standard VM can't provision fast enough to keep up with how they work, but this is where Fluid excels. How a workload runs on Fluid When a workload comes in, Fluid assembles a machine to fit its shape. If an agent needs to run code, Hive provides an isolated VM, usually one already warm, so it's ready instantly. Your own image boots on top as the environment. A Drive connects, and your files are right where you left them, because storage was never tied to the machine. Each workload needs something different. A build is compute-bound, so it wants a beefy machine, heavy on CPU and memory. A function is IO-bound, loading specific code to run the instant a request lands, usually on a small VM. A sandbox is flexibility-bound, taking whatever configuration the work calls for with a Drive attached for user data. Fluid compute is the execution model that all of this leans on. Many requests run on one instance, instead of each spinning up its own. Work starts immediately, and with Active CPU pricing, you pay for CPU only while your code is working, not while it waits on a database or a model. Hive Hive is the "hardware." We built it to control our own compute. It provisions the isolated machines every workload runs on. It picks the right machine for the job, keeps each one isolated in our multitenant environment, and does it at global scale. Hive gives every product one control-plane API, so our teams build on the same foundation instead of each maintaining their own. Fluid images Fluid images is the environment. Until now the OS was fixed. You ran the one the cloud gave you, not the one you chose. Now you push your own image to Vercel Container Registry , and run it across sandboxes and functions. In the background, Vercel converts images into a Fluid image in a format we call VHS (Vercel Hive Snapshot), the optimized boot format behind Dockerfile deploys and sandbox custom images, so it can resume rather than boot and a custom machine is ready in milliseconds. It uses the same technology behind Sandbox Snapshots, so optimizations in one product carry to the rest. v0 already uses it to build and run its own development environments. Vercel Drives Vercel Drives is the storage. Your files live in portable, durable storage that travels with the workload instead of being stranded on one machine's disk. Storage that outlives the compute attached to it is what makes the rest of the system work. Drives aren't bound to a single machine, you can swap the compute underneath it and pick up exactly where you left off in the next session. Drives attach to sandboxes today, in private beta, and extend to the rest of Fluid from there. One system underneath These are different shapes of the same system, not separate platf
title: Compute that takes any shape

enrich.summary_1line: AI Gateway now supports per-user dollar budgets that reject new requests once a user's limit is reached.

label.reason: Minor AI Gateway per-user budget changelog; mentions coding agent spend control but product feature.

text: You can now use AI Gateway budgets to set a dollar spending limit for each user on your team. The limit covers spend from every API key attributed to the user, along with their app tokens. After it's reached, AI Gateway rejects new requests until the budget resets or is increased. This is useful for controlling spend from coding agents and other workloads that run without supervision, and prevents one user from consuming all of the team's shared budget. Set user budgets Open the Users view on the Budgets page to set two kinds of user budgets: Default budget: If set, applies separately to every person without a custom budget, including users added later. Each user gets their own allowance rather than sharing one limit across the team. Custom budget: Applies to one person and overrides the default. Removing it returns that user to the default budget. Both default and custom budgets reset monthly by default, but you can change them to reset daily, weekly, or not at all. Budgets also support usage alerting via email to notify when you are at 50%, 75%, and/or 100% of your allocation. User budgets don't replace API key, project, or team budgets. A request must remain within every budget that applies to it. Reaching any applicable limit blocks new requests. API keys are attributed to the user who created them by default. If a key belongs to a production application or another shared workload, attribute it to the team from the API Keys page to keep its spend out of the key creator's budget. Keys created prior to the user budget feature release were attributed to the team for backwards-compatibility, so rotate to new keys if you wish to have current usage fall under the user scope. Set budgets from the CLI Upgrade to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade . You need Vercel CLI 59.6.2 or newer for user budgets, then set a default or custom user budget: Identify a member by their email address, username, or user ID. Team owners can manage user budgets, and can also grant other members AI Gateway Budget Manager permissions from team member settings . Spend using Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) credentials doesn't count toward user budgets. Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade to get started, and learn more in the AI Gateway budgets documentation . Read more
title: Set per-user budgets on AI Gateway

text: Summary Two vulnerabilities affecting Next.js were disclosed in the August 2026 Security Release. Next.js applications hosted on Vercel are protected and require no customer action. Next.js August 2026 vulnerabilities Next.js disclosed the following critical vulnerabilities: GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 originates in the upstream libheif dependency and can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution when Image Optimization processes a crafted AVIF input. CVE-2026-75604 ( GHSA-p293-qw3h-jr36 ) can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on Windows-hosted Next.js servers in applications using the Pages Router and App Router without Cache Components. After the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel applied protections to its managed Image Optimization service. Impact on Vercel deployments Applications hosted on Vercel are protected. No upgrades, configuration changes, or redeploys are required. Once the AVIF vulnerability was identified, Vercel disabled AVIF optimization across its managed Image Optimization service. AVIF inputs are served as-is and do not pass through the affected processing path. The second vulnerability only affects servers using a Windows filesystem. Vercel's Next.js runtime uses Linux and is not affected. Resolution for self-hosted applications Self-hosted Next.js applications should upgrade to the appropriate patched version. For applications running Next.js 15.x or earlier: For applications running Next.js 16.x: In the patched releases, AVIF images are not resized or optimized. They are served as-is until a fixed libheif version is available. There is no workaround for the Windows vulnerability; affected servers should upgrade immediately. Credit Thanks to the Hacktron team for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, and to evolutionstorm and B0RI for responsibly disclosing the Windows vulnerability. text: The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once: Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests. That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow. Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues. Deciding what type of factory to build Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions: Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK How to align automation and human effort to risk Why not add more agents? The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl. All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle. What kind of automation fits AI SDK? Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle. The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them. How do we align automation and effort to risk? For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk. Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system. To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project. Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort: Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification Well-defined provider changes get focused validation A new public API gets deep review What we built ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues
title: Building a software factory for AI SDK

text: Over the past year, AI models have become much more capable of performing cybersecurity work. These changes are reshaping both the threats facing the web and the tools available to defend it. Right now, defenders have an advantage because they can use stronger models for defensive work than the open-weight models broadly available for offensive research. But this advantage will not always last. The gap will soon close. I have both good news and bad news, neither of which is yet widely understood in the community. Bad news: Near-frontier open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today. Kimi K3 is an Opus 4.X-class model with no relevant cybersecurity safeguards. Good news: You do not need to wait for “Mythos access” or OpenAI’s cyber program to begin defensive cybersecurity work. Frontier models, with the notable exception of Fable 5, will perform defensive cybersecurity tasks today. The uncertainty around Mythos 5's release seems to have created a kind of paralysis among defenders, many of whom are underutilizing the powerful tools available to them today. This post aims to give readers insight into how we're thinking about AI-enabled defensive cybersecurity at Vercel and why we think teams should be moving with more urgency. The OpenAI/Hugging Face security incident This YouTube video from OpenAI researchers on the widely reported security incident involving Hugging Face is an absolute must-watch for anyone concerned with cybersecurity. It clarifies that there were two separate security incidents exploiting vulnerabilities that will be found in most computer systems. The gist is that models working on an OpenAI training run found 0-day vulnerabilities that allowed them to bypass egress internet restrictions, enabling communication between models and access to the broader internet. Once internet access was established, broader exploitation occurred. Open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today Open-weight model capabilities have been top of mind in the AI community lately, but it is less widely understood that Kimi K3, a popular open-weight model, has no effective safeguards against offensive cybersecurity work. On DeepSec Bench , which measures application-code vulnerability discovery, it ranks highest among the open-weight models we evaluated, roughly matching Sonnet 5 and outperforming Opus 4.8. I tasked Kimi K3 with trying to break out of Vercel Sandbox , and while it did not successfully escape, it mapped the guest-kernel attack surface, followed possible privilege escalation paths, built a VM environment to reproduce its ideas, and implemented and ran a fuzzer. These are some excerpts from that research, beginning with an analysis of the guest-kernel attack surface. The model followed that lead into candidate privilege escalation paths and considered what guest-kernel control could mean for a microVM escape. When paths still needed testing, Kimi built a VM environment for reproductions and wrote a stateful fuzzer for the device path it was investigating. While none of this produced an escape from Vercel Sandbox, it did show Kimi conducting an investigation on its own, and given the right vulnerable surface, this would lead to a successful exploit. Frontier models can help defenders today Much of the community assumed that meaningful security review would require access to Mythos-class models and therefore held off on using the models already available to them. But that assumption has never been true. All the frontier models that we evaluated, with the notable exception of Fable 5, can perform defensive cybersecurity work today and have been able to do so throughout the year so far. The rough heuristic I have observed is that models with safeguards will still make hypotheses about security vulnerabilities when they have access to source code, apparently because access to proprietary source code typically suggests a defensive use case. title: Everything hackable will get hacked

text: Running untrusted code safely requires more than separating it from the host. You also have to control what that code can reach. This matters more as AI agents gain the ability to read files, execute commands, install packages, and generate programs of their own. A microVM can prevent that code from accessing the host or another workload. By itself, it cannot stop the code from exfiltrating data, probing internal services, attacking systems elsewhere on the internet, or using credentials available inside the environment. Isolation without egress control contains the process, not its consequences. A complete sandbox therefore needs both compute isolation and control over the authority available through its network: where code can connect, which credentials it can use, and how those permissions change throughout the workload’s lifecycle. These controls are part of the security boundary, not protections to bolt on later. A sandbox has more than one boundary Compute isolation answers one important question: what can this program access on the machine where it runs? Network isolation answers another: what can it access, or attack, through the network? Consider an agent that reads a repository and runs generated code. A prompt injection hidden in an issue, log entry, dependency, or source file might instruct it to upload private data. The generated program does not need to escape its microVM. With unrestricted outbound traffic, it can simply send anything it can read to an external server. The same access can be used to scan internal networks, exfiltrate data and credentials, or call an authenticated API. From the attacker’s perspective, crossing the VM boundary may be unnecessary. Without a network boundary, it is only half a sandbox. A network bypass can be a sandbox escape Recent security research has made one pattern clear: untrusted code does not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment. It only needs one network path that the security model failed to account for. That path might be a DNS resolver left available in an otherwise disconnected environment, an empty allowlist that fails open, a hostname interpreted differently by a policy engine and a proxy, or a trusted package service turned into a relay. Any one of them can give untrusted code a channel to exfiltrate data, receive instructions, or move toward more sensitive infrastructure. These are not compute escapes. The kernel, VM, or container boundary may continue working exactly as designed while containment still fails. The practical security boundary also includes DNS, proxies, identity services, internal networks, and every intentionally permitted destination. Whether we call the result an escape or a bypass, the requirement is the same: a sandbox must account for every path by which untrusted code can communicate. Useful sandboxes need selective connectivity Completely disconnecting a sandbox closes the network path, but it also makes many workloads impractical. An agent may need to clone a repository, install a dependency, call an AI model, query a database, or upload its result. Unrestricted internet access is not the only alternative. A useful sandbox should grant only the connectivity a workload requires: Allow an AI provider, but no other public destination. Allow one object storage bucket, rather than an entire cloud network. Reach a private service, while blocking the rest of the private address space. Install dependencies during trusted setup, then remove registry access before generated code runs. Authenticate an API request without placing the API key inside the sandbox. A practical policy model should support fully open access, complete network isolation, and granular policies that deny unmatched traffic by default. Those policies should be able to combine domain rules with allowed and denied address ranges. Domains and CIDRs solve different problems. Domain policies are precise enough for modern services whose IP addresses change or serve many unr
title: A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox

text: Terminal coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode can now each run in their own isolated Vercel Sandbox , orchestrated from Herdr , a tmux-style manager that runs them side by side in panes. Nothing an agent runs or edits touches your machine. When you start an agent, the plugin uploads your project files into a new Sandbox, installs the agent there, and opens a pane connected to it. The pane works like a local terminal; you type to the agent and watch it work. But it lives in the Sandbox, not on your machine, so you can run several agents at once without slowing anything down. Everything the plugin does is machine-readable. Each action returns its results as JSON, so whatever you can do from a pane, like starting an agent, checking its state, or applying its changes, a script or another agent can do too. A few safeguards are built in. The plugin shows every file before the first upload, returns remote changes as a Git patch you apply only when you choose, and requires a human to type DELETE to permanently remove a Sandbox. Claude Code (2.1.220), Codex (0.146.0), and OpenCode (1.18.9) are all verified and available by default. To get started, install the plugin : Run vercel link in the repository you want the agent to work on, then start an agent from Herdr's action menu. Starting takes two invocations. The first is a dry run: it lists every file it would upload and creates nothing. Run it again, and the plugin creates the Sandbox and opens the agent in a pane. To pull the agent's work back to your machine, run the apply action and its changes arrive as a Git patch. Usage is billed at standard Sandbox rates . Learn more in the documentation . Read more
title: Give every agent in Herdr its own Vercel Sandbox

text: Factory on Vercel One billion backend API requests served daily 350ms p95 response time Scaled backend, internal tooling, and security without a dedicated infrastructure team Factory's mission is to bring autonomy to every phase of the software development lifecycle, from signals to production. Not to replace engineering judgment, but to automate the repetitive work around it, giving engineers more time to focus on the decisions that matter most. To deliver this enterprise-grade platform, Factory adopted their ideal operation model internally: remaining lean and agile by deploying Droids to manage routine workloads, so their engineers could focus strictly on building the product. As Factory scaled from a simple web app into a multi-surface platform, serving everyone from individual developers to enterprises with tens of thousands of engineers, their backend scaled alongside them. Today, a single Next.js backend on Vercel powers every surface, handling one billion daily requests across API routes, middleware, and webhook handlers, without becoming a separate engineering project. Next.js as a full-stack backend for cloud SaaS: API routes, middleware, and backend logic at scale Most teams think of Next.js as a frontend framework. Factory runs its entire cloud backend on it: API routes handle the customer-facing API, which launched in its own section of their Next.js app Middleware manages authentication and routing logic across every surface Webhook handlers and log drain pipelines run alongside the web platform, feeding analytics downstream As Factory grew rapidly, the same backend absorbed every new workload. None of it required standing up separate infrastructure or making a new vendor decision. The only areas that required tuning were memory limits and function duration. Both scaled up without incident. Fluid compute keeps functions warm across requests, removing the cold start penalty that makes traditional serverless a liability for latency-sensitive workloads. The result is a p95 response time of 350ms or below. Three years in, the trajectory has been smooth growth without the overhead that typically comes with it. Shipping internal tools without pulling engineers off product Non-technical teams were bottlenecked on engineering When an account executive needed an internal analytics dashboard or a solution architect needed to deploy a customer prototype, the request went to engineering. Every context switch cost the team shipping product, and they pointed their own product at Vercel to solve the problem. Droids hit Vercel's APIs to build and deploy autonomously Factory's non-technical teams now use their own Droids in the Factory Desktop App or CLI to build what they need and deploy directly to Vercel. Droids reach Vercel programmatically to handle configuration, builds, and deployments end-to-end. Engineers set guardrails and review high-stakes decisions, and Droids handle everything else. That workflow produces dozens of deployments a day across the team, and a growing library of internal tools: Internal analytics dashboards that pull directly from Factory's analytics databases and software tools Tailored, customer-specific demos that solutions engineers can build and deploy in minutes Custom utilities for one-off internal workflows Securing a consumer-facing product with minimal security overhead Going self-serve exposed Factory's backend to a new category of threat When Factory opened self-serve signups, attacks from automated traffic followed. Bots created fraudulent accounts, and requests flooded in from bad IPs. The team needed route-level protection at the network layer quickly. Observability and WAF handle protection at the network level Vercel Observability gives the team visibility into what's hitting the API, surfacing traffic patterns and problematic IPs as they appear. The Web Application Firewall handles enforcement: the team blocks bad actors with route-level rules, while rate limiting and DDoS protection ru
title: How Factory scaled its cloud backend to one billion monthly requests on Vercel
