text: Agents fetch web pages to answer questions, write code, and complete tasks. When an agent requests a page, it gets everything your browser gets, including navigation menus, stylesheets, JavaScript bundles, tracking scripts, and footer links, when all it needs is the structured text on the page. That extra markup confuses the agent, consumes its context window, and makes every request more expensive. What is content negotiation What agents need is a way to request just the text content of a page, without the browser-specific markup. Content negotiation solves this. It's a standard HTTP mechanism where the client specifies its preferred format via the Accept header, and the server returns the matching representation. Many agents already send Accept: text/markdown when fetching pages, and a server that supports content negotiation can return clean, structured text from the same URL that serves HTML to a browser. We've updated many of our pages, including our blog and changelog, to support content negotiation. This post walks through how it works, how we implemented it in Next.js, and how to add markdown sitemaps so agents can discover your content. How agents request markdown When an agent fetches a page, it includes an Accept header with its format preferences: Accept: text/markdown, text/html, */* By listing text/markdown first, the agent signals that markdown is preferred over HTML when available. This works better than hosting separate .md URLs because content negotiation requires no site-specific knowledge. Any agent that sends the right header gets markdown automatically, from any site that supports it. Try it yourself: curl https://vercel.com/blog/self-driving-infrastructure -H "accept: text/markdown" Implementing content negotiation in Next.js The implementation has two parts, a rewrite rule in next.config.ts that detects the header and a route handler that returns markdown. The rewrite checks the Accept header on every incoming request. When it contains text/markdown , the request gets routed to a dedicated markdown endpoint instead of the default HTML page: The route handler serves the markdown. Our blog content lives in our CMS as rich text, so the route handler converts it to markdown on the fly. If your content is already authored in markdown, you can serve it directly without a conversion step. The rich-text-to-markdown conversion preserves the content's structure. Code blocks keep their syntax highlighting markers, headings maintain their hierarchy, and links remain functional. The agent receives the same information as the HTML version, just in a format optimized for token efficiency. Performance benefits The HTML version of this page is around 500KB. The markdown version is 3KB, a 99.37% reduction in payload size. For agents operating under token limits, smaller payloads mean they can consume more content per request and spend their budget on actual information instead of markup. We keep the HTML and markdown versions synchronized using Next.js 16 remote cache and shared slugs, so when content updates in our CMS, both versions refresh simultaneously. Markdown sitemaps for agent discovery Content negotiation also works for sitemaps. XML sitemaps are flat lists of URLs with no titles, no hierarchy, and no indication of what each page is about. A markdown sitemap gives agents a structured table of contents with human-readable titles and parent-child relationships, so they can understand what content exists on your site and navigate to what they need. We serve markdown sitemaps for both our blog and documentation. Here's the route handler we use to generate a markdown sitemap for blog posts: For documentation or other content with nested sections, a recursive renderer preserves the hierarchy so agents understand which pages are children of which topics: You can see this in action with the Vercel documentation sitemap . For agents that don't send the Accept header, a link tag in your HTML <head> provides an alternativ
title: Making agent-friendly pages with content negotiation

text: AI agents are changing how software gets built. They clone repos, install dependencies, run tests, and iterate in seconds. Despite the change in software, most infrastructure was built for humans, not agents. Traditional compute assumes someone is in the loop, with minutes to provision and configure environments. Agents need secure, isolated environments that start fast, run untrusted code, and disappear when the task is done. Today, Vercel Sandbox is generally available, the execution layer for agents, and we're open-sourcing the Vercel Sandbox CLI and SDK for the community to build on this infrastructure. Built on our compute platform Vercel processes over 2.7 million deployments per day. Each one spins up an isolated microVM, runs user code, and disappears, often in seconds. To do that at scale, we built our own compute platform. Internally code-named Hive, it’s powered by Firecracker and orchestrates microVM clusters across multiple regions. When you click Deploy in v0 , import a repo, clone a template, or run vercel in the CLI, Hive is what makes it feel quick. Sandbox brings that same infrastructure to agents. Why agents need different infrastructure Agents don’t work like humans. They spin up environments, execute code, tear them down, and repeat the cycle continuously. That shifts the constraints toward isolation, security, and ephemeral operation, not persistent, long-running compute. Agents need: Sub-second starts for thousands of sandboxes per task Full isolation when running untrusted code from repositories and user input Ephemeral environments that exist only as long as needed Snapshots to restore complex environments instantly instead of rebuilding Fluid compute with Active CPU pricing for cost and performance efficiency We’ve spent years solving these problems for deployments. Sandbox applies the same approach to agent compute. What is Vercel Sandbox? Vercel Sandbox provides on-demand Linux microVMs. Each sandbox is isolated, with its own filesystem, network, and process space. You get sudo access, package managers, and the ability to run the same commands you’d run on a Linux machine. Sandboxes are ephemeral by design. They run for as long as you need, then shut down automatically, and you only pay for active CPU time, not idle time. This matches how agents work. A single task can involve dozens of start, run, and teardown cycles, and the infrastructure needs to keep up. How teams are using Sandbox Roo Code Roo Code builds AI coding agents that work across Slack, Linear, GitHub, and their web interface. When you trigger an agent, you get a running application to interact with, not just a patch. Snapshots changed their architecture. They snapshot the environment so later runs can restore a known state instead of starting from scratch, skipping repo cloning, dependency installs, and service boot time. Blackbox AI Blackbox AI built Agents HQ, a unified orchestration platform that integrates multiple AI coding agents through a single API. It runs tasks inside Vercel Sandboxes. This supports horizontal scaling for high-volume concurrent execution. Blackbox can dispatch tasks to multiple agents in parallel, each in an isolated sandbox, without resource contention. Create your first sandbox with one command in the CLI Explore the documentation to get started, and check out the open-source SDK . Read more
title: Run untrusted code with Vercel Sandbox, now generally available

text: Two medium-severity denial-of-service vulnerabilities were discovered in self-hosted Next.js applications. Both issues can cause server crashes through memory exhaustion under specific configurations. No data exposure or privilege escalation is possible. Applications hosted on Vercel’s platform are not affected by these issues, and require no customer action. Summary CVE-2025-59471 (CVSS 5.9) affects the Image Optimizer when external image optimization is enabled via remotePatterns . The /_next/image endpoint loads remote images fully into memory without enforcing a maximum size, allowing an attacker to trigger out-of-memory conditions using very large images hosted on an allowed domain. CVE-2025-59472 (CVSS 5.9) affects applications with Partial Pre-Rendering (PPR) enabled in minimal mode. The PPR resume endpoint accepts unauthenticated POST requests and processes attacker-controlled data, allowing memory exhaustion through unbounded request buffering or decompression. Affected Versions CVE-2025-59471 Next.js versions >=10 through <15.5.10 Next.js versions >=16 through <16.1.5 CVE-2025-59472 Next.js versions >=15 through <15.6.0-canary.61 Next.js versions >=16 through <16.1.5 Impact Both vulnerabilities can cause the Node.js process to terminate due to memory exhaustion, resulting in application downtime. CVE-2025-59471 requires external image optimization to be enabled and the attacker to control a large image hosted on an allowed domain. CVE-2025-59472 only affects applications running with the experimental.ppr: true or cacheComponents: true configuration options and NEXT_PRIVATE_MINIMAL_MODE=1 as an environment variable. Resolution Fixed in: 15.5.10 15.6.0-canary.61 16.1.5 16.2.0-canary.9 Workaround: For self-hosted deployments unable to upgrade immediately: Restrict or remove untrusted remotePatterns Disable Partial Pre-Rendering or minimal mode Apply strict request size limits at the reverse proxy layer Credit We thank Andrew MacPherson for their responsible disclosure through our bug bounty program. References GHSA CVE-2025-59471 GHSA CVE-2025-59472 Read more
title: Summaries of CVE-2025-59471 and CVE-2025-59472

text: We invited Ankur Goyal from Braintrust to share how they tested the "bash is all you need" hypothesis for AI agents. There's a growing conviction in the AI community that filesystems and bash are the optimal abstraction for AI agents. The logic makes sense: LLMs have been extensively trained on code, terminals, and file navigation, so you should be able to give your agent a shell and let it work. Even non-coding agents may benefit from this approach. Vercel's recent post on building agents with filesystems and bash showed this by mapping sales calls, support tickets, and other structured data onto the filesystem. The agent greps for relevant sections, pulls what it needs, and builds context on demand. But there's an alternative view worth testing. Filesystems may be the right abstraction for exploring and retrieving context, but what about querying structured data? We built an eval harness to find out. Setting up the eval We tasked agents with querying a dataset of GitHub issues and pull requests. This type of semi-structured data mirrors real-world use cases like customer support tickets or sales call transcripts. Question complexity ranged from: Simple queries: "How many open issues mention 'security'?" Complex queries: "Find issues where someone reported a bug and later someone submitted a pull request claiming to fix it" Three agent approaches competed: SQL agent : Direct database queries against a SQLite database containing the same data Bash agent : Using just-bash to navigate and query JSON files on the filesystem Filesystem agent : Basic file tools (search, read) without full shell access Each agent received the same questions and was scored on accuracy. Initial results Agent Accuracy Avg Tokens Cost Duration SQL 100% 155,531 $0.51 45s Bash 52.7% 1,062,031 $3.34 401s Filesystem 63.0% 1,275,871 $3.89 126s SQL dominated. It hit 100% accuracy while bash achieved just 53%. Bash also used 7x more tokens and cost 6.5x more, while taking 9x longer to run. Even basic filesystem tools (search, read) outperformed full bash access, hitting 63% accuracy. You can explore the SQL experiment , bash experiment , and filesystem experiment results directly. One surprising finding was that the bash agent generated highly sophisticated shell commands , chaining find , grep , jq , awk , and xargs in ways that rarely appear in typical agent workflows. The model clearly has deep knowledge of shell scripting, but that knowledge didn't translate to better task performance. Debugging the results The eval revealed substantive issues requiring attention. Performance bottlenecks. Commands that should run in milliseconds were timing out at 10 seconds. stat() calls across 68,000 files were the culprit. The just-bash tool received optimizations addressing this. Missing schema context. The bash agent didn't know the structure of the JSON files it was querying. Adding schema information and example commands to the system prompt helped, but not enough to close the gap. Eval scoring issues. Hand-checking failed cases revealed several questions where the "expected" answer was actually wrong, or where the agent found additional valid results that the scorer penalized. Five questions received corrections addressing ambiguities or dataset mismatches. "Which repositories have the most unique issue reporters" was ambiguous between org-level and repo-level grouping Several questions had expected outputs that didn't match the actual dataset The bash agent sometimes found more valid results than the reference answers included The Vercel team submitted a PR with the corrections . After fixes to both just-bash and the eval itself, the performance gap narrowed considerably. The hybrid approach Then we tried a different idea. Instead of choosing one abstraction, give the agent both: Let it use bash to explore and manipulate files Also provide access to a SQLite database when that's the right tool The hybrid agent developed an interesting behavior. It would run SQL qu
title: Testing if "bash is all you need"

text: Many of us have built complex tooling to feed our agents the right information. It's brittle because we're guessing what the model needs instead of letting it find what it needs. We've found a simpler approach. We replaced most of the custom tooling in our internal agents with a filesystem tool and a bash tool. Our sales call summarization agent went from ~$1.00 to ~$0.25 per call on Claude Opus 4.5, and the output quality improved. We used the same approach for d0 , our text-to-SQL agent. The idea behind this is that LLMs have been trained on massive amounts of code. They've spent countless hours navigating directories, grepping through files, and managing state across complex codebases. If agents excel at filesystem operations for code, they'll excel at filesystem operations for anything. Agents already understand filesystems. Customer support tickets, sales call transcripts, CRM data, conversation history. Structure it as files, give the agent bash, and the model brings the same capabilities it uses for code navigation. Read more
title: How to build agents with filesystems and bash

text: Last year we introduced the v0 Composite Model Family , and described how the v0 models operate inside a multi-step agentic pipeline. Three parts of that pipeline have had the greatest impact on reliability. These are the dynamic system prompt, a streaming manipulation layer that we call “LLM Suspense”, and a set of deterministic and model-driven autofixers that run after (or while!) the model finishes streaming its response. What we optimize for The primary metric we optimize for is the percentage of successful generations. A successful generation is one that produces a working website in v0’s preview instead of an error or blank screen. But the problem is that LLMs running in isolation encounter various issues when generating code at scale. In our experience, code generated by LLMs can have errors as often as 10% of the time. Our composite pipeline is able to detect and fix many of these errors in real time as the LLM streams the output. This can lead to a double-digit increase in success rates. Read more
title: How we made v0 an effective coding agent

text: Companies spend millions of dollars in time and money trying to build internal tools. They are trying to build software without actually building software, and most of the tools end up collecting dust. v0’s AI agent changes this equation. Business users can build and publish real code and apps on the same platform that their developers use, safely integrate with internal and external systems, and secure everything behind existing SSO authentication. title: Stopping the slow death of internal tools

text: In the weeks following React2Shell's disclosure, our firewall blocked over 6 million exploit attempts targeting deployments running vulnerable versions of Next.js, with 2.3 million in a single 24-hour period at peak. This was possible thanks to Seawall, the deep request inspection layer of the Vercel Web Application Firewall (WAF). We worked with 116 security researchers to find every WAF bypass they could, paying out over $1 million and shipping 20 unique updates to our WAF in 48 hours as new techniques were reported. The bypass techniques they discovered are now permanent additions to our firewall, protecting every deployment on the platform. But WAF rules are only the first line of defense. We are now disclosing for the first time an additional defense-in-depth against RCE on the Vercel platform that operates directly on the compute layer. Data from this defense-in-depth allows us to state with high confidence that the WAF was extraordinarily effective against exploitation of React2Shell. This post is about what we built to protect our customers and what it means for security on Vercel going forward. Read more
title: Our $1 million hacker challenge for React2Shell

text: See the Security Bulletin for the latest updates. Summary Two additional vulnerabilities in React Server Components have been identified: a high-severity Denial of Service ( CVE-2025-55184 ) and a medium-severity Source Code Exposure ( CVE-2025-55183 ). These issues were discovered while security researchers examined the patches for the original React2Shell vulnerability. The initial fix was incomplete and did not fully prevent denial-of-service attacks for all payload types, resulting in CVE-2025-67779 . Importantly, none of these new issues allow for Remote Code Execution. We created new rules to address these vulnerabilities and deployed them to the Vercel WAF to automatically protect all projects hosted on Vercel at no cost. However, do not rely on the WAF for full protection. Immediate upgrades to a patched version are required. Impact Denial of Service ( CVE-2025-55184 ) A malicious HTTP request can be crafted and sent to any App Router endpoint that, when deserialized, can cause the server process to hang and consume CPU. Source Code Exposure ( CVE-2025-55183 ) A malicious HTTP request can be crafted and sent to any App Router endpoint that can return the compiled source code of Server Actions. This could reveal business logic, but would not expose secrets unless they were hardcoded directly into Server Action's code. These vulnerabilities are present in versions 19.0.0 , 19.0.1 , 19.1.0 , 19.1.1 , 19.1.2 , 19.2.0 , and 19.2.1 of the following packages: react-server-dom-parcel react-server-dom-webpack react-server-dom-turbopack These packages are included in the following frameworks and bundlers: Next.js : 13.x , 14.x , 15.x , and 16.x . Other frameworks and plugins that embed or depend on React Server Components implementation (e.g., Vite, Parcel, React Router, RedwoodSDK, Waku) Resolution After creating mitigations to address these vulnerabilities, we deployed them across our globally-distributed platform to protect our customers. We still recommend upgrading to the latest patched version. Updated releases of React and affected downstream frameworks include fixes to prevent these issues. All users should upgrade to a patched version as soon as possible. Fixed in React: 19.0.2, 19.1.3, 19.2.2 . Next.js: 14.2.35, 15.0.7, 15.1.11, 15.2.8, 15.3.8, 15.4.10, 15.5.9, 15.6.0-canary.60, 16.0.10, 16.1.0-canary.19 . Frameworks and bundlers using the aforementioned packages should install the latest versions provided by their respective maintainers. Credit Thanks to RyotaK from GMO Flatt Security Inc. and Andrew MacPherson for identifying and responsibly reporting these vulnerabilities, and the Meta Security and React teams for their partnership. References Next.js Security Update: December 11, 2025 React Blog: Denial of Service and Source Code Exposure in React Server Components React security advisory (CVE-2025-55183) React security advisory (CVE-2025-55184) Read more
title: React Server Components security update: DoS and Source Code Exposure

text: See the React2Shell security bulletin for the latest updates. Summary A critical-severity vulnerability in React Server Components ( CVE-2025-55182 ) affects React 19 and frameworks that use it, including Next.js ( CVE-2025-66478 ). Under certain conditions, specially crafted requests could lead to unintended remote code execution. We created new rules to address this vulnerability and quickly deployed to the Vercel WAF to automatically protect all projects hosted on Vercel at no cost. However, do not rely on the WAF for full protection. Immediate upgrades to a patched version are required. We also worked with the React team to deliver recommendations to the largest WAF and CDN providers. We still strongly recommend upgrading to a patched version regardless of your hosting provider. Impact Applications using affected versions of the React Server Components implementation may process untrusted input in a way that allows an attacker to perform remote code execution. The vulnerability is present in versions 19.0, 19.1.0, 19.1.1, and 19.2.0 of the following packages: : react-server-dom-parcel (19.0.0, 19.1.0, 19.1.1, and 19.2.0) react-server-dom-webpack (19.0.0, 19.1.0, 19.1.1, and 19.2.0) react-server-dom-turbopack (19.0.0, 19.1.0, 19.1.1, and 19.2.0) These packages are included in the following frameworks and bundlers: Next.js with versions ≥14.3.0-canary.77, ≥15 and ≥16 Other frameworks and plugins that embed or depend on React Server Components implementation (e.g., Vite, Parcel, React Router, RedwoodSDK, Waku) Resolution After creating mitigations to address this vulnerability, we deployed them across our globally-distributed platform to quickly protect our customers. We still recommend upgrading to the latest patched version. Updated releases of React and affected downstream frameworks include hardened handling of user inputs to prevent unintended behavior. All users should upgrade to a patched version as soon as possible. If you are on Next.js 14.3.0-canary.77 or a later canary release, downgrade to the latest stable 14.x release. Fixed in: React : 19.0.1, 19.1.2, 19.2.1 Next.js : 15.0.5, 15.1.9, 15.2.6, 15.3.6, 15.4.8, 15.5.7, 15.6.0-canary.58, 16.0.7 Frameworks and bundlers using the aforementioned packages should install the latest versions provided by their respective maintainers. Credit Thanks to Lachlan Davidson for identifying and responsibly reporting the vulnerability, and the Meta Security and React team for their partnership. References Next.js GHSA React GHSA Read more
title: Summary of CVE-2025-55182

text: Summary A vulnerability affecting Next.js Image Optimization has been addressed. It impacted versions prior to v15.4.5 and v14.2.31 , and involved a scenario where attacker-controlled external image servers could serve crafted responses that result in arbitrary file downloads with attacker-defined filenames and content. Your Vercel deployments are safe by default. A patch applied on July 29th, 2025 eliminated exposure for all Vercel-hosted customers. Self-hosted deployments should upgrade to v15.4.5 or v14.2.31 to remediate the issue. Impact Under certain configurations ( images.domains or permissive images.remotePatterns ), a malicious actor could: Trigger the download of a file from a Next.js app with attacker-controlled content and filename Exploit this behavior for phishing, drive-by downloads, or social engineering scenarios This issue requires that: The target app has external image domains or patterns configured The remote server is attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced A user is tricked into clicking a crafted URL Resolution The issue was resolved by updating the image optimizer logic to avoid falling back to the upstream’s Content-Type header when magic number detection fails. This ensures that responses are only cached when confidently identified as image content and do not mistakenly reuse cache keys for user-specific responses. The fix was included in: Next.js v15.4.5 Next.js v14.2.31 Credit Thanks to kristianmagas for the responsible disclosure. References GitHub Advisory: GHSA-xv57-4mr9-wg8v Next.js Release Notes Read more
title: CVE-2025-55173

text: Autonomous coding agents are not the future. They are already here . Agents can now design, build, test, and deploy an entire full-stack feature from front end to back end without a human touching the keyboard. The reality is that while this technology has advanced quickly, Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) have not traditionally focused on the cost of tools used in development. Under current U.S. GAAP, you can capitalize certain third-party software costs if they are a direct cost of creating software during the application development stage. Historically, though, developer tools were treated as overhead because their cost could not be directly tied to capitalizable work. Under GAAP, work that meets the criteria should be capitalized. When agents perform that work, they should be treated no differently than salaried engineers. Read more
title: If agents are building your app, who gets the W-2?

text: AI bot traffic is growing across the web. Not all bots are harmful. Crawlers have powered search engines for decades, and we've spent just as long optimizing for them. Now, large language models (LLMs) need training data, and the AI tools built on them need timely, relevant updates. This is the next wave of discoverability and getting it right from the start can determine whether AI becomes a growth channel or a missed opportunity. Blocking AI crawlers today is like blocking search engines in the early days and then wondering why organic traffic vanishes. As users shift from Googling for web pages to prompting for direct answers and cited sources, the advantage will go to sites that understand each type of bot and choose where access creates value. Read more
title: The three types of AI bot traffic and how to handle them

Active CPU pricing is built on three core metrics: Active CPU : Time your code is actively executing in an instance. text: A low-severity vulnerability in the Next.js dev server has been addressed. Summary This vulnerability affects Next.js versions 13.0.0 through 14.2.29 and 15.0.0 through 15.2.1 . It includes two related issues affecting the local development server: Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking (CSWSH) and Cross-Origin Script Inclusion . Both stem from the lack of origin validation on development server resources. Impact When running next dev , a malicious website can: Initiate a WebSocket connection to localhost and interact with the local development server if the project uses the App Router, potentially exposing internal component code. Inject a <script> tag referencing predictable paths for development scripts (e.g., /app/page.js ), which are then executed in the attacker's origin. This can allow extraction of source code The root cause is insufficient origin verification on local development server resources, including the WebSocket server and static script endpoints. This issue is similar to CVE-2018-14732 , though scoped strictly to local development use. Resolution This issue was fixed in Next.js versions 14.2.30 and 15.2.2 . These releases introduce a configuration option to enable origin checks, which help prevent unauthorized cross-origin requests to the local development server. You can learn how to enable this option after upgrading to a patched version by visiting our documentation page . Note that this configuration is currently opt-in and will become the default in a future major release. Workarounds Avoid browsing untrusted websites while running the local development server Implement local firewall or proxy rules to block unauthorized access to the development server For Vercel Customers This CVE affects local development, no mitigation are required for applications in production on Vercel. Credit Thanks to sapphi-red and Radman Siddiki for responsibly disclosing this issue. References CVE-2018-14732 Next.js Documentation Read more
title: CVE-2025-48068

text: Note : This blog is outdated, please reference this page for the latest information or read the docs here . The Vercel AI Gateway is now available for alpha testing. Built on the AI SDK 5 alpha , the Gateway lets you switch between ~100 AI models without needing to manage API keys, rate limits, or provider accounts. The Gateway handles authentication, usage tracking, and in the future, billing. Get started with AI SDK 5 and the Gateway , or continue reading to learn more. Why we're building the AI Gateway The current speed of AI development is fast and is only getting faster . There's a new state-of-the-art model released almost every week. Frustratingly, this means developers have been locked into a specific provider or model API in their application code. We want to help developers ship fast and keep up with AI progress, without needing 10 different API keys and provider accounts. Production AI applications often run into capacity issues or rate limiting due to high demand. Infrastructure providers move quickly to bring models online and keep up with this demand, but this can come at the expense of performance or availability. The AI Gateway will allow you to load balance across providers, or fail over if a provider has downtime or degradation in performance. Model inference costs keep dropping and providers are competing on quality, performance, and price. The Gateway helps you quickly take advantage of these cost savings. We're taking what we've learned scaling v0 to millions of users, by quickly load balancing and switching between a mixture of providers, and turning that infrastructure into the AI Gateway. Integration with the AI SDK We built the AI SDK to create a common abstraction for AI model APIs across modalities like text, images, and audio. The AI SDK is free and open source, and works with any model or infrastructure provider. The AI Gateway is a separate Vercel product built on top of the AI SDK. We're building these products with high cohesion, but loose coupling. The Gateway will take full advantage of AI SDK features like tool calling, function arguments, streaming, retries, attachments, and structured outputs. Pricing During the AI Gateway alpha, usage is free with rate limits based on your Vercel plan tier. These rate limits are similar to the current AI SDK Playground . We plan to support pay-as-you-go pricing when the Gateway reaches general availability. Model pricing will follow the provider's market rates, updated regularly. We are also planning to explore bring-your-own-key in the future. text: In the process of remediating CVE-2025-29927 , we looked at other possible exploits of Middleware. We independently verified this low severity vulnerability in parallel with two reports from independent researchers. Summary To mitigate CVE-2025-29927 , Next.js validated the x-middleware-subrequest-id which persisted across multiple incoming requests: However, this subrequest ID is sent to all requests, even if the destination is not the same host as the Next.js application. Initiating a fetch request to a third-party within Middleware will send the x-middleware-subrequest-id to that third party. Impact While the exploitation of this vulnerability is unlikely due to an attacker requiring control of the third-party, we want to be proactive. We were already planning on removing this recursion prevention logic from Middleware—it was not supported in newer updates to Middleware to support the Node.js runtime—this disclosure expedited our efforts to bring parity between runtimes. Vercel customers are protected with mitigations already implemented within our platform environment. We still encourage teams to update to the latest Next.js patch version or their chosen backport. Other infrastructure providers which host Next.js applications are not impacted by this, as it is specific to Vercel's implementation of recursion protection. Remediation This advisory was published in alignment with our new internal process for disclosure of vulnerabilities within OSS packages, based on our postmorten of CVE-2025-29927 . We’ve patched 15.x, and offered backports for versions 12.x through 14.x, making an exception to our newly published LTS policy . We’ve also worked proactively with new partners to Next.js for early disclosure. If you are an infrastructure provider and want to work with us, please email partners@nextjs.org . Credit Thank you to Jinseo Kim ( kjsman ) and ryotak for the responsible disclosure. These researchers were awarded as part of our bug bounty program. Read more
title: CVE-2025-30218

text: At Vercel, we consistently monitor and update our security protocols to address emerging threats. A new vulnerability, known as the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset Attack ( CVE-2023-44487 ), has the potential to disrupt HTTP/2-enabled web servers. Rapid Reset is a vulnerability possible in the HTTP/2 protocol involving quickly initiating and canceling streams. It can be used to launch large denial-of-service attacks, negatively affecting performance and availability. We've taken proactive steps to refine our infrastructure and strengthen our defenses. Our improved system can now more efficiently handle the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset Attack. An essential component of our defense strategy is inline network traffic monitoring, where we identify malicious TCP connections and terminate them. Limiting abuse over a single connection has enabled Vercel to protect against HTTP/2 Rapid Reset Attack. Combining our existing system with new improvements, all applications on Vercel are even further resistant to the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset Attack. We want to assure you that your web assets are protected against the HTTP/2 Rapid Reset Attack. We're committed to consistently improving our security measures in response to new threats to ensure safety and reliability for all users. Read more
title: Strengthening Vercel's Infrastructure against HTTP/2 Rapid Reset Attacks

text: Note: This post is historical and describes Edge Functions as they existed at the time. For new projects, use Vercel Functions with the Node.js runtime and Fluid compute . The field of artificial intelligence continues to take the world by storm. Huge strides have been made in text and image generation through tools like ChatGPT, GPT-3, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion. It’s spawned a wave of exciting AI startups, many of which we’re seeing built with Vercel and Next.js . One of the most exciting developments in the AI space is GPT-3, a cutting-edge natural language processing model developed by OpenAI . With its ability to understand and generate human-like text, GPT-3 has the potential to disrupt how we perform many of our tasks. This historical walkthrough uses twitterbio.com to show how streaming changed the user experience for GPT-3 apps. For new projects, build this pattern with Vercel Functions , Fluid compute , and streaming responses. The frontend The Next.js frontend consists of a few elements: A text box for users to copy their current bio or write a few sentences about themselves A dropdown where they can select the tone of the bio they want to be generated A submit button for generating their bio, which when clicked calls an API route that uses OpenAI’s GPT-3 model and returns two generated bios Two containers to display the generated bios after we get them back from the API route Here’s what the code for our index page looks like. We have a few pieces of state that correspond to the elements mentioned above. We’re also defining a prompt—like ChatGPT, we need to send a prompt to GPT-3 to instruct it to generate the new bios. Finally, we ask GPT-3 to generate two bios clearly labeled (so we can parse them correctly) using the user-provided bio and vibe as context. The rest of our index page is comprised of the UI elements themselves: our text box, dropdown, submit button, and two containers on the bottom that we display when we get the generated bios. There's also some loading logic for the button to show a loading indicator when clicked. In addition to the UI elements and the loading logic, we have a generateBio function that’s called when the user clicks the submit button. This sends a POST request to our /api/generate API route with the prompt in the body. We get the generated bios back from the API route, save it to the generatedBios state, then display it to the user. Because we asked GPT-3 to return the text in a specific numbered format, we can split it based on the “2.” to show the user the two bios separated nicely into containers as seen below. The backend A great advantage of using Next.js is being able to handle both our frontend and backend in a single application. We can spin up an API route just by creating a file called generate.ts in our api folder. Let’s take a look at our /api/generate API Route. We get the prompt from the request body that’s passed in on the frontend, then construct a payload to send to OpenAI. In this payload, we specify some important information like the exact model (GPT-3) and how many tokens we want OpenAI to respond with (a token is approximately 4 characters). In this case, we’re limiting the max tokens because Twitter bios have a character constraint. After the payload is constructed, we send it in a POST request to OpenAI, await the result to get back the generated bios, then send them back to the client as JSON. There we have it! We built the first version of our application. Feel free to check out the code and demo for this approach. Current guidance: use Vercel Functions with streaming The original version of this tutorial migrated the example to Edge Functions to get streaming and avoid timeouts. For new AI applications on Vercel, use Vercel Functions with the default Node.js runtime and Fluid compute . This gives you streaming support, longer durations, and full Node.js API compatibility. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare post argues hosted AI agents obscure users from websites and proposes identity, reputation, and accountability mechanisms.

text:
AI agents act for millions, but servers see intermediaries that strip user visibility. This post defines the problem space and introduces a collaborative approach to safely identifying, allowing, and managing this automated traffic.

AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action? “Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser. They are usually hosted and maintained by an “Operator” as part of a managed service or consumer offering. Examples include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, and more are launching all the time. Agents can potentially take any action online that their User could, without the limits that hold humans back. They don't tire, they run around the clock, they act in parallel, and they put up with friction no person would. Much of the web, from how Sites plan capacity to how they make money, assumes those limits. Fundamentally, remotely hosted Agents are intermediaries. An intermediary is anything that sits between a User and a Site, so the Site sees it instead of the User. Agents are the newest kind of intermediary, but intermediaries have existed for a long time. Cloud browsers (hosted browsers that software controls on a User's behalf) and Proxies (services that relay a User's traffic, including VPNs) are intermediaries too. What has changed is the trajectory. Agentic traffic is growing rapidly and may eclipse traditional human browsing on the Internet in the near future. This forces a reckoning for anyone operating a Site today. Historically, a Site could simply block intermediary traffic and require Users to disable the intermediary service. That stops working when the majority of traffic is agentic. Once blocking is no longer viable, Site Operators are left with the problem that intermediaries have always created. The Site loses direct information about the User and must decide whether to trust the intermediary without it. This post covers Agents hosted somewhere other than the User's device. Local agents (e.g. OpenClaw) or Agents running in the User's own browser, on their own device, are out of scope of the primary topic addressed by this post (see below, "On open source and local Agents"). This post rests on one principle: The Intermediation Principle: The business relationship between Users and Sites, and each participant’s security responsibilities, must be upheld regardless of intermediation. A Site needs new tools to recognize, serve, and hold accountable a User acting through an Agent just as it could if that User had visited directly. The Agent, and the Operator behind it, must be recognizable and accountable too, because an Agent can do what no User could. Agents are able to scale human access almost without limit, so they create new risks, even for behavior that was previously benign. Meet Ezra. Ezra works as a personal assistant for people in her city. Her best client is Amy, a local CEO, but she also works for Bob, Charlie, and Debra. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare launched analytics and per-agent access policies for personal AI agents visiting websites, with Allow, Block on pages with ads, or Block options.

text:
Personal AI agents have changed how users interact with the web, blurring the lines between automated and human traffic. Learn how Cloudflare gives site owners visibility and control to manage personal agent access.

Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time. In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use. For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants. Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it. Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block. In Security Settings, you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block), Block on pages with ads, or Block. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available to all customers with Cloudflare One connectivity.

label.reason: Cloudflare private origins GA; mentions MCP servers and agent backends but mainly networking product news.

text:
Public traffic to private origins, with WAF, bot management, caching, and Workers, is now available to every customer with Cloudflare One connectivity.

Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins. In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin. Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers. During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group. Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins: Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Dedicated CDN Egress IPs aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing. See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations. Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN, no connector software on the origin is required. With Cloudflare Mesh, a connector runs within your private network and can serve multiple origins. Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually. The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network. The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error. For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record. POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true } Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path: { "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"], "private_routing": true } The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec, GRE, Cloudflare Tunnel, CNI, or Cloudflare Mesh. The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes. We are launching a PHP Capture the Flag challenge integrated with our Bug Bounty program to test our WAF protections. Security researchers are invited to bypass our defenses and capture the flag to help make the Internet safer.

Update — October 30, 2026: Thank you to everyone who has participated in the PHP Capture the Flag challenge. We have received a strong response from the security research community, and the submissions have helped us harden our existing php2shell WAF protections and create new detections. Details of managed-rule changes are available in the Cloudflare WAF changelog. The CTF remains open. We encourage researchers to continue submitting materially distinct, reproducible bypasses through the Cloudflare HackerOne program. We will share further information and feedback as the challenge progresses. Thank you again for your contributions. Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell: serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web. Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called full transaction detection. As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free. Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential. That’s why today we're launching the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge, run through our Bug Bounty program. We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag. We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the two PHP vulnerabilities behind php2shell. The target runs stock PHP 8.5.11 (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a Cloudflare Container, with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called /flag. The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file. Your mission, should you choose to accept it: bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag. You can use your own research tools. The challenge page has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form. This limited-time challenge is run via Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 Internet disruptions in Q3 2026, led by government-directed shutdowns and power outages.

label.reason: Quarterly internet outage review; general infrastructure interest, not his focus.

text:
An examination of global Internet disruptions observed by Cloudflare Radar during the third quarter of 2026. This review analyzes how power failures, natural disasters, and government shutdowns impacted network connectivity and traffic.

The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet, Cloudflare Radar can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, we review the disruptions detected and annotated on Radar, highlighting what happened, where it happened, and the broader conditions that shaped each event. In this post, we examine the major categories of Internet disruptions observed during the third quarter of 2026, including government-directed shutdowns, power outages and natural disasters. Between July and September, Internet disruptions were largely driven by failures in the systems the Internet depends on. Power grids failed in Cuba, Honduras, Guam, Ukraine, and several other countries. Natural disasters damaged electricity and telecommunications infrastructure from Nepal to Colombia. Government-directed shutdowns remained the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by exam-related shutdowns in Iraq, while renewed conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region showed how quickly connectivity can become part of a broader political and humanitarian crisis. Outages within the United States, Japan, and Portugal — countries with a relatively strong history of Internet resilience — remind us that no country is immune to disruption. In total, Cloudflare Radar recorded 49 disruptions during the quarter. Government-directed shutdowns accounted for 19 incidents, including 18 exam shutdowns in Iraq. Power outages followed with 14 incidents, while natural disasters accounted for five. The Internet is designed to be distributed and resilient, but that resilience still depends on electricity. When power fails, routers, mobile base stations, data centers, interconnection facilities, and the networks that connect them can fail with it. Over the past three months, that dependency was one of the clearest patterns in Radar’s disruption data. Power outages were the second-most common cause of disruptions by incident count this quarter, behind government-directed exam shutdowns. In Cuba, Internet disruptions followed the erratic patterns of an unstable power grid. Radar observed four power-related outages across the quarter, meaning connectivity was affected by grid failures at least once a month. The outages took place July 6, July 14, August 3, and a three-day blackout from September 18 to 20. The traffic volume decreases ranged from 18% on July 14 to 59% on August 3. Honduras illustrated how a localized infrastructure failure can produce national-level effects. A power failure on September 10 at an interconnection facility affected at least 11 major providers, showing how concentrated traffic exchange points can become single points of failure. The outage lasted approximately three hours, during which HTTP traffic across the country fell by 63%. Two notable exceptions were the cross-border provider Telecomunicaciones de Guatemala (AS14754) and mobile carrier Celtel (AS52262), which were unaffected. This suggests that their Honduran connectivity may rely more heavily on infrastructure outside the country. On July 5, a power outage in Sevastopol, Ukraine, caused an eight-hour blackout, with HTTP traffic dropping by 98%. A little over a month later, on August 12, drone strikes targeting energy infrastructure caused another power outage, resulting in a ten-hour Internet disruption and up to a 95% decline in traffic volume. enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare reports SGLang bug exposed cross-request KV cache data in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI from August 27 to September 9, 2026.

label.reason: Real KV cache cross-tenant leak in SGLang serving of GLM-5.3; inference serving and AI security lessons.

text:
A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.

On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions. After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it: To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid requ
title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang

enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare releases Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans that serves byte-range requests using chunk-aligned caching.

label.reason: Pingora range-request caching redesign; distributed systems interest but CDN-specific, not AI.

text:
Naive byte-range caching can waste gigabytes of origin bandwidth on small requests. We rebuilt our cache architecture in Pingora to coordinate partial fetches automatically, cutting R2 p99 latency in half.

A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale. So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%. Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule, and Cloudflare handles the rest. An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header: GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151 If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range: HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000 Content-Length: 1048576 Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it. The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it. Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration. The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post: each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone. The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key. This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming, a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range. The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology. Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently. Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora-based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers. The fix came from something Pingora was already d
title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning

enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare launches PQ GeoKey Manager in closed beta, restricting where post-quantum-protected customer private keys can be unwrapped.

label.reason: Post-quantum geo-fenced key management closed beta; niche crypto product.

text:
Cloudflare's new post-quantum GeoKey Manager protects geographically fenced decryption keys from harvest now, decrypt later attacks. Learn how we redesigned our cryptography stack to support strict data sovereignty in a post-quantum world.

Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography. While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography. Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later. For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work. Cloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security (TLS) keys back in 2017 with GeoKey Manager. This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network. GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with ciphertext policy attribute based encryption (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key. That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a NIST standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as Gateway or Tunnel. This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries. In its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used fr
title: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management

text:
Cloudflare has deployed default web application firewall (WAF) protections for newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities before public disclosure. The rules use request and response signals to stop exploit attempts and prevent exposed data from reaching attackers.

Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release. All Cloudflare WAF customers are protected against known exploit attempts if their site uses PHP's default upload progress field name. Customers who have changed session.upload_progress.name are not covered by the WAF rule. The existing rules "PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #6" protects against this vulnerability. More information to follow. October 21, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed twovulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell. The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic. Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation, OpenAI and Wiz among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell. Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic. Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives. To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability. Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog. The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users. What we know about the vulnerabilities PHP is used by almost 70% of websites. The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet. The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. enrich.summary_1line: Commerce.com enables WebMCP across almost 100,000 storefront domains on Cloudflare, with a per-merchant edge opt-out.

label.reason: WebMCP for agent shopping across 100k stores; relevant to MCP and agent tooling.

text:
Almost 100,000 Commerce.com domains now give AI agents real shopping tools through WebMCP on Cloudflare. Here's how we turned it on across every store at once, while keeping each merchant in control.

AI can write code and pass the bar exam, but it still struggles to buy a pair of shoes online. That’s because websites were built for humans, not agents. Most agents that shop for someone today work from a site’s HTML — they look at the page, guess which button does what, click, and try again when they get it wrong. This process is slow, uses a lot of tokens, and something as seemingly innocuous as a theme change can break it. Enter WebMCP: a browser standard from Google that gives AI agents structured tools on a page, like search_products. Instead of hunting for buttons, the agent calls the exact tool it needs directly, making shopping faster, cheaper, and far more reliable. Because WebMCP is still an experimental proposed browser standard in early preview, it’s currently available behind experimental Chrome flags (chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing), in Chrome Origin Trials, in some agentic browsers, and across developer environments like Cloudflare Kitesurf. In August, we launched edge implementation of WebMCP in beta. Turn it on, and Cloudflare injects a tiny script at the edge to make those tools available automatically, without site owners writing a single line of code. Commerce.com, a flexible commerce platform built for the age of AI, already uses Cloudflare to run their almost 100,000 domains. text:
Following the discovery that eight eMudhra intermediate certificates use weak keys, Cloudflare is deploying mitigations and releasing client updates. We explain the impact, our response, and what customers and developers should do next.

On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet. We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services. We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected. We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms. Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below. For developers, look beneath the SDK. An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy. Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore. This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) enrich.summary_1line: Cloudflare reports cutting its AI code reviewer's average cost per review by 68%, to $0.77, via prompt caching and model changes.
