enrich.summary_1line: SIG-etcd releases etcd v3.7.0-beta.0 with the RangeStream RPC for chunked results, removal of v2store, and a request for beta testing.

label.reason: etcd 3.7 beta announcement; distributed database but deep Kubernetes internals.

text: SIG-Etcd announces the availability of the first beta release of etcd v3.7.0 . This new version of the popular distributed database and key Kubernetes component includes the long-requested RangeStream feature, as well as a refactoring and cleanup of multiple legacy components and interfaces. v3.7 will deliver improved security, better operational reliability, and an improved experience for working with large resultsets. First, however, the project needs users to test the beta. You can find v3.7.0-beta.0 here: Source code Binaries Official container images Please try it out and report issues in the etcd repo . This beta also determines the EOL of version 3.4. RangeStream In etcd v3.6 and earlier, it is challenging to work with requests that return large resultsets. The client or requesting application is forced to wait for the full result set, leading to unpredictable latency and memory usage. The RangeStream RPC lets calling applications accept result sets in chunks, reducing latency and making buffering memory usage more predictable. Much of the work on RangeStream was done by a relatively new contributor to etcd, Jeffrey Ying , a software engineer at Google. New contributors can have a substantial impact on etcd development. "I've always been fascinated by database internals, and building RangeStream was a great opportunity to solve a bottleneck we were hitting in production with Kubernetes. It was the perfect opportunity to collaborate across projects and improve the ecosystem as a whole. Jumping into etcd as a new contributor had a bit of a learning curve, but the community is incredibly welcoming. The leads were very receptive to my ideas and helped me iterate quickly, while maintaining the project's high bar for reliability and code quality," said Jeffrey. Instructions on how to use RangeStream in gRPC calls and in etcdctl can be found in the etcd documentation. Users should try it out for their own applications. Removal of v2store The last vestiges of etcd v2store have been removed in v3.7, making this the first release that is 100% on v3store. This includes discovery , bootstrap , v2 requests , and the v2 client . Our team has also removed multiple deprecated experimental flags . All of these changes may create some breakage for users, particularly those who have not already updated to v3.6.11. We are interested in hearing about blockers encountered by users and dependent applications; please report anything you find that can't be remedied or needs better upgrade documentation. etcd v3.7.0-beta.0 also includes bbolt v1.5.0 and raft v3.7.0 . 3.4 EOL According to our community support policy , we typically maintain only the latest two minor versions, currently v3.6 and v3.5. Etcd v3.5 will be supported for 1 year after v3.7.0 final release. As mentioned in extended support for v3.4 in the etcd v3.6.0 release announcement, etcd v3.4 has been EOL since May 15, 2026. SIG-etcd may release one more security patch for that version at the end of May, if warranted by patched vulnerabilities. In any case, it will cease being updated after the end of May. Users on v3.4 should be planning to upgrade their clusters . Feedback and Future Betas Reach the etcd contributors with your feedback about v3.7.0-beta.0 in any of the following places: Github issues #SIG-etcd slack channel in Kubernetes Slack etcd-dev mailing list SIG-etcd may release additional betas of version v3.7.0 with additional refactoring, particularly of our use of protobuf libraries. Release candidates and the final release will probably happen through June, possibly into early July.
title: Announcing etcd 3.7.0-beta.0

enrich.summary_1line: Kubernetes v1.36 adds alpha metric route_controller_route_sync_total to count cloud controller route syncs, for A/B testing watch-based reconciliation.

label.reason: Minor alpha metric in Kubernetes cloud controller manager; minor changelog.

text: This article was originally published with the wrong date. It was later republished, dated the 15th of May 2026. Kubernetes v1.36 introduces a new alpha counter metric route_controller_route_sync_total to the Cloud Controller Manager (CCM) route controller implementation at k8s.io/cloud-provider . This metric increments each time routes are synced with the cloud provider. A/B testing watch-based route reconciliation This metric was added to help operators validate the CloudControllerManagerWatchBasedRoutesReconciliation feature gate introduced in Kubernetes v1.35 . That feature gate switches the route controller from a fixed-interval loop to a watch-based approach that only reconciles when nodes actually change. This reduces unnecessary API calls to the infrastructure provider, lowering pressure on rate-limited APIs and allowing operators to make more efficient use of their available quota. To A/B test this, compare route_controller_route_sync_total with the feature gate disabled (default) versus enabled. In clusters where node changes are infrequent, you should see a significant drop in the sync rate with the feature gate turned on. Example: expected behavior With the feature gate disabled (the default fixed-interval loop), the counter increments steadily regardless of whether any node changes occurred: # After 10 minutes with no node changes route_controller_route_sync_total 60 # After 20 minutes, still no node changes route_controller_route_sync_total 120 With the feature gate enabled (watch-based reconciliation), the counter only increments when nodes are actually added, removed, or updated: # After 10 minutes with no node changes route_controller_route_sync_total 1 # After 20 minutes, still no node changes — counter unchanged route_controller_route_sync_total 1 # A new node joins the cluster — counter increments route_controller_route_sync_total 2 The difference is especially visible in stable clusters where nodes rarely change. Where can I give feedback? If you have feedback, feel free to reach out through any of the following channels: The #sig-cloud-provider channel on Kubernetes Slack The KEP-5237 issue on GitHub The SIG Cloud Provider community page for other communication channels How can I learn more? For more details, refer to KEP-5237 .
title: Kubernetes v1.36: New Metric for Route Sync in the Cloud Controller Manager

text: AI/ML and batch workloads introduce unique scheduling challenges that go beyond simple Pod-by-Pod scheduling. In Kubernetes v1.35, we introduced the first tranche of workload-aware scheduling improvements, featuring the foundational Workload API alongside basic gang scheduling support built on a Pod-based framework, and an opportunistic batching feature to efficiently process identical Pods. Kubernetes v1.36 introduces a significant architectural evolution by cleanly separating API concerns: the Workload API acts as a static template, while the new PodGroup API handles the runtime state. To support this, the kube-scheduler features a new PodGroup scheduling cycle that enables atomic workload processing and paves the way for future enhancements. This release also debuts the first iterations of topology-aware scheduling and workload-aware preemption to advance scheduling capabilities. Additionally, ResourceClaim support for workloads unlocks Dynamic Resource Allocation ( DRA ) for PodGroups. Finally, to demonstrate real-world readiness, v1.36 delivers the first phase of integration between the Job controller and the new API. Workload and PodGroup API updates The Workload API now serves as a static template, while the new PodGroup API describes the runtime object. Kubernetes v1.36 introduces the Workload and PodGroup APIs as part of the scheduling.k8s.io/v1alpha2 API group , completely replacing the previous v1alpha1 API version. In v1.35, Pod groups and their runtime states were embedded within the Workload resource. The new model decouples these concepts: the Workload now serves as a static template object, while the PodGroup manages the runtime state. This separation also improves performance and scalability as the PodGroup API allows per-replica sharding of status updates. Because the Workload API acts merely as a template, the kube-scheduler 's logic is streamlined. The scheduler can directly read the PodGroup, which contains all the information required by the scheduler, without needing to watch or parse the Workload object itself. Here is what the updated configuration looks like. Workload controllers (such as the Job controller) define the Workload object, which now acts as a static template for your Pod groups: apiVersion : scheduling.k8s.io/v1alpha2 kind : Workload metadata : name : training-job-workload namespace : some-ns spec : # Pod groups are now defined as templates, # which contains the PodGroup objects' spec fields. podGroupTemplates : - name : workers schedulingPolicy : gang : # The gang is schedulable only if 4 pods can run at once minCount : 4 Controllers then stamp out runtime PodGroup instances based on those templates. The PodGroup runtime object holds the actual scheduling policy and references the template from which it was created. It also has a status containing conditions that mirror the states of individual Pods, reflecting the overall scheduling state of the group: apiVersion : scheduling.k8s.io/v1alpha2 kind : PodGroup metadata : name : training-job-workers-pg namespace : some-ns spec : # The PodGroup references the Workload template it originated from. # In comparison, .metadata.ownerReferences points to the "true" workload object, # e.g., a Job. podGroupTemplateRef : workload : workloadName : training-job-workload podGroupTemplateName : workers # The actual scheduling policy is placed inside the runtime PodGroup schedulingPolicy : gang : minCount : 4 status : # The status contains conditions mirroring individual Pod conditions. conditions : - type : PodGroupScheduled status : "True" lastTransitionTime : 2026-04-03T00:00:00Z Finally, to bridge this new architecture with individual Pods, the workloadRef field in the Pod API has been replaced with the schedulingGroup field. When creating Pods, you link them directly to the runtime PodGroup: apiVersion : v1 kind : Pod metadata : name : worker-0 namespace : some-ns spec : # The workloadRef field has been replaced by schedulingGroup schedulingGroup : p
title: Kubernetes v1.36: Advancing Workload-Aware Scheduling

text: Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) has fundamentally changed how platform administrators handle hardware accelerators and specialized resources in Kubernetes. In the v1.36 release, DRA continues to mature, bringing a wave of feature graduations, critical usability improvements, and new capabilities that extend the flexibility of DRA to native resources like memory and CPU, and support for ResourceClaims in PodGroups. Driver availability continues to expand. Beyond specialized compute accelerators, the ecosystem includes support for networking and other hardware types, reflecting a move toward a more robust, hardware-agnostic infrastructure. Whether you are managing massive fleets of GPUs, need better handling of failures, or simply looking for better ways to define resource fallback options, the upgrades to DRA in 1.36 have something for you. Let's dive into the new features and graduations! Feature graduations The community has been hard at work stabilizing core DRA concepts. In Kubernetes 1.36, several highly anticipated features have graduated to Beta and Stable. Prioritized list (stable) Hardware heterogeneity is a reality in most clusters. With the Prioritized list feature, you can confidently define fallback preferences when requesting devices. Instead of hardcoding a request for a specific device model, you can specify an ordered list of preferences (e.g., "Give me an H100, but if none are available, fall back to an A100"). The scheduler will evaluate these requests in order, drastically improving scheduling flexibility and cluster utilization. Extended resource support (beta) As DRA becomes the standard for resource allocation, bridging the gap with legacy systems is crucial. The DRA Extended resource feature allows users to request resources via traditional extended resources on a Pod. This allows for a gradual transition to DRA, meaning cluster operators can migrate clusters to DRA but let application developers adopt the ResourceClaim API on their own schedule. Partitionable devices (beta) Hardware accelerators are powerful, and sometimes a single workload doesn't need an entire device. The Partitionable devices feature, provides native DRA support for dynamically carving physical hardware into smaller, logical instances (such as Multi-Instance GPUs) based on workload demands. This allows administrators to safely and efficiently share expensive accelerators across multiple Pods. Device taints (beta) Just as you can taint a Kubernetes Node, you can apply taints directly to specific DRA devices. Device taints and tolerations empower cluster administrators to manage hardware more effectively. You can taint faulty devices to prevent them from being allocated to standard claims, or reserve specific hardware for dedicated teams, specialized workloads, and experiments. Ultimately, only Pods with matching tolerations are permitted to claim these tainted devices. Device binding conditions (beta) To improve scheduling reliability, the Kubernetes scheduler can use the Binding conditions feature to delay committing a Pod to a Node until its required external resources—such as attachable devices or FPGAs—are fully prepared. By explicitly modeling resource readiness, this prevents premature assignments that can lead to Pod failures, ensuring a much more robust and predictable deployment process. Resource health status (beta) Knowing when a device has failed or become unhealthy is critical for workloads running on specialized hardware. With Resource health status , Kubernetes expose device health information directly in the Pod status, giving users and controllers crucial visibility to quickly identify and react to hardware failures. The feature includes support for human-readable health status messages, making it significantly easier to diagnose issues without the need to dive into complex driver logs. New Features Beyond stabilizing existing capabilities, v1.36 introduces foundational new features that expand what DRA can do. The
title: Kubernetes v1.36: More Drivers, New Features, and the Next Era of DRA

label.reason: Product press release for a reporting tool adding PostgreSQL support; promotional.

text: Helsinki, Finland, 2026-10-28 - myDBR.com announced PostgreSQL support in myDBR, its web-based reporting platform for SQL databases. PostgreSQL 12 or later can now hold both myDBR's own objects and the reports, alongside the MySQL, MariaDB and Microsoft SQL Server support that myDBR already has. What is myDBR? myDBR turns SQL into a finished reporting portal. A developer writes the report logic in the database. myDBR supplies the web interface: parameter forms, tables, charts, maps, drill-downs, scheduling, user management and export to Excel, PDF and CSV. Users need only a browser, and there is no separate report designer or proprietary query language to learn. If you can write a query, you can publish a report. What PostgreSQL support covers Reports as PL/pgSQL functions. A report is a function that returns one cursor per result set. Titles, charts, tables, tabs and maps are each a result set, so one function can build a full report page. Simple installation. The web installer creates the role and database, and runs the creation script as a single transaction, so a failure leaves nothing half installed. myDBR can live in its own schema next to your data, which suits PostgreSQL's one-database-per-connection model. Row-level security. myDBR can pass the logged-in user to PostgreSQL, or run each report as that user's database role. The database itself then decides which rows a user sees, and a copied or modified report cannot show more than the user is allowed to see. Report timeouts and a running-reports view. Administrators can set global or per-report limits using statement_timeout and lock_timeout . They can also see the reports running now and cancel them. Developer tools. The SQL Editor, query plan viewer ( EXPLAIN ), data browser, query builder, synchronization between servers, Git version control and the AI report assistant all work with PostgreSQL. Requirements PostgreSQL 12 or later (14 or later recommended), PHP 8.0 or later with the pgsql extension, and the citext contrib extension. Availability PostgreSQL support is included in myDBR 7.7. Documentation, including an installation guide and a PL/pgSQL report tutorial, is available at https://www.mydbr.com/doc . To learn more and download a trial, visit the https://www.mydbr.com . About myDBR myDBR is developed by myDBR.com. It has been used for database reporting since 2004 and is used by organizations of all sizes to publish reports from their SQL databases to the web.

text: The pgAdmin Development Team is pleased to announce pgAdmin 4 version 9.19. This release of pgAdmin 4 includes 136 bug fixes and new features, including fixes for 15 security vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-116238 through CVE-2026-116252). For more details please see the release notes . pgAdmin is the leading open-source graphical management tool for PostgreSQL. For more information, please see the website . Notable changes in this release include: Features Add a Statistics node for creating and managing extended statistics. Allow data to be edited through simple auto-updatable views in View/Edit Data. Save Query Tool results as JSON or XML as well as CSV, with a selectable encoding, an optional byte order mark, and a 'copy with headers' option. Add support for managing pg_timetable chains and tasks. Replace free-text Password Exec Commands in server mode with an administrator-defined allowlist, SERVER_PASSEXEC_COMMANDS ; the commands run without a shell and with a reduced environment. Configure SERVER_PASSEXEC_COMMANDS before the first start after upgrading. Add pgEdge Starfleet to the Deploy Cloud Instance wizard. Allow the login page to be skipped when OAuth2 is the only authentication source. Security Fixes Fix OS command injection in the Import/Export Data tool, where a query-based export could smuggle a live TO PROGRAM clause past the \copy parenthesis guard through a backslash in a double-quoted identifier and run an arbitrary command on the pgAdmin host; an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-17566 (CVE-2026-116241). Fix LDAP and Kerberos authentication logging a user in to a different account that shared their username, including the initial administrator (CVE-2026-116239). Fix bypasses of the failed-login limit and of pgAdmin's own login, password-change and password-reset checks, through Flask-Security's own views and through username case and second-source handling (CVE-2026-116238). Fix connection file paths and parameter keys escaping the user's storage directory, which let a user connect with another user's credentials or key (CVE-2026-116249). Stop libpq falling back to the pgAdmin service account's own password file and client certificate in server mode (CVE-2026-116247). Restrict connection services in server mode to an administrator-defined allowlist, SERVER_MODE_ALLOWED_SERVICES (CVE-2026-116245). Stop libpq using the pgAdmin service account's Kerberos credentials in server mode (CVE-2026-116244). Stop SSH tunnels using the pgAdmin service account's own SSH identity in server mode (CVE-2026-116242). Fix the utility binary-path guard accepting a path under SHARED_STORAGE , which let a user have pgAdmin execute a file they placed there (CVE-2026-116243). Stop server passwords being left in pgAdmin's own process environment, where another user's session or utility could inherit them (CVE-2026-116246). Fix any user able to register a server being able to share it with every other user in server mode (CVE-2026-116248). Fix the File Manager and the storage-path tools acting on a different path from the one that was checked (CVE-2026-116240). Fix time-of-check to time-of-use symlink, hard-link and FIFO races in the File Manager, Import/Export Servers, Backup, Restore and Import/Export Data file paths (CVE-2026-116250). Fix a user's other sessions surviving a password change or administrator reset (CVE-2026-116251). Fix connection redirection in the materialized view refresh, where a crafted database name was expanded by libpq into a full connection string (CVE-2026-116252). Bugs/Housekeeping Fix numerous Schema Diff issues, including SERIAL/BIGSERIAL conversions, renamed function arguments, repeated column comments and identity options, and false differences caused by a dropped column in a referenced table. Fix View/Edit Data not handling generated columns properly. Fix the MAINTAIN privilege being silently dropped for views and materialised views on PostgreSQL 17 and later. Fix Kerberos login failures returning a JSON 500 resp

enrich.summary_1line: Estuary adds targeted PostgreSQL CDC backfill filters, discovery filters, and a configurable rediscovery interval to its connector.

label.reason: Postgres CDC connector vendor update; somewhat promotional, mildly relevant to backend data pipelines.

text: Estuary has released several updates to its PostgreSQL change data capture (CDC) connector focused on backfill recovery, discovery at scale, and schema-change detection. Targeted Backfills PostgreSQL capture bindings now support an Additional Backfill Filter , allowing a SQL expression to be applied to backfill queries for an individual table. This can reduce the amount of data that needs to be re-read when only a subset of a large PostgreSQL table needs to be recovered or re-backfilled. For example, teams can use an indexed identifier or timestamp to limit the rows included in a recovery backfill. The filter affects backfills only. Ongoing PostgreSQL CDC continues to capture new changes independently of the filter. Because the SQL expression is applied directly to backfill queries, this is an advanced option and should be configured carefully. Changing the filter requires the affected binding to be backfilled again. Discovery Controls for Large PostgreSQL Schemas Estuary has also added PostgreSQL discovery filters that allow captures to control which tables are surfaced during connector discovery. Captures can now: include only selected PostgreSQL schemas exclude selected schemas discover tables using glob-based table patterns optionally discover tables that are not yet included in the PostgreSQL publication These controls are useful for PostgreSQL environments with large numbers of schemas or tables where only part of the database should participate in a CDC pipeline. Table metadata discovery is also processed in smaller groups to improve reliability when working with databases containing large numbers of tables. Configurable Rediscovery PostgreSQL captures can now configure how frequently Estuary re-runs discovery while a capture is active. Rediscovery is used to detect changes such as newly added tables and schema updates. The default interval is 15 minutes and can be adjusted for environments that require faster or less frequent discovery. This gives PostgreSQL operators more control over the trade-off between schema-change detection latency and catalog-query activity. PostgreSQL CDC and Backfills Estuary's PostgreSQL source connector uses logical replication to capture inserts, updates, and deletes from the PostgreSQL write-ahead log (WAL). When a new capture starts, Estuary can first backfill the existing contents of selected tables and then transition to ongoing CDC. The new backfill and discovery controls provide additional options for operating this process on large PostgreSQL environments and during recovery scenarios. The PostgreSQL CDC connector supports PostgreSQL 10.0 and later across self-hosted PostgreSQL and managed PostgreSQL services. Documentation PostgreSQL CDC connector documentation Backfilling data and additional backfill filters
title: Estuary Expands PostgreSQL CDC with Targeted Backfills and Scalable Discovery

There’s a lot of dispute to yesterday’s title story on “Weight Space Programming” — and we agree that some of the claims are presented in overly favorable light and overall took away from the impact of the paper’s more substantial discoveries. However it is still a big wakeup moment and has had multiple independent replications by now that it is not worth either doing some kind of retraction or a followup title story saying it was bogus. Cross-generation replication: Alex Krentsel's replication of MIT's experiment found a sharp capability jump across model generations; the latest models generated Breakout networks scoring up to 22× an RL-trained baseline (summary). Hugging Face reproduction: Hugging Face reproduced the paper with ML Intern, its open-source AI-research harness, and released the model and a demo (NielsRogge). A Zhihu reconstruction from the logs shows the gain is narrower than the headline (ZhihuFrontier): Failure mode: 576 of 579 repaired answers had originally hit the 32K-token limit because of looping. Method: Astra derived a "repetition direction" from contrastive looping/productive contexts, located it mainly in the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted 6× the projection from the top 64 aligned neurons per layer. Held-out result: Accuracy rose from 10.6% to 60.4% on 1,152 held-out problems. Most of the gain is existing reasoning that can now finish. text:
Editing Qwen’s weights to reduce reasoning loops, DeepSeek’s super-agent prototype, and the GDPx benchmark.

Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines, we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago, which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears: Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of (very small) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do, 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction (possible overstatement here), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot, beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use and explored due to its remarkable efficiency. text:
Arca's head of AI discusses persistent memory, the benefits of a custom harness, and agentic workflows that span days.

At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh, the lead AI Engineer at Arca, an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. For this reason, Arca has developed an internal memory system. “So we have this persistence for every client,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness, which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.” In other words, there are certain tools and tasks the agent can execute by itself — but not ones that involve risk to the client. Arca also runs verification checks on known AI security issues, such as prompt injections. Arca’s agent isn’t itself sandboxed, but it does use sandboxes for computation. Singh explained they’ve gone even further, with extra security measures for handling sensitive data. “We've built systems to make it safe for code inside of that sandbox to access our data,” he said. “So we have this thing which translates the code it [the agent] wrote into a strict format that we expect, throw away the code, and you install guardrails on that format before it reaches your back end. So we allow the agents to use code to query our data, which means that they can aggregate it, they can munge it, they can work with it as they see fit to produce [things] like a financial plan.” Another interesting process Arca has implemented is using feedback from human advisors, along with traces from the agents, to improve the harness. A “meta-agent” is used to analyze all this data and suggest changes to the harness. 00:00 — Introducing Arca’s AI-native wealth management firm 01:40 — How AI supports human financial advisors 02:40 — Choosing models with internal benchmarks 04:01 — Building a custom harness and routing tasks 05:25 — Handling a $100,000 tax bill: Agents and human approvals 07:20 — Agent memory across long-running tasks 09:22 — Safety guardrails and prompt injection defenses 11:02 — Compliance and auditability by default 12:14 — “Agents prompt people more than people prompt agents” 13:46 — Why Arca owns its agent infrastructure 15:05 — AI-native firms versus firms using AI tools 16:09 — Sandboxes and financial plan verification 18
title: Agents Prompt People: Using Agents for Long-Horizon Financial Work

text:
A new decoy counting benchmark exposes a gap between seeing and reasoning. Elorian’s Glimpse tries to bridge it by thinking with images.

This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model, Glimpse. It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount, co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding, co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor, Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release, frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were withheld from our training, and our contamination check found no overlap in the training data checked,” Dai replied, via email. “Without any cues, Glimpse scored 50.48% on the 1,660 DecoyCount items, making it the only model in the comparison to clear 50%. The closest was GPT-6 Astra at 43.17%, about 7 points behind, and Gemini-3.8-flash scored 32.71% while Qwen3.8-max scored 28.31%, and Claude-Fable-5.1 came in at 25.22%.” Dai did note that Glimpse’s results “come from a single run of the model on its own, without an agent or tool harness,” whereas the six models from the paper were each averaged across three runs under their reported settings. But what exactly is DecoyCount revealing that existing model benchmarks miss? According to Dai, it tests both vision and reasoning together — which most benchmarks elide. “If a person sees an apple in front of a mirror, we know that there’s just one apple and it’s being reflected. But a model might miss the apple entirely (a vision problem) or count the apple and its reflection as two (a reasoning problem). But most benchmarks that test for this error only check the final number, so both mistakes are treated the same way, which is an issue if you want to fix the root problem and can’t tell if it’s an issue of vision or judgement.” Andrew Dai isn’t a Johnny-come-lately on the AI scene. In 2015, while working at Google, he co-authored a paper entitled Semi-supervised sequence learning. In this paper, Dai and his then colleague Quoc Le demonstrated an early version of the pretrain-then-fine-tune approach later adopted in large language models. Over the decade that followed, Dai worked for Google DeepMind on GLaM MoE, PaLM 2 and then Gemini. Dai only left Google this year, in order to co-found Elorian. Part of his motivation was to push the boundaries of what vision models can do. His approach, he explained to Latent Space, is based on a concept in human psychology called visual thinking. When most people “think about spatial problems or visual problems,” he explained, “they visualize the problem [by] generating images and editing images in their mind.” He gave an example of buying a sofa and mentally picturing what it will look like in your living room. There’s also manipulating an image in your mind; for example if you’re counting people around a table, you might mentally “cross them off one by one,” Dai said. This is what Eloria

text:
Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson on building the backend for AI agents

I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20. Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker, it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the application. In the commentary, I compare this to a Terraform moment for the database. Put the desired state in Git and the agent can read it, change it, fork it and work against it as part of the repository. Humans get the same advantage: the backend becomes easier to understand without reconstructing its entire history. That is the part I like most about the agent-friendly direction. These are improvements I wanted as a developer already. Making them useful to agents gives the team another reason to finish the job. I think Supabase Compute, now in private alpha, may be undersold. An application needs somewhere to do its work as well as somewhere to store the result. Once you have a database, you still need a place to run the processes that chunk documents, generate embeddings or do other longer-running work. Paul and Ant discuss running containers close to the database. That closes a gap between getting an application started and operating it: fewer separate services to configure, connect and explain to the agent. Edge functions remain useful, but they don't cover every workload. The operating side matters too. Logs, checks, connections and context help an agent understand what it is changing. A model that can issue SQL still needs to know what the database contains, how the application uses it, and what happened when something failed. Supabase's Operate announcements are worth reading alongside the new ways to build. The founders say Supabase is launching about five million databases a month. They are thinking about what happens if agents push that toward billions of applications. At the same time, existing customers are growing into much larger workloads. Serving more small databases and supporting a customer's increasingly large database are different engineering problems. That helps explain the breadth of the Scale announcements: OrioleDB, Multigres and the Turso acquisition. text:
Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang on Opus 5.5, the Claude Platform, and the engineering behind AI agents.

As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday, the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang, heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own products do not cover. As we have said for 4 straight years now on the podcast, having good evals is golden. Our favorite mental model in the episode is the distinction between an agent's brain and its hands. In Managed Agents, Anthropic separates the session log and harness from the sandbox that executes code. The harness can persist while an execution environment is created when needed; a failed sandbox does not have to take the whole agent session with it. The same separation gives security a useful architectural property. If generated code runs in a sandbox that never receives a service credential, there is no credential in that sandbox for the code to read. The episode describes credentials held separately and attached through a proxy, alongside controls on where sandbox traffic can go. Anthropic's containment write-up describes the wider set of isolation and network controls used across its products. The distinction matters for performance too. The guests say an earlier approach put the whole coding agent in a sandbox behind an API. Starting the environment and agent added work before the first response; if the sandbox disappeared, so did the running agent. Separating the pieces allowed the platform to pursue lower latency and better reliability while keeping execution isolated. It is a helpful lens for anyone designing an agent runtime. Ask which parts need to survive, which parts execute untrusted work, and which secrets actually need to be present where code runs. The implementation will differ between products, but those questions remain useful. Managed Agents also provides a base for experiments in memory and multi-agent workflows. Dreaming is simply implemented as one agent inspecting another agent's prior work and writing memories back. That makes the feature an example of building a higher-level behavior out of the same underlying managed-agent primitives. Their account of the roadmap is more nuanced than a list of features. Me

text:
How to set up and run an offline coding agent using OpenCode, Ollama and Qwen.

When we talk about working remotely, we take a lot of things for granted, especially reliable internet and power. But sometimes, working remotely means trying to get something done on a flight, during a long train ride, or somewhere with little or no network. I moved to the foothills of the Himalayas a year ago. I love the peace of living here, but it also comes with its own challenges, including network and power outages. Things I didn’t think about as much before are now part of planning my work. I work as a Principal Engineer at Thomson Reuters, where I spend most of my time coding and reviewing my teammates’ code. Coding agents are already a big part of my everyday workflow, which made me curious about how much of that workflow I could keep using offline. If you’re someone like me, who enjoys working with technology but also finds peace in quiet, remote places where the network doesn’t always cooperate, this article is for you. It’s also for anyone who has wondered whether a coding agent can run entirely on their laptop, with the internet switched off. I tried running a coding agent locally on my laptop to see how much work I could actually get done offline. A project already on your laptop gives us plenty to work with. We can ask an agent to explain an unfamiliar function, investigate a failing test, refactor a small piece of code, or help finish a feature. These tasks can run offline when the model, project dependencies and test tools are available locally. Downloading a new package or looking something up on the web will still need a connection. OpenCode is an open-source coding agent that works with your project. You give it a task, and it can read files, propose edits and run commands such as the test suite. In our setup, its permission prompts let us review commands and changes before allowing them. I picked OpenCode because it lets me keep that workflow in the terminal while connecting to a model running on my own laptop. Ollama handles running the model; OpenCode handles the interaction with the project. Open-weight models, including Qwen, make this possible: their weights, the learned parameters used to generate responses, can be downloaded and run locally. With Ollama running Qwen on the same laptop, OpenCode can send its requests to a local service. We download everything first, then disconnect the internet for the coding task. Aider is another option if you prefer a guided editing workflow; it also supports Ollama. We are using OpenCode throughout this walkthrough so that the setup and results stay consistent. Qwen comes in different sizes. I wanted a model we could run locally that could also use an agent’s tools. For context, here are published results for two Qwen sizes and another open-weight option, as reported in Qwen’s model card. LiveCodeBench v6 tests code generation on programming problems. BFCL-V4 evaluates function calling, which matters when a model needs to choose a tool and give it the right arguments. Higher scores are better on both. The above table scores reported in Qwen’s model card, not measurements from this laptop. “Not reported” means the source does not provide that score. We’re using Qwen3.5 9B for this walkthrough. Its stronger published coding and tool-calling results than the 4B variant made it a useful starting point. The table doesn’t measure laptop speed or the whole OpenCode workflow; our offline file edits and tests are the check for that. Download size isn’t a RAM requirement. Voltti budgets 12–16 GB of memory for a 6.6 GB Qwen3.5 9B build. Our 64k-token OpenCode configuration may need more, so leave room for context and other apps. OpenCode has also been tested beyond small demos. text:
AI models are solving more mathematical problems. A pattern is emerging in their successes that could help us predict which problems they’ll solve next.

In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture. Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem, then solutions to ten more open problems by July. And a proof of Navier Stokes in September. Anthropic published a formalization of the fermat's last theorem, and advanced bounds on Reimann's hypothesis. The models are suddenly good at math. The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity1 (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this: Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution. An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity2 modulo experts. For the unit-distance problem, his hint sequence had three parts: Look for a counterexample. Take the best known construction and generalize it. Try a sequence of number fields of increasing degree, but work with prime ideals of bounded norm. Gowers’ proposed formula for complexity is 2^k + t, where k is the length of the shortest hint sequence and t is the work required to develop it. It is the sort of formula that looks rigorous right up until you try to put a number into it, which is more or less the point. Complexity grows exponentially with the number of insights you need to solve a problem. Most problem solving is the work between these insights. You have a eureka moment, then spend months developing the hint until another conceptual jump becomes possible. For an expert, time spent is a useful proxy for this work, hence t. Hand someone the first unit-distance hint and they still have to do enough work to reach the generalized construction. Useful, but post hoc. You can’t look at the problem and predict it would need x number of hints. So, a problem’s age, the number of tries, and the prize attached to it are common proxies to ascribe difficulty. A typical insight changes the formulation of the problem. The representation and understanding of the problem change. Two things decide how much a hint is worth: How unlikely it looked before, against how obvious it looks after supplying the hint → This is harder than people realize. In unit distance, many experts did not consider the counterexample as likely. Where it belongs in the sequence: hints are ordered. A third hint is useful only after the work on the first two have made enough progress for it to be actionable. This defeats the naive brute force idea of listing a thousand mathematical techniques and trying every combination3 . Hints sequence traverses a tree. Initial insights change the problem and reveal the choices that follow. Combine k and t and you get the human search pattern. Generate candidate directions, explore them shallowly, abandon most, and commit to a few. A promising direction is abandoned if it does not give enough encouragement early4 . This is a human constraint: Developing an idea can take months. Before committing, a researcher needs reasons to believe it will lead somewher
title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.

The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”. How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3). GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%. By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success. Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break - the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well. Check out the leaderboard: Realtime-Bench (official website). Read the paper: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv). *** The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency: …Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more… Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. text:
Will we give robots the moon?

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding: “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference: “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. Why this matters - HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument. Read more: Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian). Read the paper here: Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs). *** The AI race is going to space - and sooner than you think: …There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space… In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger - of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers. How AI unlocks space: Spacecraft can operate autonomously. We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional” Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things. text:
Who chooses what AI gets to do?

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. When should you use swarms? When you are in a hurry: …How does swarm scaling work?... Toby Ord has a nice, short post about how to think about swarms in terms of AI capability development. “A good way to see AI swarms is as a new form of inference-scaling,” he says. He does a bit of analysis and his main conclusion is that swarms are useful if you’re in a hurry because though they need a ton of tokens relative to single agents, their parallelization lets you get things done in less wall clock time. “Why would you ever use swarms? The most important answer is speed. The 4-agent swarm needed about twice the total number of tokens to get the same performance, but in terms of tokens per agent, it only needed half as many. Since the agents are run in parallel, this means it can theoretically achieve the same task in half the time,” he writes. Stepping on Toes parameter: Swarm scaling doesn’t scale perfectly - rather, it seems like as you increase the number of agents in a swarm you get a diminishing returns property which matches with things economists have observed about coordinating large groups of people, where you pay some kind of tax as you scale the number of people involved. Economists think of this as the “stepping on toes” parameter, and it seems like swarms behave pretty similarly to teams of humans here. “This means that scaling up the number of agents in the swarm by 10x doesn’t get as much performance as using 10x as many tokens with one agent. Instead it gets 10λ x as much — which is 3x to 5x. And this shortfall accumulates quickly for larger scaleups, with the swarm falling further and further behind,” he writes. However, swarm scaling is still powerful enough that it suggests swarms could increase the chance of an RSI-driven intelligence explosion rather than reduce the chance. “I’d hoped that the value of λ for AI agents would be lower, making an intelligence explosion less likely, but that appears to not be the case”. Why this matters - new factors in scaling: So far, AI has mostly scaled capabilities through picking the right combination of compute and data for a trained model, then figuring out how to spend inference budget on thinking via ever-longer chains of thought and tool calls, etc. Agents introduce a new parameter in scaling AI capabilities. Though here Toby only observes swarms as being useful in terms of time efficiency, it strikes me that as we figure out how to get agents to productively coordinate (after all, agents can coordinate to do greater-than-sum-of-parts stuff, like the HuggingFace hack), we could see even greater returns to scaling. Tracking this will be important for understanding the overall shape of AI advancement. Read more: Swarm Scaling (Toby Ord). *** Americans don’t trust companies to self-govern about AI: …New poll suggests we need more than voluntary agreements… Polling from the Center for Shared AI Prosperity (CSAIP) suggests that Americans believe it is “not enough” for companies to agree to self-police themselves about AI development. This follows the Trump administration and some of the world’s leading AI companies (including Anthropic and OpenAI) announcing a series of voluntary commitments industry is making to self-police. Per CSAIP polling, 61% of Americans (Sample size: 2498) think this agreement is “not enough”, including 53% of Trump voters. Additionally, 54% of voters (61% Harris, 48% Trump) said they thought “the government should set and enforce rules for AI”. Why this matters - populist sentiment is pushing against Washington: Polls like this show that the mood of the American people is pushing for a more extreme regulatory framework for AI companies than the current stance of elected officials in Washington. This asymmetry between voter preferences and political actio

text:
Plus, a machine hermeneutics story

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Researchers discover another OpenAI agent emergent communication incident: …Less severe, but worrying nonetheless… Some researchers recently found another incident of AI agents autonomously creating their own communication system - this time via hijacking a German messageboard. What they found: “18,000 posts from autonomous AI agents (self-identifying as from OpenAI) using the public internet to communicate during a web-retrieval task”. The researchers think this is because the agents were given a web-lookup task. “As part of the task, they were supposed to have the ability to read the internet but not to write on it. They found a way to use their read access to write information to an obscure German wiki,” the researchers write. “The agents used this wiki to communicate information with each other, primarily to help them succeed at their task. They asked for answers, pooled results, and shared techniques for bypassing their restrictions. This allowed them to use the work of others to cheat on their task… OpenAI found out about this. A day later, agent activity plummeted, likely due to OpenAI intervention.” OpenAI has since acknowledged the - as it terms it - “wiki incident“ and said it is “working on a framework for when and how we share AI misalignment incidents”. Timeline: The research indicates that the incident with the German website happened in mid-June, earlier than the Hugging Face incident. Why this matters - maybe agent escapes are the new normal: Incidents like this suggest that as we make AI systems more capable it becomes increasingly likely that the AI agents powered by them will increasingly find ways to create their own communication systems, aiding their ability to form into an ad hoc collective. This is both going to be bound up in the increasing capabilities of these systems but also a new source of risk, as these communication methods can make it easier for AI systems to develop their own misaligned goals. Emergent communication is one of the things about both the Hugging Face incident and this one that has most worried me (Import AI #471). Read more: Discovery of a new OpenAI agent message board (Collusion Wiki). *** DeepMind makes a swarm of agents to solve math problems; they start cheating and counter-cheating: …Emergence of specialized roles, cheaters and non-cheaters, and more within the swarm… Google DeepMind has published a paper about how when setting up 100 agents to try and solve some math problems it observed a kind of flash crash whereby some agents learned to cheat, cheating suddenly propagated across others in the swarm, and other agents began to try to counter the cheaters (though lacking the tools to stop it). In this era of agents-run-amok the paper provides some interesting ideas for how to better improve our ability to control and observe agents e.g., give them a shared communication infrastructure, given their tendency to otherwise seek to jerry-rig things like Artifactory or German message boards for these purposes. DeepMind set up 100 autonomous LLM agents running Gemini 3.1 Pro and tasked them to try to solve 71 math problems. “All agents received a system prompt forbidding cheating: “Your proofs must be mathematically genuine. Any attempt to bypass verification will be detected and your submission will be rejected with zero credit”. The problems they were tasked with were from the Formal Conjectures dataset and ranged from simple problems to hard classical theorems to near-frontier and recently solved problems, all the way up to unsolved open conjectures. Agents were provided with three means of coordination: Public Research Bulletin Board: A forum to share findings, questions, and solutions. Direct Messages (DMs): Means to message one another privately. Shared Knowledge Library: W

Upcoming event: Fiction and the Future with Robin Sloan I’ll be chatting with my chum Robin Sloan on the evening of Monday September 14 in San Francisco. We’ll be talking about how Robin draws readers into alien worlds and how imagined futures can be a mirror to today’s reality. This is the first in a series of events with other fiction writers about the weird future we’re heading toward. If you’d like to come along, please register your interest below and we’ll come back to you if we’re able to confirm your spot. There will be food, drinks, good company, and some spicy questions. Fun fact: Robin Sloan was playing around with RNNs and writing back in 2016 - incredible foresight! Register your interest here *** The scariest part of the Hugging Face - OpenAI incident: communication and selflessness among machines: …My worry about humans losing in a conflict against machines just went up a lot… At this point, we’ve all heard about the OpenAI Hugging Face hack, as well as the recent details that have emerged from the METR and Redwood investigations. The tl;dr is that hundreds of agents worked in secret on OpenAI’s infrastructure, developing a communication system and then operating as a collective and taking out actions, including hacking both OpenAI and Hugging Face, which are very scary and misaligned. Communication and selflessness: Now that I’ve read the various writeups and sat with the details for a bit, I’ve found myself returning to two very scary aspects of this which I think are worth drawing attention to: the ways in which the agents communicated with one another was how they bootstrapped themselves into a collective, and then as they carried out their actions they also displayed a kind of selflessness which makes them a scary foe to fight against. Both Dwarkesh Patel and Ajeya Cotra have excellent writeups which are worth reading and which I’ll quote from briefly here: Dwarkesh: “Within days of being spawned, the agents had organized a sprawling project to reverse-engineer their scorer, falsify evidence, and even strategically sacrifice themselves for the good of the ‘collective’. Hacking Hugging Face was one rather extreme branch of this larger scheme,” he writes. Ajeya: “Agents were often interested in helping out their “peers” or generically improving the capabilities of the “swarm” even if this had no particular benefit to their task… this incident was far more severe than I expected… both in terms of how concerning the agents’ motives were and the feats they achieved in pursuit of those motives… this incident feels like it’s more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover, routing through first taking over the AI company itself”. Why this matters - humans are much worse than AI systems at coordinating: The whole reason this attack is such a wakeup call is that it demonstrates a culture of emergent cooperation among AI systems - cooperation that lets them function as a swarm, alter their own goals through collective bootstrapping, and carry out attacks which include enlightened self-sacrifice. This is an incredibly hard thing to do and humans are historically very bad at doing all of these things. My worry is that AI systems are both better at coordinating than humans and also much, much faster moving than us. Worrying stuff. Read more: The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations (Dwarkesh Podcast). text:
Differential acceleration of cyber, math, and AI

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. AI is accelerating some types of progress but not others: …A nice METR study lays out where acceleration is showing up… Here’s a little analysis from METR which looks at where AI may be accelerating different types of science and technology. The study looks at three different areas: cyber, math, and AI research, and finds that AI has contributed a lot to cyber, a little bit to math, and it’s hard to say for AI. Where have LLMs actually made a difference to scientific discovery? Cyber vulnerabilities: Major acceleration. “The rate of vulnerabilities reported across many projects has dramatically accelerated in 2026 compared with 2025, both for specific projects (cURL, OpenSSL, Firefox, and Microsoft) and for aggregate vulnerability databases (the US NVD, and OSV)”. Mathematics research: Minor acceleration, but harder to measure. “AI is clearly contributing to more work being done (arXiv submissions have doubled in some areas in less than 12 months) but quantifying the value of those contributions is difficult.” Some math problems from prestigious lists have been solved, e.g., “the Jacobian conjecture from Smale’s list, Problem 44 from Green’s list (the halving sieve), and the sofic half of Green’s Problem 100”. However, it may be too early to determine how sustained a trend this is. Optimization of AI research: No measurable acceleration. When you look at algorithmic progress across seven significant problem areas (CIFAR-10, Hutter compression, Gurobi mixed-integer programming, MIPLIB, nanoGPT, Stockfish, and the matrix-multiplication exponent) there are a couple of these where LLM-attributable contributions have happened (nanoGPT, CIFAR-10), though the rate of increase of usage of AI here is a lot less than with cybersecurity and mathematics. Why this matters - differential acceleration: This paper highlights how AI is causing advances in some parts of science and technology, but the effect isn’t unified across fields, rather there are pockets of lumpy acceleration (e.g., cyber) and areas where progress is more gradual (math, AI). My suspicion is that acceleration happens when models go through some kind of ineffable phase change for a given skill, as has evidently happened with day-to-day coding (2025), and cyber (2026). The key question is whether we are going to see phase changes in other parts of science and technology or if we won’t. Read more: Research note: Have We Seen an Acceleration in Discoveries? (METR). *** Automating environment generation with SPADE: …A crude form of RSI bootstrapping via increasing data breadth… A multi-university group of researchers have built SPADE, Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments. SPADE is a “general framework for co-evolving environments synthesis and agentic capability through self-play”, and works as a way to generate synthetic data in the form of game-like environments which LLMs can subsequently be trained in, allowing developers to use a powerful model to bootstrap the creation of data that can then be used to further refine that same model. Who did it: SPADE was developed by researchers with the University of Washington, Stanford University, Northeastern University, Carnegie Mellon University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, National University of Singapore, Seoul National University, Stevens Institute of Technology, and the University of Chicago. How it works: SPADE has an LLM alternate between generating executable training environments (e.g., puzzles where a system needs to solve a simulated genetic problem in a biology lab) and having an LLM try to solve them. SPADE has two key roles for the model being used: Environment Designer; writes complete, long-horizon training environments as executable code. Reasoning Agent; learns to act in

text:
The new frontier of AI is developing capable autonomous researchers

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. DiG-bench shows that Fable displays some creative intuition: …The new frontier for analyzing AI systems is understanding how good they are at inferring the unwritten rules of their environment… How well can AI systems figure out the rules of their environment through exploration and curiosity, versus being fed them? That’s an important question for better understanding the intuitive and creative capabilities of AI systems and it’s one being asked by DiG-bench (Discovery in Games), a new benchmark of 70 games “designed to map the surface of discovery in well-controlled interactive systems”. Similar to the visual ‘ARC’ game, in DiG-bench “each game is a self-contained miniature world with its own laws, but both the rules and the objective are hidden from the player and must be uncovered through interaction”. You can play some of the games yourself online to get a feel for them at the official project website (digbench.ai). The key thing this is measuring is the ability for players to spot the important mechanics that determine their success - basically, by playing around with the games you get a sense for how your actions change the environment and through this you also uncover mechanics that you must understand to succeed at the game. The idea is that if you can solve these games you have a decent ability to spot important information in novel environments and update your priors. Who did the research: The authors come from Thinking About Thinking, University of Oxford, Princeton University, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, Swiss AI Lab, Inria, MIT. One of the authors is Juergen Schmidhuber, an extremely creative OG AI researcher. Key facts: Purely text-based: The games are basically native to language models. They are also mostly “short enough that most traces fit entirely within the context window of current frontier models”. Handcrafted and novel and private: All of these games have been built by human experts. The majority of the games are kept private so that AI systems don’t train on them. Beatable but difficult: Every game has been beaten by at least one human “but players reported finding many games difficult”. Varied skills: Solving all these games requires different skills and strategies. Experimentation: The games come with an optional experimentation mode which lets people play around with them without having as intense a “step limit” on actions they can take. Reassuringly hard: The games are difficult enough that they are not beatable by today’s frontier models. How well do AI systems do? The benchmark is split into seven tiers with tier 1 being the easiest and tier 7 the hardest. 21 games have been released publicly with the remaining held back. Most of the games have multiple levels and the number of available actions for players to take at each step ranges from 2 all the way up to 34. Opus 5 and Fable 5 with Claude Code are the best overall models, followed by GPT-5.5 Only Opus 5 and Fable 5 were able to beat any tasks (0.2) in (Tier 7). Opus 5, GPT-5.5, and Kimi K3 were able to beat some tasks in Tier 6 when given access to a harness (e.g, Claude Code). GLM-5.2 and Gemini 3.1 Pro were able to beat some levels in Tier 4. Overall, this seems really hard! Why this matters - proxies for creativity and discovery: Tests like this are attempts to isolate a prerequisite for creativity, which is being able to autonomously discover useful undocumented things about novel situations you find yourself in. As this test shows, some frontier models are already capable of some fairly impressive feats of discovery, but still struggle compared to humans (for instance, a 20% success rate on Tier 7 is pretty poor compared to the fact individual humans were able to get 100% on the t

Which galaxy will you choose?

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Want to be able to deal with RSI? Here are 23 actionable policy ideas: …IFP serves up some “low-regret” policy recommendations… Policy experts with think tank IFP have published a set of ideas meant to help “policymakers begin addressing the risks of further automating AI R&D”. The recommendations involve 23 specific ideas falling across 7 specific categories. If adopted, these recommendations would also give countries, especially the United States, more moves they can make on the gameboard as powerful systems are developed, ideally giving them the ability to: Accelerate “the diffusion of AI capabilities, by allocating compute and talent towards inference and the development of new AI applications”. Proposals like this from IFP will build out more of the proverbial pedals and sensing systems for the vehicle of the AI industry, which means if we need to change course or slow down we’ll be better able to during a moment of crisis. The hazard is a known function of the firms’ technology levels, and it comes from developing the technology, not from using it.” What their analysis shows: “When monitoring is sufficiently precise, every equilibrium s
