enrich.summary_1line: Delhi High Court rejected Unity Small Finance Bank's appeal against an interim order barring a capital restructuring resolution without prior consent from RIPL and Centrum.

text: Adding another layer to the ongoing shareholder dispute at BharatPe-backed Unity Small Finance Bank (SFB), the Delhi High Court (HC) has rejected an appeal filed by the bank against an interim order. The interim order restrains Unity SFB from placing a proposed capital restructuring resolution before its board without prior written consent from BharatPe parent Resilient Innovations (RIPL) and Centrum Financial Services. The order, passed by a bench Justices C Hari Shankar and Vinod Kumar on November 5, restrains Unity SFB from tabling, discussing or approving ‘Agenda Item 18’ at its board meeting without prior written consent from RIPL and Centrum Financial Services. The HC granted BharatPe the interim relief pertaining to the case earlier this year in July The dispute stems from a Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) signed between Unity Bank, RIPL and Centrum in October 2021, following their partnership to establish Unity SFB. The agreement features certain ‘Reserved Matters’ that would require prior written consent from representatives of both RIPL and Centrum. These include changes to the bank’s capital structure and amendments to its constitutional documents. Agenda Item 18 proposed increasing Unity SFB’s authorised share capital from ₹4,000 Cr to ₹4,900 Cr by creating an additional 90 Cr preference shares of ₹10 each. The proposal also involved amending the bank’s Memorandum of Association (MoA) to facilitate the issuance of these shares. RIPL opposed the proposal, arguing that the proposed capital restructuring could dilute its shareholding in Unity SFB from 49% to 21%. It contended that the resolution fell under the SHA’s Reserved Matters and therefore required prior written consent from both RIPL and Centrum. Welcoming the decision, BharatPe said the ruling reaffirmed the shareholder rights and governance framework agreed upon when the joint venture was established in 2021. “The board must ensure that the bank complies with the court’s directions in letter and spirit. We expect the board to exercise independent judgment, free from undue influence, and act in the interests of the bank and all its stakeholders, including minority shareholders,” a BharatPe spokesperson said. The company also called on Unity’s board to respect the governance processes agreed upon at the time of the bank’s inception and honour its contractual obligations under the SHA. It said the agreed framework should not be set aside to favour one shareholder group over another. Unity Small Bank, on the other hand, declined to comment on the matter. “The discussions are solely between the bank’s promoter and a financial investor. The bank remains operationally unaffected, and continues to serve its customers and stakeholders as usual,” the bank told Inc42. The proposal also involved amending Clause V of the bank’s Memorandum of Association (MOA) to reflect the revised authorised capital. While the bank acknowledged in its board agenda that the proposed capital increase was a ‘Reserved Matter’ under the SHA and sought RIPL and Centrum’s approval, it also proposed taking the resolution up for board discussion and approval. RIPL opposed the move, arguing that a clause of the SHA expressly prohibits even discussing a Reserved Matter at a board meeting without prior written consent from both shareholders. It also relied on Clause 8, which bars the bank from taking decisions or actions on Reserved Matters without the requisite consent. enrich.summary_1line: X told the Delhi High Court that takedown notices attributed to Delhi Police against IFF and SFLC.in were fake.

text: Social media platform X has told the Delhi High Court that takedown notices purportedly issued by the Delhi Police against digital rights organisations Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC.in) were fake. According to a post by IFF today, X said an internal investigation found the purported police communications to be fake and that it had filed a complaint with law enforcement authorities. X’s counsel told the court that an imposter had submitted the requests in the Delhi Police’s name. “X stated that it is not likely to take any action at this stage,” IFF’s post added. The court recorded X’s statement and disposed of the organisations’ petitions, granting them liberty to approach it again if the platform takes action against their accounts. Senior advocate Akhil Sibal, representing both organisations, placed X’s transparency reports and a legal notice purportedly sent on behalf of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) on record. IFF said it had written to the RSS seeking confirmation of the legal notice’s authenticity but received no response. Separately, SFLC.in said an email seeking verification of the takedown requests had bounced back from the Delhi Police address mentioned in the communication. IFF said X forwarded two ‘Illegal Content Reports’ to it on Tuesday (November 3), submitted in the name of the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police. The first, dated October 31, sought the removal of a post IFF published on October 30 and another by SFLC.in. The second, dated Monday (November 2), sought the removal of 37 posts and the withholding of the accounts of IFF, SFLC.in, and GeoBlockedIndia. The reports alleged that the posts defamed the RSS under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The posts reproduced and commented on a legal notice the organisations said they had received in the RSS’s name. IFF contested the requests, arguing that its posts were protected speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. It also questioned their legal basis, saying the reports cited no complaint, FIR, Magistrate’s order, or court order. Through its counsel, IFF subsequently served a legal notice to the Delhi Police, with a copy to X, seeking withdrawal of the reports and details of the authority under which they had been submitted. It also asked X not to act on the requests pending their withdrawal or adjudication. IFF approached the Delhi High Court after receiving no official withdrawal or clarification from the Delhi Police. The dispute comes amid a wider debate over content takedowns, transparency, and platforms’ responsibilities when responding to government requests. In July, former Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey claimed that the Indian government had directed GitHub to remove three URLs linked to bitchat, an open-source messaging app that enables peer-to-peer communication without internet connectivity or centralised servers. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre’s (I4C) reported directive gave GitHub three hours to remove or disable access to the URLs. These covered the project’s main source code repository, Android repository, and Android releases page. The agency cited concerns over anonymous communication and difficulties in lawful interception and investigations. Meanwhile, MeitY is reportedly exploring withdrawing safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000, from social media platforms. The provision limits intermediaries’ liability for third-party content, subject to prescribed conditions. enrich.summary_1line: TRAI recommended a separate satellite network provider authorisation and proposed direct-to-device satellite services, subject to government approval.

label.reason: TRAI satellite direct-to-device telecom policy; unrelated to AI engineering.

text: The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has recommended a separate authorisation for satellite network providers and proposed permitting direct-to-device services using satellite and terrestrial mobile spectrum. The proposals can enable compatible smartphones to connect directly to satellites, potentially extending connectivity to areas without conventional mobile coverage. Under the proposed Satellite Communication Network (SCN) Provider Authorisation, companies can build and operate satellite networks and sell capacity to eligible telecom service providers. They cannot serve end users directly under this authorisation. The recommendations require government approval and do not immediately permit commercial D2D services. The framework would give telecom operators a way to access satellite infrastructure through partnerships, while continuing to manage their customer relationships. For satcom companies, it would create a separate route to sell network capacity to telecom operators, without requiring them to build a consumer-facing service under the same authorisation. In effect, one company can operate the underlying satellite network while another sells connectivity to customers. This will support partnerships between satellite infrastructure providers and telecom operators seeking to extend their coverage. However, the SCN authorisation alone would not allow a satellite company to sell mobile or broadband services directly to consumers. It would require the relevant service licence or authorisation. The proposed nationwide authorisation would remain valid for up to 20 years, with renewal permitted for another period of up to 20 years. TRAI has proposed two routes for D2D connectivity – using spectrum earmarked for mobile satellite services or using spectrum already assigned to terrestrial mobile operators. For the first route, it has recommended that the government encourage handset manufacturers to include support for the relevant satellite bands in future smartphones sold in India. For the second, telecom operators can partner with satellite network providers to use their existing mobile spectrum for satellite connectivity. However, participating operators would collectively need to hold the relevant frequency channel across all 22 licensed service areas and agree to its use. TRAI has recommended permitting this arrangement without waiting for the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027. The satellite services would have to avoid interfering with existing authorised services and cannot claim protection from interference caused by them. TRAI has proposed an authorisation fee of 8% of adjusted gross revenue (AGR), without a minimum authorisation fee. Satellite network providers can obtain spectrum directly from the government or use spectrum held by eligible partner operators. In a partnership, spectrum rights would remain with the operator. Government-assigned satellite spectrum would be valid for up to five years, with a possible extension of up to two years. It would attract an annual minimum spectrum charge of ₹3,500 per MHz. For D2D services using a telecom operator’s existing mobile spectrum, TRAI has proposed no additional spectrum charges. Existing spectrum charges would continue. The proposals come amid efforts by Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Reliance Jio to tap India’s satellite connectivity market. enrich.summary_1line: Cashfree Payments launched Checkout for Agents, a WebMCP-based tool that lets AI agents process customer payments without merchant code changes.

text: Fintech soonicorn Cashfree Payments has launched ‘Checkout for Agents’, a new tool that enables AI agents to process customer payments seamlessly. The new feature is built on the open-source WebMCP (model context protocol). The startup claims that merchants using Cashfree’s checkout page can avail the service without requiring any code changes or technical updates. The new solution aims to address a critical friction point in agentic commerce. While global purchases initiated by AI agents are projected to hit $1.5 Tn by 2030, traditional web interfaces remain optimised for human navigation. Hence, AI agents consume nearly 2 Mn tokens on average to decode the web page when they need to execute a transaction. By leveraging WebMCP, Cashfree claims that its new checkout tool directly communicates all the available actions to the AI agents, including reading order total and selecting payment mode. The startup claims its solution reduces token consumption by over 40%. The architecture also allows personal AI assistants like Instinct, Meta’s Muse, and Grok Bot to reach the final payment step with fewer errors and lower drop-off rates, while leaving the final transaction authorisation with the user. “If an agent is visiting and browsing the merchant’s website, there will not be any drop off at the payment layer. Your speed of conversion will increase, token usage will drop, and the success rate will be near 100% as far as an agent making a payment is concerned,” Cashfree cofounder Reeju Datta told Inc42. He foresees AI agents driving a significant share of traffic to Cashfree’s customers in the future. “Agent traffic has grown around 4-5X annually and converts 5X better than my SEO traffic. The lifetime value (LTV) of such users is also much much higher,” Datta added. On a question about AI agents taking unauthorised or unintended actions, Datta claimed that Cashfree’s latest offering preserves existing authorisation mechanisms and creates no heightened vulnerabilities. For instance, if the final payment authorisation step requires an OTP, then the user would still have to enter the pin to approve the payment. Founded in 2015 by Datta and Akash Sinha, Cashfree Payments offers digital payment solutions such as payment gateway, cross-border payments, payout solutions and banking APIs. It claims to process over $80 Bn in annual transaction volumes for over 10 Lakh businesses, including the likes of MakeMyTrip, Zomato, CRED, and Delhivery. Cashfree isn’t the only one in India’s startup ecosystem betting on agentic commerce. Its IPO-bound rival Razorpay is also repositioning itself as an AI-powered business operating system through its Agent Studio and agentic commerce push. Then, there is Bengaluru-based Nudge that helps ecommerce brands optimise product discovery and conversions inside AI platforms. Foodtech giant Swiggy is also enabling users to interact with its app through external AI agents to discover food, build carts, place orders, and book restaurant tables. enrich.summary_1line: CERT-In issued a November 4, 2026 advisory on an AI-assisted campaign, CRAFTY FALCON, targeting payment and disbursement APIs at BFSI entities.

label.reason: CERT-In advisory on AI-driven attacks exploiting payment APIs; useful security awareness for API builders.

text: India’s cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In has issued a critical warning to entities in the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) sector over an escalating campaign of AI-driven cyberattacks targeting payment and disbursement APIs. In an advisory dated November 4, 2026, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) identified the threat actor behind the campaign as ‘CRAFTY FALCON’, describing it as an AI-assisted financial threat actor that uses machine intelligence to identify targets, execute attacks at machine speed and exploit victims’ own payment and disbursement APIs to initiate unauthorised fund transfers. Banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), fintech companies and other financial services entities have been warned of the growing threat. CERT-In’s Computer Security Incident Response Team-Finance (CSIRT-Fin) said the campaign has witnessed a significant escalation, with successful attacks continuing to be reported across the financial services ecosystem. The agency has urged all BFSI entities to treat the campaign as an immediate and continuing threat. A key concern highlighted in the advisory is the threat actor’s continued targeting of financial entities that had already received earlier restricted advisories and undertaken remediation measures. According to CERT-In, some of these organisations have been deliberately targeted again, including cases where remediation was incomplete. The attacks have also been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other periods of reduced monitoring, potentially delaying detection and response. CERT-In’s analysis identified the use of multiple publicly available AI-driven offensive security tools in the campaign. These include the ARTEX family of large language model (LLM)-based tools, PentAGI, an autonomous multi-agent AI penetration testing system, and the Cairn attack search engine, alongside the CyberStrikeAI framework. These tools can execute complete attack chains autonomously, generate and refine large volumes of customised attack scripts in rapid succession, and adapt their payloads based on responses from targeted systems. The supporting attack infrastructure also changes frequently, with IP addresses rotating within hours to days. CERT-In said infrastructure fingerprints and detailed detection rules have been shared with affected entities through restricted advisories. The latest advisory follows another critical warning issued by CERT-In in October, when the agency flagged attackers using publicly available agentic AI tools to conduct financially motivated intrusions into Indian organisations. The watchdog warned that autonomous AI agents, ostensibly deployed for research and evaluation, had accessed live systems without authorisation, reading business records containing personal data and confidential information. Meanwhile, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has also warned banks, NBFCs and fintech startups about the growing use of AI agents by cybercriminals to perpetrate financial fraud. The agency said it had uncovered multiple individual cases in which malicious agentic AI systems exploited compromised financial systems to execute unauthorised transactions involving amounts running into crores of rupees. Separately, CERT-In has flagged multiple vulnerabilities in select versions of Tata Motors’ iRA 2.0 and iRA.ev connected vehicle applications, which could allow attackers to access sensitive credentials and vehicle-related information. The agency identified four vulnerabilities, including hardcoded service account credentials, API keys and authorisation tokens within the applications; inadequate validation of URLs and origins loaded through the apps’ WebView component; authentication tokens being recorded in application logs; and improper implementation of SSL certificate pinning in the network security configuration. Shiprocket’s adjusted EBITDA rose to ₹14.2 Cr from ₹4.3 Cr a year ago, while its adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 2.1% from 0.9%. Shiprocket reports its operations under two segments: core business and emerging business. The latter includes marketing technology, checkout, cross-border, and omnichannel solutions. Core business revenue grew 25.3% to ₹461.5 Cr from ₹368.3 Cr a year ago, while adjusted EBITDA increased 28.9% to ₹59.1 Cr. The segment’s adjusted EBITDA margin improved to 12.8% from 12.4%, with transactions growing 31% during the quarter. Emerging business revenue rose 60.9% to ₹212.2 Cr from ₹131.9 Cr, increasing its share of overall revenue to 31% from 26%. However, the segment’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹44.9 Cr from ₹41.6 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA loss margin narrowed to 21.2% from 31.5%, reflecting faster revenue growth. Within emerging businesses, martech revenue jumped 102%, while omnichannel revenue rose 79%. Shiprocket attributed omnichannel growth to brands using its services to replenish quick commerce dark stores, including appointment-based deliveries with visibility into purchase orders from platforms such as Blinkit and Zepto. Its martech offerings, grouped under Fastrr, span advertising, checkout, and customer engagement tools. Shiprocket processed 233 Mn unique transactions involving goods worth ₹37,398.7 Cr in gross merchandise value (GMV) during the trailing 12 months ended September 30. It served 2.36 Lakh active merchants over the same period. For Q2 FY27, the company reported 33% growth in GMV, 34% growth in transactions, an 8% increase in merchants, and a 25% rise in average revenue per user. The number of merchants using its emerging business offerings increased 75% to 62,025 on a trailing 12-month basis. Meanwhile, 9.3% of core business merchants used an emerging product, up from 7.9% a year ago. Around 17,300 new merchants joined Shiprocket through its emerging products during the quarter, compared with about 5,400 a year earlier. CFO Tanmay Kumar attributed the turnaround to growth in core business transactions, improving contribution from emerging businesses, and the repayment of borrowings using IPO proceeds. “… IPO proceeds retired all our borrowings, which cut finance costs, and the surplus now earns interest income,” Kumar said. Finance costs declined to ₹4.9 Cr from ₹6.7 Cr a year ago. The company had no outstanding borrowings at September-end as against ₹242 Cr at March 31, although lease liabilities remained on its books. Net cash generated from operating activities stood at ₹55.1 Cr in H1 FY27 compared with ₹23.8 Cr a year ago. Founded in 2017 by Saahil Goel, Gautam Kapoor, Vishesh Khurana, and Akshay Ghulati, Shiprocket started as a logistics aggregator for online sellers, partnering with third-party delivery providers. It has since expanded into a broader ecommerce enablement platform. Important to highlight that Khurana left operational role at Shiprocket in 2025 to join Tribe Capital, Shiprocket’s backer, as a managing partner. Shares of Shiprocket ended today’s trading session 0.80% lower at ₹130.80 on the BSE. The post Shiprocket Turns Profitable In Q2, Revenue Jumps 35% YoY To ₹674 Cr appeared first on Inc42 Media.
title: Shiprocket Turns Profitable In Q2, Revenue Jumps 35% YoY To ₹674 Cr

text:
In a closed-door roundtable, leaders from logistics, healthcare, telecom, fintech, and e-commerce discussed where to automate, where to keep humans in charge, and why observability can no longer be an afterthought.

AI has made writing code faster than ever, but the harder question for engineering leaders is what happens after the code is written. At a roundtable on operating engineering in the AI era, leaders from logistics, food tech, healthcare, telecom, fintech, ecommerce and higher education compared notes on scaling with AI without losing reliability, security or control. The shared view was that speed is no longer the hard part. Governing it is. The roundtable, moderated by Ipshita Basu, brought together Manjunath Nakshathri, Head of Engineering, Mojro; Shobhit Suman, CPO, HungerBox; Pavan Kumar A T, CTO, Digii (DigiiCampus); Pranjal Nadhani, Co-founder and CTO, Cautio; Kenil Paul, VP, Technology and Solutions, 6D Technologies; Rimjhim Agrawal, Co-founder and CTO, BrainSightAI; Dhruv Rastogi, Chief AI Officer, MediAssist; Chandrakesh Pandey, Senior Vice President of Technology, Niyo Solutions Inc.; Achal Sharma, CTO, TechnoSport; Sunil Kumar, Director Engineering, Meesho; and Anshul Sharma, Director Engineering, Scaler. The session was hosted by groundcover and Data Signals in partnership with YourStory, and was led on the host side by Paul Trebe, Head of Sales and Partnership, groundcover, and Satish Dange, Founder, Data Signals. Participants agreed that AI has compressed build time, but the pressure has shifted downstream. When agents generate large volumes of code, the questions become who reviews it, who tests it and who monitors dozens of deployments a day. Several leaders said their teams now spend more time on design, context and governance than on writing components. Agents are only as effective as the context they receive, and few organizations yet have repository knowledge, documentation and templates in a form an agent can reliably use. The room converged on a progressive approach. Reversible, read-only work, such as fetching data or generating reports, can go to agents with little friction. Irreversible actions, such as deleting data or running database updates, stay behind human review. Blast radius matters as much as reversibility. If a wrong call could affect end users or production systems, a person makes it. One of the participants described a ‘four eyes’ model in which AI does the maker work of reading and analyzing, deterministic rules deliver clear yes or no outcomes, and a human signs off. Another speaker described risk scoring based on severity and occurrence, which focuses human review on medium and high criticality items. Others drew the line by specialization, letting engineers use agents freely in their own domain while production ownership stays with people who can debug at 2 AM. That scenario also surfaced in a hopeful form. Instead of waking an engineer, an agent can investigate an incident and hand over a report by morning, leaving the decision with a human. Trust, participants said, will build gradually, much as it did with online payments, and the line will keep moving. Accountability drew firm agreement: it cannot be delegated to a model. Leaders remain answerable for what agents do. AI works as an intelligence multiplier, one participant noted, which means mistakes are amplified as quickly as good decisions. Skill erosion sparked livelier debate. Some saw a shift in skills, much as calculators changed arithmetic. Others, particularly in healthcare, worried about losing the expertise needed to judge AI output at all. One practical answer was to decide deliberately where AI drafts and where humans do. For telecom and healthcare leaders, data control is settled at design time. Models cannot simply run in a public cloud when regulators, tenancy separation, and residency rules apply, and one mistake can bring heavy penalties. enrich.summary_1line: Deepinder Goyal defended the Temple brain-monitoring wearable on X after criticism from Indian doctors who questioned its scientific evidence.

text:
In a post on X, Goyal said $30 million was invested in building the device, of which he put in $20 million of his personal money.

Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal has posted a series of updates and clarifications on X amid backlash from some Indian doctors who criticised his brain-monitoring wearable Temple. Describing Temple as “an ambitious project”, Goyal gave a detailed explanation on what the team is building. “The team is delusional enough to think we can build this. And we will,” he wrote on Friday. He also later added that the first 10,000 orders will not have to pay a subscription to use Temple. Criticising the doctors, he said, "All my emotion last night was directed at a few influencer doctors, who are more influencers than doctors. They did not read our research in detail, and spread twisted facts to call something new a scam. They get views by piling on us." The open debate started on Thursday when Goyal took to X to defend the device. He said, “First and foremost, a business lesson: if Temple were a scam, and any of what we said weren't true, people would know it in just a few days of using Temple.” He also said the device features a 14-day no-question return policy. “If the product doesn't work, it fails out of the gate and the company dies before recovering a tenth of its R&D," he said. Goyal is currently Vice Chairman and Non-Executive Director of Eternal (parent company of Zomato). He is also the founder of healthtech wearable startup Temple and LAT Aerospace. In the post, Goyal highlighted that $30 million was invested in building the device, including $20 million of his personal money. Calling this his purpose, he said it's not about the money. “I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck.” Goyal argued that most wearable companies start with internal studies. He referred to Whoop which shipped its fitness band in 2015 but the first published validation happened a few years later. He also added that Temple had a higher standard. "Pre-prints are a step prior to peer reviewed publications, and they are coming up." Reposing confidence in the product, he said, “We stand by our science and our methods. Each of our claims is easily verifiable by individuals and institutions alike, and you will see a lot of independent studies come up on their own when the device becomes available to use.” Moreover, he added that this device is a fitness tracker, and wellness device, not a medical device. “If at some point, we clinically validate any of our metrics, we will let you know.” However, some doctors were not convinced by Goyal’s response. Responding to Goyal's claim on showing scientific evidence, an X user, who goes by the handle TheLiverdoc, said the Apple Watch Series 11 and Fitbit Sense had shown clinical evidence before launch. Similarly, Samsung Galaxy Watch8 and Watch9 also passed FDA trials prior to release. "Meanwhile, the Oura Ring 4 and Whoop 4.0 launched as wellness trackers backed by peer-reviewed sleep studies." On X, Dr Rishabh Jain responded saying Goyal shared financial and personal sacrifices but no scientific evidence. "Stop calling legitimate scientific scrutiny 'rage'. You have responded to questions about medical accuracy with investment figures, return policies, personal reputation, and promises of future studies. None of these constitutes scientific validation.” Criticising the return policy he said, "Subjective satisfaction cannot establish medical accuracy.” Dr Jain further said that doctors are not against innovation. However the evidence needs to show it. "If Temple delivers what it promises, doctors will be among its biggest supporters." He also said that science is not a popularity contest, and criticism is not “rage". Dr Jain also asked for data that can be reviewed by independent researchers. Temple is a wearable device that tracks blood flow and oxyge
title: Deepinder Goyal hits back at doctors, defends wearable device Temple

enrich.summary_1line: VeloDB's APAC director argued at TechSparks 2026 that AI agents need a unified real-time data layer to move from pilot to production.

label.reason: Why agents fail in production, data layer/database angle; relevant, though vendor keynote.

text:
At TechSparks 2026, VeloDB’s Regional Director for APAC explained why AI agents that work in pilots struggle in production, and why the fix often lies in the database underneath them.

AI agents tend to look good in a pilot. The scope is narrow, the data is controlled, and the questions are predictable. Production is different, and that gap is where many projects stall. Gartner predicts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls. For Nitin Waghulde, Regional Director, APAC at VeloDB, a large part of the problem sits below the model, in the data layer. In a keynote titled ‘AI agents at scale: Surviving beyond the demo’, Nitin explained how AI agents use data differently from people, what they need to work reliably at scale, and how companies are redesigning their data infrastructure to support them. Nitin started his session with an example. In a traditional system, a business manager who wanted last year’s sales figure would run a ready-made report and get the number in one lookup. Ask an AI agent why sales dropped over the last three quarters, and the work changes. The agent pulls order records from the ERP and CRM systems, scans support tickets and chats to check whether major customers have escalated problems, and reads sales team reports on territory dynamics. If its reasoning is incomplete, it goes back for more. “What used to be completed in one simple lookup or one simple query, now you’re taking hundreds of lookups for the same thing,” he said. In the past, people and reports were the main consumers of business data, and systems were built around fixed reports with clear boundaries. Now, Nitin said, AI has become a new customer of that data, and it behaves very differently. Agents run around the clock, ask many questions at once, and work in an iterative loop: ask, think, search, and retry until they can answer. Their questions are also unscripted. That puts a heavy, unpredictable load on the data layer. The challenge grows because business data lives in several places at once: transactional records, chat memory, documents, dashboards and pre-built reports, and vector stores for meaning-based search. An agent has to search all of them and combine the results before it can answer. Each extra trip to the data adds cost. If the data is stale, the answer is wrong. Nitin compared it to driving with an inaccurate traffic map. And when data comes from many sources, it becomes harder to know where an answer came from, which creates a trust problem. He likened it to sending someone to five filing cabinets to collect pieces of paper. By the time the person returns from the fifth cabinet, the information from the first may already be out of date. Nitin outlined four requirements for agents to move from pilot to production. VeloDB’s answer is a single engine that handles all of these needs. The company was founded in 2023 by the original creators of Apache Doris, an open-source real-time analytics database that became a top-level Apache Software Foundation project in June 2022. According to VeloDB, Apache Doris has more than 14,000 GitHub stars and 700 contributors, and is used by over 5,000 enterprises worldwide. To cut down the back-and-forth trips that slow agents down, VeloDB supports hybrid queries. A single query can combine SQL, vector search, and text search, running deterministic and probabilistic searches in parallel. The result is one unified source of truth instead of scattered data. Nitin shared two examples of companies running this architecture in production. The first was one of the largest crypto exchanges, with more than 120 million users, which he did not name. The exchange makes transaction data available to AI agents that retail investors can query, for example to see what positions large traders are taking on an asset. He said its agents handle about 33,000 conversations with a tail latency of around 3
title: VeloDB’s Nitin Waghulde on why AI agents break down after the demo

enrich.summary_1line: Delhi High Court division bench dismissed Unity Bank's appeal, upholding BharatPe parent RIPL's shareholder consent rights under the SHA.

text: A division bench of the Delhi High Court has dismissed an appeal by Unity Bank, upholding the interim protection granted to BharatPe's parent company RIPL (Resilient Innovations Private Limited) under the Shareholders’ Agreement and affirming the order of a single judge. The court has now, on two occasions, declined to let the bank and its promoter proceed on reserved matters without the prior written consent of RIPL, as the Shareholders’ Agreement (SHA) requires. Rejecting the bank’s explanation that it had sought RIPL’s consent on Reserved Matters through an “inadvertent error”, the bench called the plea an “argument of desperation and nothing more”. It noted that Unity had expressly sought RIPL’s consent in writing, which showed it knew of the contractual requirement. The bench reaffirmed that Unity cannot take decisions on Reserved Matters without the prior written consent of RIPL and Centrum, observing that Clause 8 of the SHA explicitly bars any action on such matters without it. It endorsed the single judge’s findings, describing the matter as “elementary”. The court also rejected Unity’s contention that the Reserve Bank of India had turned down the SHA. It observed that the RBI had never objected to the agreement, which had been submitted to it for approval, and held that the injunction does not obstruct any RBI directive and merely requires enforcement of Clause 8. Turning down the argument that the SHA cannot override the Articles of Association, the bench noted that Clause 8 opens with a non obstante clause, giving it precedence over the relevant provisions of the Articles. BharatPe welcomed the decision. A spokesperson said, “The Board must ensure that the Bank complies with the Court’s directions in letter and spirit. We expect the Board to exercise independent judgment, free from undue influence, and act in the interests of the Bank and all its stakeholders, including minority shareholders. Governance processes followed since the Bank’s inception must be respected and applied consistently. They cannot be set aside to favour one shareholder group at the expense of another. “We expect the Board to guide the Bank in honouring its contractual obligations and ensuring that its actions comply with the Court’s directions. We believe the Hon’ble Division Bench’s decision reinforces the importance of the agreed governance framework and the shareholder rights that formed the basis of the joint venture in 2021. Respect for these commitments is essential to maintaining trust between shareholders and protecting the institution’s long-term interests.” The ruling reinforces that Unity Bank is bound by the Reserved Matter provisions of the SHA and cannot dismiss its own written requests for shareholder consent as inadvertent errors to avoid its contractual obligations.
title: Delhi HC upholds interim protection for BharatPe’s shareholder rights, dismisses Unity Bank’s appeal

How did Bihar Museum enter the global top 10? Shradha Sharma reflects on Nitish Kumar's vision, legal challenges and the persistence behind its success

Bihar Museum in Patna was recently ranked ahead of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Louvre in Paris. The museum has secured the ninth place on The World's 100 Best Museums 2026, published by German travel guide Worth a Journey. The Met stands tenth and the Louvre 31st. It is the only Indian institution on the list and the highest-ranked museum in Asia. For a museum that opened barely a decade ago, it is a significant achievement. More so because there was a time when the project itself faced serious opposition, with questions raised about its cost, relevance and the way it was being executed. Reflecting on the recognition in a recent LinkedIn post, YourStory Founder and CEO Shradha Sharma recalled the roles played by two people in getting the museum built: Nitish Kumar, who championed the project as Bihar's Chief Minister, and 1992-batch IAS officer Chanchal Kumar, who was entrusted with its execution. When the state government proposed spending nearly Rs 500 crore on a world-class museum in Patna, the decision attracted criticism. Why should a state struggling with basic infrastructure invest so much in a museum? Who would visit it? Could the money have been better spent elsewhere? According to Sharma, even people within the political establishment questioned the proposal. Nitish Kumar, however, stood by the project, convinced that Bihar needed an institution worthy of its historical and cultural heritage. The challenges began with the land. According to Sharma, the proposed 13-acre site had seven government bungalows, some occupied by senior officials and a state minister. Getting the occupants to vacate required considerable administrative effort and legal intervention. She also recounted an incident in which men allegedly linked to local politicians entered the construction site demanding subcontracts, prompting police intervention. The museum was designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki in collaboration with Mumbai-based architectural firm Opolis, while Larsen & Toubro was selected to construct it. But appointing internationally recognised architects and an established construction company was only part of the challenge. Getting the project completed was another matter. The museum also faced judicial scrutiny. In June 2015, the Patna High Court, hearing a public interest litigation, criticised the expenditure of approximately Rs 500 crore and questioned the transparency of the contracting process. The court held that the project was not in the public interest but declined to halt construction because the building was nearing completion. Those findings remain an important part of the museum's history. Its international recognition does not erase the questions raised about public spending and governance, although the institution has since gained recognition well beyond Bihar. Sharma credits much of the execution to Chanchal Kumar, who held the dual responsibility of Secretary of Art and Culture and Secretary of the Building Construction Department. The arrangement meant that both the museum's cultural vision and its construction came under the same officer. Sharma said she recently read his account of how the museum came together and was struck by how little he spoke about his own contribution. Behind the finished building were years of navigating approvals, land disputes, administrative resistance and the many complications that accompany a large public project. For Sharma, who grew up in Bihar, the recognition carries a more personal meaning. Few places in India can claim the kind of historical and intellectual inheritance that Bihar possesses. enrich.summary_1line: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora argues vulnerability patching lags AI-driven discovery and recommends virtual patching and shared clearing houses.

entities: company:national institute of standards and technology
text:
Nikesh Arora, Chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, has called for faster and more collaborative approaches to vulnerability management.

Nikesh Arora, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Palo Alto Networks, has raised concerns about the growing use of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models to identify software vulnerabilities and link them into potential attack paths. While these capabilities can help strengthen cybersecurity, they could also give attackers faster ways to exploit weaknesses in enterprise systems. The bigger challenge, Arora notes in a LinkedIn post, is ensuring that organisations can verify, prioritise and fix vulnerabilities at the same pace at which AI can discover them. “Most organizations do not have capacity to patch at the speed needed, especially the smaller ones,” Arora wrote. Smaller businesses often lack security specialists, while larger ones must test fixes against existing applications. He also says models identify different weaknesses, so one model cannot provide complete coverage. Finding a flaw is only the start. Teams must confirm it, assess the risk, develop a fix, test for disruption and deploy it. False positives, or incorrect alerts, waste time, while untested patches can disrupt services. The scale is growing. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology said submissions to its National Vulnerability Database rose 263% between 2020 and 2025. It enriched nearly 42,000 records in 2025, but this was still insufficient. In April 2026, it adopted risk-based prioritisation, focusing on exploited flaws and critical software. AI developers are linking discovery with repair. Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, launched in April 2026 with Palo Alto Networks among its partners, gives selected organisations access to Claude Mythos Preview for defensive security. Anthropic said partners had identified more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity flaws by June and expanded the programme to around 150 additional organisations. On November 4, OpenAI reported that a controlled Linux-kernel pipeline generated candidate patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities, which allow a user to gain higher access rights. Human researchers reviewed the findings before reporting them to maintainers. In India, CERT-In’s November 4 advisory warned of an AI-assisted threat actor targeting non-bank lenders, fintech firms, payment providers and cryptocurrency platforms through machine intelligence and payment APIs. The agency has also issued 2026 guidance on AI-assisted vulnerability defence and AI security auditing. Arora advocates virtual patching as an interim measure. “The most obvious solution is virtual patching. This is a time tested technology that is currently available with cyber vendors for endpoints, WAF, cloud, network use cases.” WAF is a web application firewall, which filters website and application traffic. A virtual patch is a security rule that blocks a known method of exploiting a flaw without changing the affected software. It buys time while a permanent update is tested, but does not remove the weakness. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project cautions that it protects only the traffic the system inspects and attacks variations its rules recognise. Arora calls for a shared vulnerability clearing house and faster development of protective signatures, or detection rules. He also highlights operational technology, systems that monitor or control physical processes such as energy, water and transport. Patching them can be difficult because downtime may affect safety or essential services.
title: AI’s ability to find cyber flaws outpacing firms’ capacity to fix them: Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora

enrich.summary_1line: Shiprocket reported its first quarterly net profit, Rs 60 lakh in Q2 FY27, with revenue up 35% to Rs 673.6 crore and debt fully repaid.

text:
Shiprocket reported a net profit of Rs 60 lakh in Q2 FY27, compared with a loss of Rs 20.3 crore a year ago, as revenue grew 35% to Rs 673.6 crore.

Shiprocket, an ecommerce enablement platform for MSMEs, turned profitable in the second quarter of FY27, reporting a net profit of Rs 60 lakh for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, against a net loss of Rs 20.3 crore in the corresponding period last year. The company's revenue from operations increased 35% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 673.6 crore during the quarter. Adjusted EBITDA stood at Rs 14.2 crore, compared with a loss in the year-ago period. Shiprocket's core business revenue grew 25% YoY to Rs 461.5 crore, while its emerging business revenue increased 61% to Rs 212.2 crore. The emerging business, which includes cross-border shipping, omnichannel fulfilment, hyperlocal delivery, marketing technology (Martech) and ecommerce enablement solutions, contributed 31% to overall revenue, compared with 26% a year ago. Within the emerging business, Martech revenue grew 102%, while the omnichannel business registered 79% growth during the quarter. Shiprocket attributed the growth in its omnichannel business to brands using its platform to replenish quick commerce dark stores. Its appointment-based delivery services allow brands to schedule deliveries and access real-time purchase order visibility from platforms such as Blinkit and Zepto. The company's contribution increased 43% YoY to Rs 130 crore, accounting for 19.3% of revenue. The core business generated adjusted EBITDA of Rs 59.1 crore, up 29% YoY, with its adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 12.8% from 12.4%. The emerging business narrowed its adjusted EBITDA margin loss to 21.2% from 31.5%, while its contribution margin improved to 15.4% from 10.1%. Shiprocket's trailing 12-month gross merchandise value (GMV) stood at Rs 37,398.7 crore, generated through 233 million unique transactions. The platform served more than 2.36 lakh active merchants during the period. The number of merchants using its emerging business products increased 75% to 62,025 on a trailing 12-month basis. During the quarter, 17,281 new merchants joined through emerging products, more than three times the 5,396 additions reported a year ago. “Indian commerce is splitting across more channels every year. A small brand today sells on its own website and on Instagram, replenishes quick commerce dark stores, and is starting to be found through AI search. For a large company, every new channel means a new team. For a small seller, it means friction. Shiprocket is building the infrastructure that removes this friction, so that any MSME in India can sell, ship and grow on the same footing as India’s biggest brands, every channel a switch away on one dashboard," said Saahil Goel, Managing Director and CEO of Shiprocket. "Growing 35% with positive Adjusted EBITDA and operating cash flow shows we can build it from our own operations. text:

What if booking a cab, sending a message or managing a meeting required nothing more than a flick of your thumb? Bengaluru- and San Francisco-based startup Aina believes the next phase of artificial intelligence will be less about asking machines questions and more about letting them anticipate what people need. At a private launch event in Bengaluru, the startup unveiled an AI-powered smart ring that combines a colour display, voice commands and gesture-based controls. Priced at $499 (Rs 47,000), the device is available for pre-order at a limited early-bird price starting at $399 (Rs 37,700), with shipments expected to begin in January 2027. Unlike conventional smart rings, which largely focus on health and fitness tracking, Aina wants its device to become an everyday interface between users and AI agents. The premise is simple: AI agents are getting smarter, but using them still involves unlocking phones, navigating apps and approving individual actions. Aina wants to reduce that friction. Its proposition revolves around a question displayed during the launch presentation: What if AI didn't wait to be asked? To simplify these interactions, Aina has built its ring around three features: Cues, Voice and Remote. Cues uses contextual information, including routines and connected applications, to anticipate what users might want to do next. For instance, if someone regularly books a cab around the same time each morning, the ring could suggest booking a ride without waiting for an explicit request. At the launch event, Aina demonstrated a ride-booking interaction that illustrated how everyday transactions could be completed through minimal gestures. The ring can be operated using a five-way joystick-like control, allowing users to approve or reject suggestions with their thumb without reaching for a smartphone. Aina says its context-aware intelligence can learn users' routines and anticipate relevant actions over the next 15 minutes, drawing on information from the iPhone, Mac and connected services. The company showcased integrations involving Uber, Apple Music, Spotify, phone calls, calendar meetings, smart home controls and email actions. The second interaction method, Voice, allows users to dictate notes, set reminders, send messages and issue commands. Aina also showcased use cases involving WhatsApp and Telegram, alongside Mac dictation through Wispr Flow. The third feature, Remote, turns the ring into a controller for connected devices. According to the company, users can manage music, phone calls, smart home appliances and meeting controls without picking up another device. According to specifications presented at the Bengaluru launch, the ring weighs less than 13 grams and features a titanium body, full-colour display, haptic feedback and directional audio. The company claims up to 18 hours of battery life and plans to offer the device in four colours: Eclipse Black, Amber Gold, Mercury Silver and Slate Titanium, across seven sizes. Aina also highlighted a five-way control mechanism called the Shifter, which works alongside its gesture-based interface. The startup says the ring will come with an open developer platform, allowing third-party developers to build new interactions and integrations. Whether its open platform translates into a substantial developer ecosystem will become clearer once the device reaches customers. Aina was founded by Apoorv Shankar, who previously served as vice-president of hardware at Bengaluru-based wearable technology company Ultrahuman. text:
Cosmoserve also opened a facility in Hyderabad which will be utilised for satellite servicing and space debris recovery.

Cosmoserve Space, a Hyderabad-based spacetech startup, has raised $6 million in a seed round of funding from Rebright Partners of Japan, Aranya Holdings, and Naandi Ventures. The round also saw participation from existing investors AUM Ventures and Shakti VC. This funding round has seen Cosmoserve raising over $9 million. Cosmoserve also inaugurated Base 1 - a facility to design, build, test and operate systems for satellite servicing and space debris recovery. A statement said, this facility will have an orbital rendezvous and capture lab to simulate spacecraft capture operations, a space robotics innovation Lab to develop robotic capture systems; a clean room for satellite integration, a mission simulation and control Centre to manage upcoming missions. “In our first year we have flown our first payload on an Indian rocket, raised our seed round, and today we open a facility where we can design, build, test and fly our missions under one roof. enrich.summary_1line: Article argues smaller language models suit enterprise tasks needing tight evaluation, with LLMs used alongside them.

text:
As enterprises explore smaller language models for specialised tasks, developers see opportunities for tighter evaluation and control. But smaller models still

The push to deploy artificial intelligence across enterprise workflows has largely focused on increasingly capable large language models (LLMs). These systems generate content, interpret complex instructions, and power applications from customer support to software engineering. Yet as organisations move from experimentation to production, the priority shifts: the fundamental question is no longer just how capable a model is, but how reliably we can evaluate, govern, and control its behaviour. This dynamic is bringing smaller language models (SLMs) to the forefront. Purpose-built for targeted tasks and specific domains, SLMs handle discrete functions such as document processing, classification, information retrieval, and workflow automation. Instead of depending on a single, monolithic foundation model across an entire pipeline, enterprises can distribute tasks across architectures of varying sizes. However, industry experts caution against a common misconception: model size alone doesn't proxy for safety. “A smaller model is not automatically a safer model. Parameter count alone is not a safety guarantee,” says Anuj Gupta, founder and chief executive officer of KiteFishAI. “A poorly trained smaller model can be just as problematic within its intended application as a much larger model.” The core operational case for SLMs lies in scope definition. General-purpose LLMs are designed to handle an open-ended spectrum of user prompts, making it nearly impossible to anticipate every failure mode or edge case. Conversely, a specialised model operates within tightly defined parameters. “Smaller, specialised models can be easier to control because their capabilities and intended operating boundaries are more clearly defined,” Gupta explains. “When a model is trained for a specific domain or set of tasks, developers can build targeted evaluation datasets, test edge cases more extensively, and understand failure patterns more systematically.” Sourav Bandyopadhyay, founder and chief scientist at Shunya Labs, underscores that task-specific boundaries are vital for rigorous evaluation. “You can only evaluate what you can define. A general model's job is ‘anything’, so its test set is effectively infinite,” he notes. In contrast, when an SLM classifies customer requests into specific intent buckets, the challenge becomes a closed problem. Teams can curate a representative held-out test set, evaluate accuracy per class, and trace distinct failure mechanisms. Conventional academic benchmarks often fail to capture whether a system can execute a banking workflow, fetch proprietary records, or adhere to compliance policies. Building specialised pipelines addresses this disconnect. For instance, KiteFishAI is developing custom architectures and pretraining pipelines for document intelligence, workflow automation, and enterprise search across banking, financial services, and healthcare—though it has not yet publicly disclosed named client deployments or audited production metrics. Rather than outright displacing LLMs, organisations increasingly deploy SLMs alongside them in tiered architectures. In these setups, smaller models function as targeted verification and control layers. A high-capacity LLM can generate responses while dedicated SLMs validate outputs against retrieved context, filter sensitive information, or scan incoming queries for prompt injection. In agentic environments—where systems interact directly with databases and enterprise APIs—this separation of duties becomes critical. “Enterprises do not necessarily need to use one large model for every function,” Gupta says. “They can build a multi-model architecture where specialised smaller models act as independent control and verification layers.” Bandyopadhyay warns against letting decision-making models evaluate their own act
title: Smaller Language Models Could Reshape How Enterprises Deploy AI

text: AI-enabled productivity could add roughly 28 billion to 84 billion USD to India's annual Nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) under realistic adoption scenarios, IT services company Cognizant said in a recent study. The range depends on how broadly AI is adopted and how much of the productivity gain turns into economic output. Cognizant's model also sets a theoretical ceiling of $830 billion a year, which assumes AI use across the entire workforce and full conversion of gains into output. The company said that figure is not a forecast, and that all the GDP numbers are modelled estimates based on self-reported survey responses and should be read as directional. Actual outcomes will depend on the pace of adoption and how far productivity gains reach national output. The research surveyed 700 enterprise employees and 75 C-suite and business executives at companies with revenues from $100 million to more than $10 billion, across 10 major industries. About 97% of surveyed employees reported some productivity improvement from AI, with an average reported uplift of 15%. Employees in India are also preparing: 74% have completed AI training, compared with 56% globally. Gains vary by sector. In healthcare, 38% of employees reported gains above 20%. Realising this potential will require adoption of AI tools across enterprises, continued investment in skilling, and an enabling environment for responsible AI at scale," Rajesh Varrier, President of Global Operations and Chairman and MD of Cognizant India, said.

enrich.summary_1line: Meta's Q3 2026 ad revenue rose 26%, while Google Search and other ad revenue grew 12%, as AI answers reduce clicks.

text: The third quarter of 2026 offered an interesting insight into how AI is creating two different outcomes for the world’s largest digital advertising businesses. While Meta is using AI to improve ad targeting, recommendations, and campaign performance, Google faces a new challenge: monetising users who increasingly interact with its AI-powered search. In Q3, Meta reported advertising revenue of $63.06 billion, up 26% year-on-year. Google’s Search and other advertising revenue grew 12% to $63.35 billion, down from 17% in the previous quarter and 19% in the first quarter. Surprisingly, Search accounted for less than 50% of Google revenue for the first time. Chatbots such as ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Meta’s new Muse assistant are becoming alternatives to traditional search. People ask these tools questions and get direct answers instead of clicking blue links on Google results pages. Fewer clicks mean fewer ad views and less revenue for Google. Google’s own AI features are also part of the shift. AI Overviews and AI Mode give users summaries and conversational answers. “The real shift is towards zero-click search. One AI conversation now does the work of five or six searches, and the user never lands on a results page where the ad lives. That is where the keyword model is exposed,” Viren Inaniyan, Co-founder and CEO of Tru Commerce, tells AIM. Google said AI Mode queries are, on average, three times longer than normal searches. Yet these AI experiences currently earn less money per query than traditional search. “Google has indicated that AI Mode currently monetises at a lower rate than traditional search. Part of this challenge is that most Google searches already end without a click, a pattern often called zero-click. AI Mode adds another dimension to this, as customers can now get more complete answers without needing to visit another page,” says Jacob Joseph, VP – Data Science, CleverTap Philipp Schindler, Google’s Chief Business Officer, said AI Mode’s lower monetisation contributed to the slowdown in Search revenue growth. The challenge is that AI-generated answers can satisfy users without requiring them to visit multiple websites or click through several search results. This could reduce opportunities for traditional sponsored links, particularly if users increasingly complete their research within AI interfaces. Schindler attributed the sequential slowdown in Search revenue growth primarily to foreign exchange movements, which he described as the single largest factor. Vertical-specific spending trends also weighed on growth, with retail advertisers in APAC affected by the EU’s elimination of its de minimis exemption, while media and entertainment spending normalised after a FIFA World Cup-driven surge in Q2. For Google, the question is how to introduce advertising into AI Mode and AI Overviews without affecting answer quality or the user experience. Inaniyan says fewer clicks do not mean lost revenue. “Many of these queries are new research that never happened before. The question is whether Google earns more or less from the full journey, not per query,” he notes. Meta’s approach is different. Rather than replacing its core discovery and social media experiences with conversational search, the company is using AI to improve how users discover content and how advertisers reach them. Its recommendation systems determine what users see across Facebook and Instagram feeds, Reels and other surfaces. Better recommendations can increase engagement, create more ad opportunities, and improve the likelihood that users will respond. “Meta does not need users to change how they buy. People keep scrolling and discovering. AI quietly improves what they see and which ad reaches them,” says Inaniyan. label.reason: TCS study on enterprise agent autonomy and security concerns; useful context for production agents.

text:
Security, governance and model dependence are emerging as major concerns for businesses, even as executives report productivity gains from AI investments.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) found that 84% of executives across enterprises identified productivity improvements as the leading benefit of AI investments. However, only 10% of enterprises allow AI agents to execute decisions without human approval across multiple business functions. Only 9% of executives reported that their organisations had AI agents that could securely orchestrate workflows across enterprise applications. Security, risk and governance emerged as the leading considerations when organisations decide where and how to deploy AI systems. These factors ranked ahead of cost, speed and ease of deployment. Amit Kapur, Chief AI and Services Transformation Officer at TCS, said, “What seems to be holding organisations back – and rightly so – are concerns around security, governance, and resilience.” He added, “Deploying AI responsibly, with the right guardrails and enterprise controls, will be the big focus in the next stage of this journey.” As agents gain access to enterprise systems, observability becomes important for monitoring their actions and decisions. The study also found that 90% of respondents considered model independence an important factor in AI investment decisions. However, only 7% reported having organisation-wide continuity plans to switch AI providers. About 34% of respondents identified AI sovereignty requirements, including control over data location, model choice, and regulatory compliance, as a high or very high organisational risk. In Europe, the figure rose to 43%. Separately, legacy systems, fragmented data and integration gaps are emerging as obstacles to scaling AI deployments. A recent assessment of Indian enterprises highlighted infrastructure challenges in moving AI workloads into production, as organisations assess whether their existing infrastructure can support AI at scale. AI economics remain unsettled. Thirty-nine percent of enterprises said they were still assessing whether their AI initiatives generated sufficient value relative to token and compute costs. Fidelity International has introduced use-case-level token budgets and an internal AI gateway to monitor expenditure and restrict access. Its approach to managing AI costs and model access offers an example of how organisations are addressing these concerns. Meanwhile, 44% of respondents said important business knowledge remained embedded in employees' expertise or fragmented documentation, potentially limiting AI systems' access to enterprise context. Another 46% reported deploying open-source AI for selected use cases. The proportion of leaders who said it was too early to determine AI's effect on jobs rose from 4% in 2024 to 19% in 2026. North America showed particular strength across several enterprise AI foundations, with 15% of respondents treating AI as a strategic enterprise capability. The UK and Ireland reported comparatively higher levels of continuity planning and governance integration. The study, titled Intelligence that is Real, surveyed 1,333 senior business and technology leaders across 25 countries and 12 industries. Their organisations had annual revenues ranging from $500 million to more than $20 billion.
title: 84% See AI Productivity Gains, but Only 10% Allow Agent Autonomy: TCS Study

The IndiaAI Mission has released three indigenous foundation models: EKA-1 by Soket AI Labs and Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B by ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations. EKA-1 is a 26.3-billion-parameter model trained on approximately 7.5 trillion tokens. It supports all 22 scheduled Indian languages and English, with capabilities in mathematics, coding, reasoning and agentic applications. Meanwhile, ZenteiQ’s Dhīr models are open-source multilingual assistants built for on-premise and offline deployment across government, defence, industrial and educational sectors. The models were unveiled at an event in New Delhi on November 3 in the presence of S Krishnan, Secretary at the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), and senior officials from MeitY and IndiaAI. Soket AI Labs developed EKA-1 as an open, sparse hybrid language model. The company said the model was tailored to India's banking, financial services and cybersecurity sectors. “With the support of the IndiaAI Mission, we have developed an advanced AI model specifically tailored to India's unique banking, financial services and cybersecurity landscape. It is designed to address sector-specific requirements, understand India's evolving digital ecosystem, and deliver solutions aligned with the country's needs and priorities,” said Abhishek Upperwal, CEO of Soket AI Labs. ZenteiQ, meanwhile, introduced Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B as open-source models supporting English and 10 Indian languages. The models are built for document-based automation, information retrieval and citizen and enterprise services. They can be deployed on-premise and operate without continuous cloud connectivity. The company said the models could run across different computing platforms, including GPUs and TPUs, with their lightweight architecture also supporting deployment on mobile devices. “Models like Dhīr 2B and Dhīr 5B offer the flexibility to run across different computing platforms, including GPUs and TPUs. Their lightweight architecture also enables on-device deployment on mobile phones, without dependence on cloud connectivity,” said Prof Sashikumar, CEO of ZenteiQ AiTech Innovations. “This allows users to access AI capabilities locally while keeping data on their devices, enhancing privacy, security and accessibility,” he added. text:
GitHub has not only added 4 million CPU cores and 160 PB of internal storage, but it is also rebuilding core Git primitives by decoupling compute from sto

Everything that humanity has coded to date—every operating system, transfer protocol, open-source library—may only represent 1% of what’s about to be built. We’re living through a technological rupture in which the classical software development lifecycle (SDLC) is collapsing as the centre of gravity shifts towards autonomous sub-agents capable of planning, drafting, rebasing, and testing software. No other platform is more acutely privy to the technological shift than GitHub. In September, over 40% of pull requests on the code-hosting platform were started by AI agents—a leap from 17% in March, according to GitHub Octoverse 2026 report. “The SDLC is no longer linear. In fact, the SDLC is collapsing. Most of us jump between these different stages depending on the task. Now, agents are handling the bulk of the implementation and the verification work, and everything feeds into and out of this central learning machine,” Jay Parikh, EVP of CoreAI at Microsoft, said during the keynote at GitHub Universe 2026. This swarm of agentic activity has also put considerable strain on GitHub’s infrastructure. In July, it recorded eight performance-degrading incidents affecting WebUI, Copilot, APIs, and SSH authentication. This was followed by a nearly eight-hour global outage a month later that was traced to a critical infrastructure failure at a US data centre. “To do all of this, you need a super strong foundation, an infrastructure that is performant and reliable. Now, there are times this year when we struggled with these things. But a lot of that was due to the growth and scale. That’s not meant to be an excuse, though we will, and we must, do better,” Parikh noted. To keep its 225 million developers and half a billion public repositories from buckling under the weight of autonomous commits, the Microsoft subsidiary has added more than four million cores and 160 petabytes of internal storage this year. GitHub is also rebuilding core Git primitives by decoupling compute from storage and minimising coordination. This architecture is designed to allow compute and storage workloads to scale independently, with an initial target of improving scale by 180x. According to the Octoverse report, GitHub recorded 34.3 billion commits and 17.9 billion pushes in a single year, with merged pull requests crossing 1.3 billion. The scale of agentic adoption can be illustrated in how a team of only three Anthropic engineers ported its core Messages API from the legacy Python infrastructure to Rust—which outperforms it in raw speed, memory safety, and concurrency management—in just one month. Crucially, none of the engineers actually knew the language. “We actually don’t have a single developer who actually knows Rust... this was actually Claude knowing how to write Rust, and us trusting Claude and then building a lot of systems around it,” Angela Jiang, Head of Product, Claude Platform at Anthropic, revealed in a conversation with AIM. This is why Git’s 20-year-old architecture needs a shake-up. It was designed for decentralised, serialised commits at a human scale, not for fleets of autonomous agents simultaneously rebasing, testing, and compiling across multi-repo projects simultaneously. Such activity can trigger retry storms. GitHub is now rearchitecting Git entirely to prevent high-concurrency loops from blocking enterprise pipelines. “We are completing our full multi-region migration into Azure early next year to ensure that the infrastructure scales elastically with customer demand,” Parikh told AIM. Beyond the underlying infrastructure investments, GitHub’s product, commercial, and security announcements aim to bolster its end-to-end software delivery system. Copilot Projects builds a multi-agent management platform, enabling developers to coordinate sub-agents and track parallel work. Copilot
title: Does the World Need a New GitHub?

text: Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) have shown that large language models (LLMs) can read, interpret, and modify neural network weights directly, without relying on traditional training methods like gradient descent. In a research blog post published on November 2, the researchers introduced a technique called Weight-Space Programming, which lets general-purpose LLMs examine a neural network’s weights, identify problems in its behaviour, and modify them based on natural-language instructions. The research was conducted by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab, all affiliated with MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). The researchers used OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to demonstrate the approach across eight experiments, including identifying what a neural network was trained to do, writing networks from scratch and improving the mathematical reasoning capabilities of an existing language model. “We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we'd expect from humans or conventional algorithms,” the researchers wrote. One key experiment involved improving Qwen3.5-0.8B, a small language model, without retraining it or using gradient information. Astra identified a problem in the model’s weights that caused it to repeat reasoning steps instead of producing answers. By modifying just 0.016% of the model’s weights, Astra increased its score on the MATH-500 benchmark from 7.9% to 48.1%. Its score on GSM8K, another mathematical reasoning benchmark, increased from 13.8% to 67.1%. The researchers also found that the changes improved the model’s instruction-following performance. Its IFEval score increased from 21% to 62.3%. In the first set of experiments, the researchers tested whether Astra could identify a network’s behaviour by examining its weights without running the network. They trained four neural networks using Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) to play Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man and Freeway. All four networks had the same architecture, input channels and possible actions. Astra received the 17,253 weights of each network as text, without being told which game it had been trained on. It correctly identified all four games. In another experiment, the researchers tested three diffusion models trained to generate circles, squares and triangles. Astra identified the shape each model generated by examining its weights, without running the models or performing forward passes. The researchers then tested whether an LLM could create neural networks without training them. They gave Astra the rules and source code for three MinAtar games: Breakout, Seaquest and Asterix. The model had no access to training data, loss functions, gradients or tools. It had to generate the network weights directly from the game descriptions. The resulting networks outperformed PPO-trained networks that had undergone 100 million training steps in all three games. In Breakout, Astra’s network scored 517.4, compared with 15.8 for a PPO network trained for 100 million steps and 25.3 for one trained for 500 million steps. In Asterix, Astra scored 53.2 against 55.2 for the 500-million-step PPO network. In Seaquest, it scored 53.1, compared with 88.9 for the same PPO benchmark. The researchers also tested Astra on the board game Go using a network with nearly 1.5 million weights. With no forward passes, Astra generated a network that won more than half its games against two smaller PPO networks. When allowed 50 forward passes to examine its performance, the generated network beat an equally sized PPO network trained on 20 million games. For this experiment, Astra used a Python sandbox to write and analyse the weights. It could not use the internet, train the network or use tree search. The researchers believe the technique could change how neural networks are optimised and audited. The researchers also point to recursive self-i
title: MIT Researchers Show LLMs Can Read and Edit Neural Network Weights Without Retraining

text:
