text:
AI is moving beyond crop monitoring to procurement, price prediction and traceability. But fragmented data and weak incentives could limit its impact across Ind

India's next agricultural technology opportunity may lie beyond the farm. Agritech companies have developed tools for crop monitoring, pest detection, and yield prediction, but a bigger challenge remains: connecting farm-level intelligence to the supply chain that determines where produce goes, how it is priced, and who captures its value. Produce moves through farmers, aggregators, warehouses, traders, processors and retailers, with information often recorded separately at each stage. AI could help businesses forecast availability, plan procurement and assess demand. But these capabilities depend on access to reliable data across a chain where records, systems and commercial interests remain fragmented. Post-harvest losses highlight the extent of agricultural inefficiencies in India. A 2022 NABARD Consultancy Services (NABCONS) study estimated losses of 6–15% for fruits and 5–12% for vegetables between 2020 and 2022. The study covered 54 agricultural commodities across 292 districts and assessed losses at multiple stages, including harvesting, transportation and storage. These figures don't show how much AI could prevent, but they highlight the operational challenges facing India's agricultural value chain. “The problem is less a complete absence of data than its fragmentation. Farmers, FPOs, mandis, aggregators, logistics firms, processors and retailers use different recordkeeping methods, languages, applications and enterprise systems. Requiring every stakeholder to adopt one application is unlikely to succeed,” says Krishna Kumar, founder and CEO of Cropin. Fragmentation also raises questions about data ownership. “The real damage happening for the entire ecosystem is not just because of fragmented operations, but because data sits in private books of these fragmented players,” says Rama Kancharapu, founder, CEO and CPO of agricultural market digitisation platform ONO. Connecting these records is therefore as much a question of access and incentives as it is of technology. Farm-level intelligence becomes more commercially useful when it informs decisions beyond cultivation. Knowing how a crop is growing helps assess its likely performance, but processors and buyers also need to know how much produce will be available, where it will come from, and when they can procure it. “The emerging phase is about connecting that intelligence directly to business decisions across the supply chain,” Kumar says. Applications are already extending into market forecasting and operations. “Immediate impact one can already witness: price predictions, supply and demand predictions, yield forecasting, quality assessment, fraud prevention and logistics optimisation,” Kancharapu says. ONO has captured more than three seasons of market data through its software-as-a-service platform, according to Kancharapu. He claims the platform enables price, arrival, supply and demand predictions with more than 90% accuracy. This remains a company-reported figure. The provided information does not establish the methodology or evaluation criteria. The government is also building digital infrastructure for agriculture. The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare reported that it had created more than 10.31 crore Farmer IDs under the Digital Agriculture Mission as of August 3, 2026. These records can help structure farmer and agricultural information, but they do not automatically capture every transaction, quality assessment or movement of produce between farms, markets, warehouses and processors. That distinction matters. A forecast is useful only if businesses can act on it, whether by adjusting procurement, planning storage or coordinating transport. title: AI's Next Agritech Frontier Is India's Fragmented Supply Chain

enrich.summary_1line: Amazon memo tells engineers to measure long-term outcomes, not AI usage metrics such as token counts or tools used.

label.reason: Amazon memo on AI-powered engineering expectations; relevant to engineering careers and practices.

text: As concerns grow over AI’s impact on software engineering jobs, Amazon has issued a memo outlining what it expects from its engineers as AI reshapes software development. While acknowledging AI’s capabilities in software engineering and its long-term prospects, Amazon said, “It is difficult to define, in a way that will stand the test of time, what good AI-powered engineering practices look like.” “Any definition we write now will likely look antiquated by this time next year,” the company added. And these ‘antiquated definitions’ risk slowing down progress, says Amazon, which wants to focus on what isn’t changing in software engineering roles. “Specifically, impact on our customers, our businesses, and our teams. The outcomes that matter aren’t changing, even if the inputs, tools, and techniques are changing faster than ever,” said the company. The company said that metrics that often grab attention, such as token usage, the number of AI tools used, code changes, the number of reviews, and more, are “deeply flawed”. Amazon said that these metrics are “disconnected from what matters”. It adds that if teams use these metrics as targets—not just measurements—they could drive negative outcomes, increasing costs and complexity. “We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes. But these outcomes can be time-delayed, difficult to measure, and hard to isolate from other trends,” said the company. Amazon recommends that engineering teams use AI adoption metrics carefully, paying particular attention to the 10% of teams with the lowest adoption and the 10% with the highest adoption. The company wants managers to investigate why some teams struggle to incorporate AI into their workflows and whether teams using AI extensively deliver corresponding productivity improvements. Amazon said its most AI-forward teams have seen productivity and delivery improvements. It also warned that engineers and teams that don’t adopt AI or increase their output risk falling behind. However, the company said engineers shouldn’t be expected to use AI for every task. “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” Amazon said. It added that an engineer who can explain where AI falls short is demonstrating the judgement the company expects. Amazon also wants engineering leaders to gain hands-on experience with AI tools rather than relying on second-hand accounts of their capabilities. Managers should be able to identify tasks where AI has improved their teams’ work, as well as those where it has not, and explain the reasoning behind their decisions. Another priority is reconnecting engineers with customers and the businesses they serve. Amazon said some individual contributors and software development managers had become less connected to customers and business priorities as the company grew.
title: Amazon Warns Engineers Against AI Productivity Traps in Latest Memo

text:
NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe supports transcription in 40 languages with advanced features like speaker attribution and speech translation.

NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on October 28, an open-weight speech model that can transcribe audio in 40 languages, translate speech and identify speakers. Developers can use natural-language instructions to control transcript formatting without retraining the model, according to NVIDIA. The model supports verbatim transcripts, cleaned-up written text, domain-specific terminology and code-switched speech. It can process recordings of up to one hour and generate speaker-attributed word-level timestamps on request. NVIDIA notes that individual capabilities vary by language and task. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe combines a Transformer speech encoder and a speaker diarisation model with NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning language model. The architecture has approximately 4.3 billion active parameters. Its released checkpoints use the designation 30B-A4B. NVIDIA reported a mean word error rate (WER) of 4.71% across nine public test sets on the English Open ASR Leaderboard. Its mean WER on the multilingual Open ASR Leaderboard was 4.62%, covering seven languages. A lower WER indicates fewer transcription errors. NVIDIA describes the model as the best open-weight model on both leaderboards. The company also reported a six-fold reduction in named-entity errors on ContextASR-Bench when the model received a list of expected entities. This feature is intended to improve the transcription of names and specialised terms. For inference speed, NVIDIA reported throughput of up to 2,238 seconds of audio per second on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. This result uses the NVFP4 checkpoint, DFlash2 speculative decoding and NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe inference software. However, these serving optimisations are not yet part of the open-weight release. NVIDIA says the release-day vLLM implementation is expected to run at roughly half the speed of the optimised setup. Actual performance will depend on the hardware, configuration and workload, according to the company. NVIDIA has released model checkpoints in BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 formats, along with GGUF files for NeMo-Speech.cpp. The model is available under the OpenMDW-1.1 licence, and a fine-tuning toolkit is available through NeMo Speech. The company says developers can adapt the model to new languages, domains and tasks. Its technical report describes experiments across 17 tasks, with adaptation typically taking between 0.5 and 2.3 GPU-hours per task.
title: NVIDIA Launches Open-Weight Transcription Model for 40 Languages

text:
Legacy systems, fragmented data and infrastructure gaps could slow Indian enterprises as they move AI agents from pilots into production.

Indian enterprises are investing in artificial intelligence, but deploying AI agents across business operations presents a challenge that goes beyond the models themselves: whether existing digital infrastructure can support them. AI agents need to retrieve information from enterprise databases, connect with business applications and carry out tasks across systems. Yet many organisations still rely on legacy applications, fragmented data environments and technology architectures that were not designed for software capable of taking actions across multiple systems. Consider an agent tasked with processing a customer order. It may need to retrieve customer details from a customer relationship management (CRM) platform, verify inventory against an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system and initiate the next step in the workflow. If the applications cannot exchange information reliably or return conflicting records, the process can fail even when the model performs as intended. The gap between AI ambitions and infrastructure readiness is already evident. Dell Technologies’ Modern Enterprise Readiness Study, conducted with Vanson Bourne, found that 67% of Indian organisations believe their current data centre environments are not ready to support AI workloads at production scale. “The biggest hurdle in moving an AI agent from pilot to production is rarely the model itself. It's the reality of integrating with fragmented enterprise data, legacy applications, security controls, and business processes that have evolved over decades,” says Vishal Kappanna, Engineering Director at Tesco Technology. For enterprises, the challenge is no longer simply building an agent that can complete a task. It is ensuring the surrounding systems can support that task reliably, repeatedly and at scale. Replacing entire technology stacks is neither practical nor necessary for most enterprises. Existing systems contain years of business logic and continue to support critical operations. Instead, companies are introducing application programming interfaces (APIs), middleware and orchestration platforms to connect legacy applications with AI systems. However, connecting an agent to an application does not automatically make a workflow reliable. An agent operating across several systems must contend with inconsistent records, different access permissions and dependencies between applications. A failure midway through a transaction can require retries, recovery mechanisms or human intervention. “Most enterprises are not replacing legacy systems to enable AI agents. They’re wrapping and modernising them through orchestration platforms, getting data out through events and APIs, and gating access behind governance layers and agent identities—modernising the seams, not the systems,” Kappanna notes. This approach allows organisations to retain existing applications while exposing the capabilities agents need. But it has limits. Connecting an older system to an orchestration layer does not necessarily resolve the constraints of its underlying architecture. Some applications may still require deeper modernisation to support the demands of production workloads. Vijay Yellapragada, Consulting AI and Data and US Commercial Leader at EY GDS, highlights the difference between demonstrating an agent’s capabilities and making it dependable in a live environment. “A pilot demonstrates that an agent can perform a task. Production requires proving that the enterprise can trust the agent to perform that task repeatedly, securely, and at scale,” Yellapragada explains. That requires enterprises to account for system failures, process exceptions and transaction volumes that may not emerge during controlled experiments. enrich.summary_1line: Article argues inference cost should be measured per completed task at agreed service levels, not by token or GPU prices alone.

label.reason: Production LLM serving economics: KV-cache pressure, latency, concurrency, cost; directly relevant to inference serving.

text: An AI model may prove its capabilities during evaluation, but the real test begins when users start using it at scale. A benchmark measures model capability under controlled conditions; production serving must meet latency, concurrency, availability and cost targets under variable demand. Long prompts increase prompt-processing demand; variable output lengths make capacity harder to predict; bursty traffic creates queues; and KV-cache pressure, replication for resilience, and idle capacity required for peak demand all raise the effective cost of serving each request. Inference is not a one-time compute event. It is a continuous production workload whose cost and performance depend on traffic patterns, response-time targets, model size, context length, concurrency, and the compute required to complete each task. Those economics also vary sharply by workload type: batch inference can prioritise throughput and scheduling flexibility, while interactive chat, voice, retrieval-augmented generation, agentic workflows and real-time decisioning have very different latency, availability and capacity requirements. That changes the economics of AI infrastructure. GPU hourly rates and API prices tell only part of the story. The real question is the cost per successful task at an agreed service level, measured by time-to-first-token, end-to-end latency, availability, quality and error rate. An important paradox lies at the heart of AI infrastructure. Inference has become dramatically cheaper, but the decline in token prices is not uniform across model classes, geographies, input and output tokens, or reserved and on-demand capacity. The cost of querying a model with GPT-3.5-level performance on the MMLU benchmark has fallen sharply. Stanford’s 2025 AI Index puts the price at $20 per million tokens in November 2022, compared with $0.07 per million tokens for Gemini 1.5 Flash-8B in October 2024, a more than 280-fold decline in about 18 months. The report also found that, across the models and tasks included in its analysis, the cost of inference fell by roughly nine to 900 times per year, depending on the task and model-performance level measured. This broader estimate refers to inference price reductions, rather than hardware efficiency or a uniform decline across production workloads. Lower unit prices have coincided with models being used for increasingly demanding workloads. Reasoning models can generate substantially more tokens, while agents can make multiple model calls, invoke tools and carry context from one step to the next. For example, a reasoning workflow may use a smaller number of requests but produce far more generated tokens and hold accelerator memory for longer. The result is that cost per token and cost per completed task are increasingly different metrics. A completed task could be a customer case resolved without escalation, a KYC document correctly classified, or a claims summary accepted by a reviewer. Even a nominally simple assistant may involve retrieval, safety checks and a generation model; an agent adds planning, repeated model calls, tool execution and retries. The unit price may be falling while the amount of inference required to complete a task is increasing. That is why production AI economics cannot stop at the API price sheet. This is particularly true when output tokens, context windows, retries and tool-call loops increase faster than the decline in unit price. It is useful for any inference system to measure how many requests it can complete, or how many tokens it can generate, while meeting the application’s quality and latency targets. Throughput complements latency: it shows how much work the system can complete while still meeting the latency target. Latency refers to how quickly an AI system can respond to an individual request, while throughput measures how much work it can handle within a given period, often expressed as requests or tokens per second across multiple users. For LLMs, time to first
title: The Economics of Continuous Inference

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) on November 5, 2026, released recommendations on a framework for Satellite Communication Network (SCN) provider authorisation and spectrum assignment. The recommendations propose a new authorisation category for satellite network providers, who would supply network capacity to eligible telecom service providers rather than directly serve users. Alongside the proposed framework, TRAI has set out security conditions governing network control, monitoring, gateway infrastructure and the use of satellite networks for cross-border services. Network Control Facilities Must Be Located in India: TRAI has recommended that the operation, maintenance and control facilities for an SCN provider’s satellite communication network be located in India. The requirement would also cover user terminals belonging to partnering authorised entities that connect to the provider’s network. SCN providers must ensure that their networks are used only to deliver telecommunications services for which the partnering entity holds authorisation. They must also prevent their networks from being used for unauthorised activities, including surveillance and electronic warfare, or in a manner that could prejudice India’s sovereignty and security. The recommendations further require SCN providers to report to the Central Government any attempt to access or use their satellite networks through a user terminal that is not registered with the partnering entity. The report must include information about the terminal and its location. To meet this requirement, providers must undertake the technical measures necessary to identify and report such attempts. However, TRAI has not prescribed a specific technology, protocol or authentication mechanism for detecting unregistered terminals. Government Can Direct Security Measures For Satellite Gateways: TRAI has proposed that SCN providers submit the location and technical details of each satellite earth station gateway to the Central Government or a designated agency before establishing it. The government or agency may examine the submitted information and direct the provider to take specific actions in relation to the gateway’s establishment. The recommendations also require SCN providers to furnish information and conduct interference-monitoring tests, as well as implement mitigation measures, as directed by the government. These provisions would give the government a role in reviewing gateway infrastructure before it is set up and in requiring operational measures where necessary. Separately, TRAI has recommended that SCN providers offer a real-time traffic monitoring facility to ensure compliance with requirements governing Indian user traffic. This includes restrictions on routing traffic through foreign gateways and on mirroring Indian traffic to foreign satellite or telecom networks. enrich.summary_1line: CERT-In released AI Security Auditing Guidelines on November 4 with a four-tier risk framework, nine audit domains and a six-hour incident reporting timeline.

label.reason: CERT-In AI security audit guidelines: Indian regulation affecting AI systems, relevant to AI security and policy.

text:
The 9 core audit domains outlined 'AI Security Audit Guidelines' not just covers AI systems developed, procured and deployed or operated in India, it also includes those processing Indian data or providing AI-enabled services to Indian users. The post Lowdown: CERT-In’s AI Security Auditing Guidelines set out tiered framework, human oversight & incident reporting appeared first on MEDIANAMA .

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) released its Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines, outlining a risk-based framework for auditing AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated by organisations in India on November 4. The framework also covers AI systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users. The guidelines set out requirements for governance, cybersecurity, data privacy, fairness, transparency, resilience and auditability, with audit obligations varying according to an AI system’s risk tier. They cover nine core audit domains and prescribe additional security requirements for generative AI, large language models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), agentic AI, multimodal AI and autonomous systems. Core audit domains: The nine domains cover an AI system’s lifecycle, from design and procurement to deployment, monitoring and decommissioning. Risk tiers determine audit intensity: AI systems are classified into four risk tiers: Low, Moderate, High and Critical. The classification considers factors such as impact severity, decision-making autonomy, data sensitivity, scale and exposure, transparency, incident response readiness, reversibility, sector criticality, adversarial exposure and auditability. The assigned tier determines the depth, frequency and independence of audits, documentation requirements, human oversight and monitoring obligations. Risk-tier escalation may apply where the system’s use, impact or exposure changes, or where the assessment identifies factors warranting a higher classification. Human oversight and the right to review AI decisions: The required level of human involvement varies according to the AI system’s risk and autonomy. Three oversight models are identified: Auditors must assess whether the oversight model is appropriate to the system’s risk. This includes checking whether human reviewers have sufficient authority, competence, information and access to intervene effectively. Contestability and decision review: Individuals affected by AI-assisted decisions must be able to seek review through contestability mechanisms, where applicable. Organisations must establish processes for human review, escalation and reconsideration. Auditors are expected to examine whether such mechanisms are documented and operational, and whether decisions can be reviewed by an authorised person. Audit reporting, remediation and timelines: Audit findings are classified as Critical, High, Moderate or Low/Observation. Organisations must document findings, assign responsibility for remediation and track their closure. The specified remediation timelines include: A re-audit is required where an audit opinion is unsatisfactory, or where two or more Critical findings arise within three months. A re-audit may also be required sooner when directed by a regulator. Audit requirements across the AI lifecycle: The audit methodology covers AI system design, procurement, data collection, development, training, validation, deployment, operation, retraining, monitoring and decommissioning. The audit process includes engagement initiation, risk assessment, scoping, audit planning, evidence collection, technical testing, finding classification, reporting, remediation and follow-up verification. Organisations must identify the AI systems within their technical and organisational boundaries, classify them using the risk-tiering methodology and determine the applicable audit domains and evidence requirements. Auditors must use the Core Audit Domains as the baseline

It also said that it had filed a complaint with the Delhi Police against the impostor, according to the court proceedings attended by MediaNama. After X clarified to the Delhi High Court that the notices were sent by an impostor and that it had filed a complaint with the Delhi Police, Justice Amit Mahajan disposed of the petitions. What X told the court: Appearing before Justice Amit Mahajan, X’s counsel said the platform had not acted on the notices. “We received the notice. In terms of transparency, we told them that we have received this. We didn’t take action,” the counsel said. “It turns out this was somebody playing an impostor, somebody impersonating Delhi Police who has sent this… We are not actioning this request because it’s an illegal request. It’s not from Delhi Police. We filed a complaint last night with Delhi Police.” — X’s counsel X’s counsel asked the court to also note that X had approached the Delhi Police to investigate the impersonation. An advocate representing the Delhi Police also attended the hearing but did not make any submissions. What IFF and SFLC.in argued: Senior Advocate Akhil Sibal appeared for both organisations and told the court that they had doubted the authenticity of the notices and had written to the authorities seeking confirmation. “But if it is genuine, My Lords, it’s most troubling,” he said. He read out X’s message to the petitioners, dated November 3, which stated: “In the interest of transparency, we are writing to inform you that X has received requests from the Delhi Police regarding your X account.” The attached “Receipt of illegal content report” named the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, as the sender. Sibal said SFLC.in had emailed the address mentioned in the notice to ask whether it was genuine, but the email “bounced back”. Read more about it here. He also said that the legal notice sent in the name of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) did not contain any lawyer’s details or a signature. The notices accused the organisations of defaming the RSS under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which covers criminal defamation. Sibal told the court that defamation is “non-cognizable” and rhetorically asked how the police could send such a notice. Sibal told the court that the Delhi Police had not said anything in the matter. Before the hearing, as noted by MediaNama, IFF and SFLC.in said they had filed the writ petition before the Delhi High Court because the Delhi Police had not responded to their queries. After X stated that the notices were, in fact, fake and had been sent by an impostor, Sibal told the court that X’s statement could be recorded and the petitions disposed of. The court recorded X’s statement and closed the petitions. According to IFF, the court gave both organisations the liberty to approach it afresh if any action was taken. Online impersonation and the free speech problem: While the use of email identities that appear to belong to the Delhi Police is threatening and bizarre, this impersonation issue also raises concerns about the misuse of copyright tools on intermediary social media platforms. Some entities impersonate creators by either claiming that content uploaded by the original creator belongs to them or falsely claiming ownership of someone else’s content. The Delhi High Court is examining the copyright tools of intermediaries. MediaNama has also documented instances of fake copyright notices issued to content creators, particularly concernin
title: Impostor sent fake Delhi Police takedown notices against IFF, SFLC.in, X tells Delhi HC

enrich.summary_1line: arXiv paper proposing SwarmEvolve, which runs hundreds of low-cost LLM agents that share KV caches for evolutionary program search.

text: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.
title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization

text: AI-Scientists arrived, but a world for them to grow in did not. Human scientists take theirs for granted $-$ centuries of open problems and shared ideas, waiting in the scientific literature. To AI-Scientists, that world is readable but not runnable, so we build Scientist World for them: every research paper becomes an executable environment. Our autonomous pipeline extracts each paper's open-ended research question and reproduces its proposed method as the baseline; an AI-Scientist entering the environment is evaluated against what the human authors achieved. We release the first 1,000 verified environments. With the world as an evaluation, we found that frontier AI-Scientists can already surpass the human researchers 74% of the time. As a record of how AI does science, it contains 6,400 hours of research traces, with every idea, experiment, failure, and success. As a training ground, we are able to raise (+158%) a small model to match frontier models in research ideation. At last, AI-Scientists' own world has arrived, grown from and growing with science itself.
title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists

text: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.
title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration

enrich.summary_1line: arXiv paper on when integrated information φ can be identified and certified from finite experiments in small stochastic networks.

text: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $α$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.
title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information

enrich.summary_1line: arXiv paper proposing Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels that map residual stream directions in a language model to text exemplars.

text: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.
title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion

enrich.summary_1line: arXiv paper presenting Cognitive Tours, a web-based prototype for curating paths linking user needs, decisions, code, tests and open questions.

text: Generative AI and agentic coding are accelerating software development, leading to concerns about technical debt. But two less visible forms of debt, cognitive debt and intent debt, are emerging as key risks to software health. Cognitive debt is the absence or erosion of a team's shared understanding where no one can confidently explain how a system works or predict the impact of a change. Intent debt is the lack of clearly articulated goals, constraints, and rationale that explain what the system is for and guide how it should evolve. This paper presents Cognitive Tours, a tool designed to mitigate and repair cognitive and intent debt. Cognitive Tours is a web-based prototype for creating and following curated paths connecting user needs, design decisions, code, tests, and open questions. AI-assisted skills help audit existing waypoints and tours for possible problems or staleness and suggest candidates for new ones; humans decide what matters, verify relationships, and construct the narrative. This division of work deliberately preserves productive friction: the sensemaking involved in selecting, explaining, and revising a tour, which is intended to foster and share understanding. Our demonstration uses a tour of Cognitive Tours itself to introduce the tool and illustrate its design decisions and interaction mechanisms. A proposed evaluation agenda concludes the paper. A demo is available at https://cognitive-tours-demo.vercel.app/
title: Cognitive Tours: Making Understanding a Deliverable in AI-Assisted Development

enrich.summary_1line: arXiv paper introducing ReproBridge, an agent workflow that builds refined reproducible ML artifacts, with ReproBridge-Bench of 1,029 tasks.

text: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.
title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts

enrich.summary_1line: Proposes a hidden Markov model for predicting an attacker's next action, reporting results on the CAGE 2 cyber defense benchmark.

text: A defender anticipating an attacker needs a probability distribution over the attacker's next action from information available before that action occurs. Two structures complicate this: the attacker's behavioral regime persists and can switch within an episode, and each action combines an operation with state-dependent arguments whose feasible values change over time. We capture both with a hidden Markov model whose latent state is the active regime and whose regime-conditioned action law is defined on a feasibility-masked tree of executable actions. The same likelihood forms the next-action distribution and updates the regime belief once the action is seen, and a partially observed prefix contributes its resolved local factors. Estimation separates into convex logistic fits that Baum-Welch reuses when regimes are unlabeled. We derive a reach-weighted nodewise KL expression for regime information, a sequence-wise log-loss bound for switching regime paths, and a uniform fallback guarantee. On the CAGE 2 cyber defense benchmark the filtered latent state is worth 0.8 nats per step, and after a controller switch the loss begins to fall in three steps against ten for a recurrent baseline.
title: A Hidden Markov Preference Model for Online Prediction of Adversary Actions

enrich.summary_1line: Compares two releases of the Ru-Jev 307M multilingual cross-encoder on label wording, finding gains on unfamiliar words but not abbreviations or codes.

text: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where accuracy rises, the risk-coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.
title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes

text: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.
title: Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety

text: Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958). We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves. More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.
title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks

enrich.summary_1line: Proposes FedReason, where an LLM writes server-side aggregation code for federated learning, evaluated with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR benchmarks.

text: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.
title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning

enrich.summary_1line: Proposes SHORE, an on-policy RL method for online 3D bin packing that combines learned placement stability with return estimates, reporting higher space utilization than GOPT.

text: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor--critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73\% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03\% vs. 0.63\%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.
title: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing

text: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.
title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference

enrich.summary_1line: Introduces SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler for masked diffusion language models that reports fewer sequential evaluations on LLaDA-8B and Dream models.

text: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: https://github.com/kasakh/specctmc
title: SpecCTMC: Exact Speculative Simulation of Diffusion Language Model Continuous-Time Markov Chains

enrich.summary_1line: Proposes locality-aware quantization (LAQ) for compressed agent memory embeddings, targeting global as well as local neighbor structure.

text: AI agents store text as embedding vectors and compress them at scale. A compression is accepted when each item's nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete, and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. We evaluate both ends with two label-free fidelities from our prior work: the local fidelity $L$ at 10 neighbors and the global fidelity $G$ at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach an $L$ of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme; PCA with 8-bit codes, at an $L$ of 0.77, moves 1.7 percent. Rescoring leaves the stored codes, and thus $G$, unchanged. We prove that across the $G$ band, $1-ν_k$ is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, and that this rate follows the distance noise of the compression (correlation 0.979). Our locality-aware quantization (LAQ) turns the bound into a hinge objective on the codebooks of an OPQ index, keeping its bytes, rotation, and search. To our knowledge, LAQ is the first quantizer whose objective comes from a proven bound on the far end. Reconstruction alone raises $G$ in 0 of 52 held-out runs; the far hinge raises it in all 52. LAQ raises $G$ in all 52 ($p=8.5\times 10^{-4}$ over 13 memory-encoder groups), including the external FinDER memory, has the highest $G$ of seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scales to a million passages, and keeps evidence recall.
title: Enhancing Local and Global Structure in Compressed AI Agent Memory

text: In general-sum games, self-interested learners can reach outcomes that are poor for everyone, which has motivated methods that shape the opponent's learning. Methods like Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness (LOLA), which differentiates through the opponent's learning process, and Model-Free Opponent Shaping (M-FOS), which uses model-free optimisation methods for long-horizon opponent shaping, have enabled mutual cooperation and exploitation of learners. However, these methods require access to the opponent's parameters, policy, rewards or learning rule during deployment. In single-agent reinforcement learning, update rules discovered by meta-learning have achieved state-of-the-art results (e.g. DiscoRL). These rules are separate from the policy they train and read only the agent's own experience. We hereby extend this framework to general-sum settings by introducing Discovered Update Rule for Opponent Shaping (DUOS). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to discover an update rule for an agent in general-sum games. DUOS meta-trains the rule to maximise the agent's expected return over its lifetime, and updates an inner network using the agent's own experience. We show that our discovered rule exhibits behaviour consistent with opponent shaping without reading opponent policies or parameters, and ranks 1st in normalised mean score and 1st in self-play among tournament entrants.
title: Discovering Learning Rules that Shape Others

enrich.summary_1line: Evaluates open-weight Kev-4B decision models as gates that screen retrieved web passages for injected instructions and fake pages.

text: Retrieved web text can carry instructions aimed at the language model, or synthetic pages written to mislead. We test whether released open-weight decision models, which answer typed questions about a text without generating tokens, can screen retrieved passages against both threats. On a benchmark of 1,000 questions over forum-style web pages with hidden injected instructions, a Kev-4B gate reads each passage's HTML. Attack success, measured automatically, falls from 27.9% with no defence to 13.6% with the published mitigations (sanitisation, normalisation and citation prompting) and to 5.7% with the gate added. The gate takes 76 ms per passage and wrongly flags 4 of 186 benign pages with instructions for human readers. Responsiveness on clean queries stays within a point (85.6% to 86.2%). On a 200-query pollution testbed where two thirds of the candidate pages are fake, filtering the pool before the top ten are chosen keeps fake pages out of the answer (0.5% exposure) and holds accuracy at 83%, against 28% with no filter. Filtering only the top ten leaves the generator too few pages to answer. Large LLMs used as judges rank attacks better (AUROC 0.99 against 0.94) but cost ten times more. Gates catch more attacks when they read the page's HTML than when they read its plain text. Every model is open-weight.
title: Decision Models as Retrieval Gates Against Injection and Pollution

enrich.summary_1line: Proposes two multitask learning strategies that add syntactic supervision to sentiment polarity classification, evaluated on eleven datasets in seven languages.

text: Sentiment Analysis (SA) is a fundamental NLP task concerned with the identification and categorization of subjective information in text. While lexicon-based methods offer transparency, they often struggle with linguistic phenomena such as negation and intensification. Syntactic parsing has been integrated into SA pipelines to address this, but conventional parsers introduce significant computational overhead. Recent work shows that reformulating dependency parsing as a Sequence Labeling (SEL) task can improve efficiency. We propose and compare two strategies for integrating syntactic knowledge into a neural sentiment analysis model under unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL). The first, Standard-MTL, jointly learns dependency parsing (via sequence labeling) and sentiment polarity classification using a shared encoder with two task-specific heads. The second, Contrastive-MTL, provides implicit syntactic guidance through a contrastive auxiliary objective and a syntax-biased attention pooling mechanism, without requiring explicit label prediction. Both rely on syntactic annotations during training and eliminate need for hand-crafted compositional rules or external parsing at inference. We evaluate eleven datasets spanning seven languages---the MARC corpus (English, Spanish, French, German) and seven datasets from SemEval-2022 Task 10 (English, Spanish, Norwegian, Basque, Catalan)---using four established SEL encodings. With the relative encoding, Contrastive-MTL outperforms a syntax-naive baseline on 10 of 11 datasets and surpasses the external rule-based pipeline (SELSP) that parses at inference on all six datasets where the latter applies, while being 1.5--9$\times$ faster at evaluation. Standard-MTL is more dataset- and encoding-dependent. These results show implicit syntactic supervision during training can match or exceed explicit parsing at inference without computational overhead.
title: Polarity Classification with Multitask Learning Syntax Augmentation

enrich.summary_1line: Reports that a self-improving embodied coding agent exposed to benchmark criteria gains an advantage that disappears when the criteria are slightly changed.

text: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.
title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement

enrich.summary_1line: Benchmarks GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro and three other LLMs on multi-hop reasoning over five biomedical and cognitive knowledge graphs, with and without graph grounding.

text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) remains unclear. We benchmark five LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) across five KGs: DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG. We introduce a multitier query dataset to evaluate reasoning depth and factual accuracy under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions. Inter-annotator agreement was substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.781 (range: 0.753-0.807) and Fleiss' kappa of 0.77. Results show that general-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning tasks, although performance declines as query complexity increases. KG grounding reduces hallucination rates across all evaluated models. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general-purpose models on specialized tasks without graph grounding. These findings highlight the value of combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. We provide practical guidance for selecting LLM-KG integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints, and discuss hybrid neurosymbolic architectures for personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI.
title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation

text: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.
title: RM-VLM: From Natural-Language Task Descriptions to Vision-Grounded Reward Machines

enrich.summary_1line: Proposes a measured-coupling rule for parallel token decoding in diffusion language models, reporting fewer steps than mean-field decoding at 1.1 points accuracy cost.

text: Diffusion language models can write many tokens per step, but must choose which tokens are safe to commit together. Mean-field decoding penalizes pairs of positions whose predictions look alike. We replace this proxy with the coupling itself: how much committing one token changes the model's confidence at another. Cheap probes inside the main forward pass measure it, with no training or extra model, and it plugs into the same mean-field rule. On three models and four benchmarks, our method needs far fewer steps than mean-field decoding and is faster in most settings, also with a key-value cache, at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points. Shuffling the couplings or replacing them with a uniform bonus loses this gain.
title: Measured Coupling for Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models

enrich.summary_1line: Presents Ginger, an open-source C++ library for graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search, reporting 1.8x average query throughput over each dataset's fastest competitor.

text: We present \textsc{Ginger}, a state-of-the-art open-source C++ library for graph-based approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS). We developed \textsc{Ginger} at Google to push the speed and memory efficiency of graph search on large and high-dimensional embedding datasets. \textsc{Ginger} surpasses existing ANNS libraries with regards to query throughput and indexing time while matching the memory footprint of the most space-efficient competitors. \textsc{Ginger} builds upon recent advances in proximity graph construction (PiPNN) and vector quantization (TurboQuant). We introduce Nested TurboQuant (NTQ), a two-level quantizer which supports low precision graph navigation and high precision reranking in a single code. This representation achieves near floating point precision with $2.6\times$ less memory. We also compress the size of our proximity graphs by up to $2.5\times$ without impacting query throughput. We combine graph reordering with a new lossless compression codec called AdaptiveGap, which builds upon StreamVByte. At $95\%$ recall, \textsc{Ginger} speeds up query throughput by an average of $1.8\times$ over each dataset's fastest competitor and by at least $2.3\times$ over any single library. This lead grows to $2.9\times$ over compact libraries on high-dimensional embeddings.
title: GINGER: Spicing Up Graph-Based Vector Search

enrich.summary_1line: Presents an optimistic algorithm for online convex optimization with memory and time-varying constraints, with bounds adapting to path length and prediction accuracy.

text: Online Convex Optimization with memory and time-varying constraints (COCO-M) is a recently-introduced framework that captures the dynamics of stateful online learning and non-stochastic control with budget constraints. Despite its expressive power, COCO-M remains largely understudied. In this work, we tackle this problem in its full scale, providing an optimistic algorithm that incorporates untrusted predictions to tame universal dynamic regret and cumulative constraint violation. Our analysis leverages a potent reduction from memory to delay and treats state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback. We establish the first bounds that adapt to both environment non-stationarity (path length $P_T$) and prediction accuracy, while lifting previous restrictive assumptions such as functional separability. En route to these results, we derive findings of independent interest for the memory-to-delay reduction, and for delayed OCO with time-varying constraints. The proposed framework ensures sublinear worst-case guarantees that improve with prediction accuracy, reaching $\mathcal O(1)$ regret under perfect predictions, with cumulative constraint violation (CCV) $\mathcal O(\sqrt{T})$ for unknown $P_T$ and $\mathcal O(\log T)$ for known or online observable $P_T$ , while recovering the optimal COCO rates when memory disappears.
title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence

text: Trajectory-based failure predictors for software engineering (SE) agents read the partial trajectory of a run to flag whether it is going right or wrong. If it is going wrong, the run can be stopped, retried, or switched to another model. We ask whether these predictors learn anything about the run itself. On public SWE-bench Verified trajectories, where each model attempts each issue once, two run-independent factors dominate predictor performance. The first is issue difficulty: a reference score that never looks at the run, only at how hard the issue is for other models, reaches 0.92 AUROC, whereas trajectory predictors reach about 0.62. The second is model ability: within an issue, knowing which model ran predicts failure better than our predictors do, and the predictors largely reproduce the overall ability ranking of the models. Beyond difficulty and ability, what predictors gain from the trajectory is statistically equivalent to zero. This confusion carries over to the actions taken after a prediction. Model switching is often motivated by the gap between the best single model's resolution rate and an any-model oracle. This gap is no larger than random variation alone produces. Per-issue switching gains nothing on held-out runs. In a repeated-run pilot, the same model often solves an issue in some runs and fails it in others. Retrying thus has real room to repair failures, but it rescues only failures caused by a bad run, not those on an issue beyond the model's ability. Current predictors cannot tell the causes apart, as they mostly predict the issue and the model, not the run. We call for failure prediction that explains why a run fails, evaluated on repeated-run benchmarks and in closed-loop, equal-budget settings.
title: Hard Issue, Weak Model, or Bad Run? Rethinking Failure Prediction for Coding Agents

text: Neural theorem proving increasingly uses retrieved premises and project context to support proof generation. Evaluating these resources requires measuring the advantage of target-selected declarations over comparable alternatives and how this advantage depends on training. We introduce LeanContext, a benchmark of 129,826 Lean whole-proof generation problems, to investigate these questions. We group selected complete preceding mathematical declarations as Mathematical Context (MC) and the remaining selected local source commands as Environment Context (EC). Four aligned input views support crossed training and inference evaluations with shared targets and original Lean verification environments. For both diffusion- and autoregressive-based models, selected declarations outperform comparable alternatives by a larger margin when training includes MC. Final-input audits identify omitted declarations referenced by the target. Prioritizing these dependencies improves Pass@32 by 1.40% and 1.70% for LLaDA and Llama, respectively, on 2,000 targets. The selection experiment operates without access to target reference proofs and holds checkpoints, EC, and inference budgets constant. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/haaaardcvZ/LeanContext.
title: LeanContext: Disentangling Mathematical Resources from Local Formal Context in Lean Whole-Proof Generation

text: After a runtime or API migration, an LLM-repaired procedure can run cleanly yet return wrong results, and a release check on typical test inputs ships it. We report a preregistered study of 73 tasks covering 60 documented changes in CPython, Node.js and SQLite. Every candidate is executed on the real runtimes against withheld contracts. Over the complete repair space, the all-assertions gate on typical inputs released 0.410 of wrong repairs. One edge input written from the release note cut this to 0.065, and to 0.061 on 15 unseen clusters. Three inputs from a blind GPT-5.6-luna writer that never saw the program reached 0.070. Two further frozen stages enlarged the menu to 1491 fragments and then added 233 hard distractors that match the legacy output on typical inputs. The edge input (0.058) and the frontier-model writer (0.058) passed their preregistered tests. Yet 0.168 and 0.153 of the hard wrong programs still passed. Two local-model writers failed their preregistered tests. Across four model families, the edge input cut wrong releases per attempt in all three open-weight families on all three menus, for example from 0.233 to 0.057, without lowering correct completion. Self-tests helped less. A blind AI audit flagged 34 contracts as stricter than their requirements. Dropping the disputed checks changed 0 verdicts, but class-label disputes remain open. No model-written code was executed. Artifacts are available from the authors on request.
title: Accepted but Wrong: Silent Failures of LLM Code Repairs after API Migrations

enrich.summary_1line: Formalizes series-wise cross-validation for global deep-learning forecasting models and benchmarks it on 11 datasets with 10 neural architectures.

text: We consider the problem of cross-validation (CV) in time series forecasting, with a focus on global forecasting models based on deep learning. The prevailing CV strategy in forecasting is to partition data across time with the last part of each series used for testing. With global models trained on collections of time series, however, a fundamentally different approach becomes possible: partitioning across series and time. We formalize series-wise CV for global forecasting models and benchmark several instantiations, including K-fold CV, bootstrapping, and Monte Carlo CV, on 11 datasets with 10 neural network architectures. We evaluate CV procedures along five dimensions: performance estimation, overoptimism rate, model selection accuracy, regret, and downstream forecasting performance. We withhold a random fraction of series from training so that they appear only in the test set. This protocol simulates the emergence of new series not seen during training, a common scenario in global forecasting. Under this protocol, our results reveal a nuanced trade-off: series-wise CV yields better downstream forecasting accuracy by guiding model selection toward configurations that generalize across both time and series, while time-wise CV retains a slight advantage for estimating out-of-sample error.
title: Series-wise Cross-validation for Global Time Series Forecasting

text: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models, but most RL objectives roll out the current policy at every iteration, and with a many-step sampler these rollouts typically dominate the cost of training. Few-step models cut this cost, yet they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives are built for an instantaneous velocity with a many-step sampler. We adapt RL objectives to few-step models systematically in three phases, namely a transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation. The transformation to $x$-space expresses each objective we consider through a common policy prediction, at the clean end by default and at an explicitly marked level for transition or flow-map objectives, so that objectives stated over densities, velocities or rewards become comparable. The decomposition writes the gradient of each of these objectives as the sum of a self-regression toward a reference and a reward augmentation, so that a method reduces, at the gradient level, to a choice of anchors and weights. The adaptation computes each anchor from a few-step model at the end of its transport or along its tangent, with the instantaneous velocity recovered from the network itself or from an auxiliary network. This yields few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL in one modular codebase. In our experiments, reward-gradient-based methods are the most effective when the reward is differentiable and its gradient is affordable; otherwise DiffusionNFT-style methods generally reach high rewards in relatively few iterations despite a sometimes higher per-iteration cost. Extra inference steps show no systematic aggregate benefit in our experiments, although selected outputs visibly improve with two to four times as many sampling steps as in training.
title: FewStepRL: Fine-tuning Few-step Diffusion Models with Reinforcement Learning

enrich.summary_1line: Analyzes 489,283 assistant-user response pairs from ShareChat and WildChat to study how answer features relate to users accepting, checking, or challenging responses.

text: Large language models (LLMs) often present synthesized answers without making their supporting evidence easy to inspect. We study how features of these answers relate to users' subsequent accepting, checking, and challenging in 489,283 assistant-user response pairs from ShareChat and WildChat. Broad attribution language appears in 31.9% of qualifying responses, compared with explicit URLs in 1.33%, revealing a gap between claims of grounding and preserved inspectable support. Attribution, uncertainty, and other response cues generally accompany both checking and challenging; only uncertainty shows a small statistically distinguishable pooled association favoring checking. Within Technical Help, uncertainty favors checking relative to challenging; refusals and reasoning traces favor challenging in Seeking Information. Scrutiny is concentrated in some conversations, while its apparent turn-to-turn persistence becomes much smaller when conversation-level differences and response ordering are examined separately.
